opt4: "Both small and great have forsaken the fountain of living waters: their fountain is broken, and there is none righteous;"
correct: "Every one of them is gone back: they are altogether become filthy; there is none that doeth good, no, not one."
explanation: God's diagnostic evaluation leaves zero exceptions: total depravity has contaminated the entire human race ('no, not one'). Psalm 53:3 (KJV) - "Every one of them is gone back: they are altogether become filthy; there is none that doeth good, no, not one."

question: What callous dietary metaphor describes the casual persecution of God's people in Psalm 53:4?
opt1: "who swallow up the poor like ravening wolves: they consider not the judgment of heaven"
opt2: "who eat up my people as they eat bread: they have not called upon God."
opt3: "who devour the heritage of Jacob like locusts: they offer no sacrifice unto the Almighty"
opt4: "who trample down the afflicted like grapes in the winepress: they despise the holy ark"
correct: "who eat up my people as they eat bread: they have not called upon God."
explanation: Persecuting God's saints has become as natural and routine to the wicked as eating daily bread, entirely devoid of prayer. Psalm 53:4 (KJV) - "Have the workers of iniquity no knowledge? who eat up my people as they eat bread: they have not called upon God."

question: What sudden panic and gruesome military defeat overtakes the persecutors in Psalm 53:5?
opt1: "They fled when no man pursued: for the angel of the Lord smote their host with sudden pestilence;"
opt2: "Panic seized their princes in the night: for an earthquake swallowed their war chariots, and their pride perished;"
opt3: "There were they in great fear, where no fear was: for God hath scattered the bones of him that encampeth against thee: thou hast put them to shame, because God hath despised them."
opt4: "Terror overtook their captains at the gates: for fire fell from heaven upon their tents, and none escaped;"
correct: "There were they in great fear, where no fear was: for God hath scattered the bones of him that encampeth against thee: thou hast put them to shame, because God hath despised them."
explanation: An irrational supernatural dread grips the arrogant army; their besieging corpses are left unburied, bones bleached and scattered across the field because God despises them. Psalm 53:5 (KJV) - "There were they in great fear, where no fear was: for God hath scattered the bones of him that encampeth against thee: thou hast put them to shame, because God hath despised them."

question: What national yearning for redemption from Zion concludes Psalm 53:6?
opt1: "Let the horn of David be exalted in Jerusalem: when the Lord scattereth the heathen, his priests shall sing;"
opt2: "Arise, O Lord, and plead the cause of thy chosen seed: when the tribes enter into rest, Judah shall be crowned;"
opt3: "Send forth thy light from the sanctuary, O God: when thy kingdom is established, the earth shall be at peace;"
opt4: "Oh that the salvation of Israel were come out of Zion! When God bringeth back the captivity of his people, Jacob shall rejoice, and Israel shall be glad."
correct: "Oh that the salvation of Israel were come out of Zion! When God bringeth back the captivity of his people, Jacob shall rejoice, and Israel shall be glad."
explanation: David looks beyond present humiliation to the ultimate Messianic restoration out of Zion, sparking universal joy across all Jacob. Psalm 53:6 (KJV) - "Oh that the salvation of Israel were come out of Zion! When God bringeth back the captivity of his people, Jacob shall rejoice, and Israel shall be glad."

question: What primary theological difference distinguishes Psalm 53 from its twin, Psalm 14?
opt1: Psalm 14 uses the covenant name 'Yahweh' (LORD) four times, whereas Psalm 53 exclusively uses the transcendent name 'Elohim' (God) throughout
opt2: Psalm 14 was written by Solomon, while Psalm 53 was written by Moses during the wilderness wanderings
opt3: Psalm 53 contains fifteen additional verses detailing the genealogies of the patriarchs
opt4: Psalm 14 is a royal wedding song, while Psalm 53 is a national harvest hymn of thanksgiving
correct: Psalm 14 uses the covenant name 'Yahweh' (LORD) four times, whereas Psalm 53 exclusively uses the transcendent name 'Elohim' (God) throughout
explanation: Psalm 53 is the Elohistic redaction of Psalm 14, fitting Book II of the Psalter (Psalms 42-72) where Elohim is overwhelmingly preferred over Yahweh. Psalm 53:2 (KJV) - "God looked down from heaven upon the children of men, to see if there were any that did understand, that did seek God."

question: What is the musical term 'upon Mahalath' in the title of Psalm 53 generally understood to signify?
opt1: A joyful dance accompaniment performed on tambourines at the Feast of Tabernacles
opt2: A mournful, melancholy tune or sickness/sadness (from the Hebrew root chalah, to be weak or sick), reflecting the spiritual disease of human depravity
opt3: A triumphant battle march sounded on silver trumpets by the sons of Aaron
opt4: An Egyptian harp mode reserved exclusively for coronation banquets
correct: A mournful, melancholy tune or sickness/sadness (from the Hebrew root chalah, to be weak or sick), reflecting the spiritual disease of human depravity
explanation: 'Mahalath' points to a sorrowful, plaintive melody appropriate for lamenting the spiritual sickness and moral contagion of universal depravity. Psalm 53:Title (KJV) - "To the chief Musician upon Mahalath, Maschil, A Psalm of David."

question: What significant textual difference occurs in verse 5 of Psalm 53 compared to Psalm 14:5-6?
opt1: Psalm 53 mentions David's victory over Goliath in the valley of Elah
opt2: Psalm 53 deletes all references to the poor and replaces them with kings
opt3: Psalm 53 adds 'where no fear was' and describes God scattering the bones of the besieging encampment, reflecting a dramatic military deliverance
opt4: Psalm 53 adds an imprecatory curse against the cities of the Philistines
correct: Psalm 53 adds 'where no fear was' and describes God scattering the bones of the besieging encampment, reflecting a dramatic military deliverance
explanation: Psalm 53:5 specifically introduces the unburied bones of the besieger scattered by God, likely adapted to commemorate a historic siege deliverance such as Sennacherib's overthrow. Psalm 53:5 (KJV) - "There were they in great fear, where no fear was: for God hath scattered the bones of him that encampeth against thee: thou hast put them to shame, because God hath despised them."

question: What does the Hebrew term 'Nabal' translated 'fool' in Psalm 53:1 fundamentally denote?
opt1: An uneducated laborer who cannot read the Hebrew Torah scrolls
opt2: A foreign pagan who does not understand the language of Canaan
opt3: A simple child who has not yet reached the age of religious accountability
opt4: A person of moral perversity, spiritual rebellion, and closed-hearted senselessness toward God, rather than mental deficiency
correct: A person of moral perversity, spiritual rebellion, and closed-hearted senselessness toward God, rather than mental deficiency
explanation: In Hebrew wisdom literature, a 'Nabal' is not intellectually incapable, but morally degenerate - deliberately choosing godlessness and practical atheism. Psalm 53:1 (KJV) - "The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God. Corrupt are they, and have done abominable iniquity: there is none that doeth good."

question: What double plea for deliverance and vindication opens Psalm 54:1?
opt1: "Deliver me, O Lord, from the sword, and protect me by thine outstretched arm;"
opt2: "Hearken, O Almighty, unto my cry, and avenge my cause with thy lightning;"
opt3: "Preserve my soul, O King of Zion, and break the power of mine enemies;"
opt4: "Save me, O God, by thy name, and judge me by thy strength."
correct: "Save me, O God, by thy name, and judge me by thy strength."
explanation: David stakes his life upon the divine Name (God's revealed covenant attributes) and calls upon God's omnipotent strength to vindicate his cause. Psalm 54:1 (KJV) - "Save me, O God, by thy name, and judge me by thy strength."

question: How does David plead for God's attentive audience in Psalm 54:2?
opt1: "Hear my prayer, O God; give ear to the words of my mouth."
opt2: "Bow down thine ear from heaven, O Lord; consider the groaning of my heart;"
opt3: "Look upon my affliction, O Most High; and receive the petitions of my lips;"
opt4: "Be not silent unto my tears, O God; and answer me in the day of trouble;"
correct: "Hear my prayer, O God; give ear to the words of my mouth."
explanation: Direct, personal urgency: David implores God to hear his vocalized prayers and incline His ear to every spoken word. Psalm 54:2 (KJV) - "Hear my prayer, O God; give ear to the words of my mouth."

question: How does David describe his adversaries and their utter disregard for God in Psalm 54:3?
opt1: "For the Philistines compass me about, and violent men set snares for my feet: they fear not the Lord. Selah."
opt2: "For strangers are risen up against me, and oppressors seek after my soul: they have not set God before them. Selah."
opt3: "For false brethren have betrayed my hiding place, and bloodthirsty men pursue me: they worship idols. Selah."
opt4: "For the hosts of Saul hunt me as a partridge, and cruel princes thirst for blood: they mock the covenant. Selah."
correct: "For strangers are risen up against me, and oppressors seek after my soul: they have not set God before them. Selah."
explanation: Though the Ziphites were fellow Judeans, their treacherous betrayal made them act like alienated 'strangers' who completely banished God from their conscience. Psalm 54:3 (KJV) - "For strangers are risen up against me, and oppressors seek after my soul: they have not set God before them. Selah."

question: What dramatic triumphant confession of divine alliance marks the turning point in Psalm 54:4?
opt1: "Lo, the Lord hath heard my weeping: the Almighty campeth around my tent;"
opt2: "Verily God hath sent his angels: the Holy One will preserve my footsteps;"
opt3: "Behold, God is mine helper: the Lord is with them that uphold my soul."
opt4: "The Lord of hosts is on my right hand: I shall not be moved by the multitude;"
correct: "Behold, God is mine helper: the Lord is with them that uphold my soul."
explanation: Faith shifts David's focus from treacherous pursuers to the invisible sovereign Protector: God Himself is his supreme Helper and upholder. Psalm 54:4 (KJV) - "Behold, God is mine helper: the Lord is with them that uphold my soul."

question: What divine retribution according to covenant fidelity does David anticipate in Psalm 54:5?
opt1: "He will consume their chariots with fire: and shatter their bows in his wrath;"
opt2: "He shall bring down their pride into the dust: and scatter their armies like chaff;"
opt3: "The Almighty will plead my cause with plague: and blot out their memory from the earth;"
opt4: "He shall reward evil unto mine enemies: cut them off in thy truth."
correct: "He shall reward evil unto mine enemies: cut them off in thy truth."
explanation: God's covenant 'truth' guarantees that unrepentant treachery will boomerang back upon the heads of those who practice evil. Psalm 54:5 (KJV) - "He shall reward evil unto mine enemies: cut them off in thy truth."

question: What voluntary worship and praise of the divine Name does David vow in Psalm 54:6?
opt1: "I will freely sacrifice unto thee: I will praise thy name, O LORD; for it is good."
opt2: "I will pay my solemn vows in Zion: I will magnify thy power among the nations;"
opt3: "I will offer ten thousand bullocks upon thine altar: I will exalt thy mercy for ever;"
opt4: "I will sing a new song upon the ten-stringed lyre: I will bless thy holiness before all people;"
correct: "I will freely sacrifice unto thee: I will praise thy name, O LORD; for it is good."
explanation: David promises a spontaneous freewill offering (nedavah) accompanied by wholehearted adoration of Yahweh's Name because of its inherent goodness. Psalm 54:6 (KJV) - "I will freely sacrifice unto thee: I will praise thy name, O LORD; for it is good."

question: What confident completed deliverance and victory does David celebrate in Psalm 54:7?
opt1: "For the snare is broken and we are escaped: the Lord hath preserved my soul alive;"
opt2: "For he hath delivered me out of all trouble: and mine eye hath seen his desire upon mine enemies."
opt3: "For the mountain of safety is established: and my feet stand in a large place;"
opt4: "For the horn of my salvation is exalted: and the ungodly are fallen into their own pit;"
correct: "For he hath delivered me out of all trouble: and mine eye hath seen his desire upon mine enemies."
explanation: Prophetic perfect tense: so certain is God's deliverance that David speaks of escaping all trouble and seeing the collapse of his foes as already accomplished. Psalm 54:7 (KJV) - "For he hath delivered me out of all trouble: and mine eye hath seen his desire upon mine enemies."

question: What historical betrayal by David's fellow Judeans is recorded in the title of Psalm 54?
opt1: When the Philistines took David in Gath after he feigned madness before Achish
opt2: When the men of Keilah shut their gates against David after the harvest
opt3: When the Ziphites came and said to Saul, Doth not David hide himself with us? (1 Samuel 23:19)
opt4: When Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel and revolted in Hebron
correct: When the Ziphites came and said to Saul, Doth not David hide himself with us? (1 Samuel 23:19)
explanation: The clan of Ziph repeatedly betrayed David's secret hiding places in the wilderness of Ziph to King Saul (1 Sam 23:19; 26:1). Psalm 54:Title (KJV) - "To the chief Musician on Neginoth, Maschil, A Psalm of David, when the Ziphims came and said to Saul, Doth not David hide himself with us?"

question: What musical instrument instruction is indicated by the term 'on Neginoth' in the superscription of Psalm 54?
opt1: Blown on wind flutes and reed pipes
opt2: Sung exclusively without musical instruments (a cappella)
opt3: Chanted to the rhythm of brass finger cymbals
opt4: Accompanied by stringed instruments (such as the lyre and harp)
correct: Accompanied by stringed instruments (such as the lyre and harp)
explanation: 'Neginoth' (plural of neginah) directs that the psalm be played to the accompaniment of plucked stringed instruments. Psalm 54:Title (KJV) - "To the chief Musician on Neginoth, Maschil, A Psalm of David ..."

question: How does the theological concept of God's 'Name' frame both the beginning and conclusion of Psalm 54?
opt1: The psalm opens by seeking salvation through God's Name (v. 1) and concludes by promising freewill praise to God's Name because 'it is good' (v. 6)
opt2: The psalm forbids pronouncing the sacred Tetragrammaton under penalty of death
opt3: The psalm declares that God's Name will be revealed only after the exile
opt4: The psalm claims that David's own name will be praised alongside God's Name
correct: The psalm opens by seeking salvation through God's Name (v. 1) and concludes by promising freewill praise to God's Name because 'it is good' (v. 6)
explanation: The divine 'Name' encompasses God's revealed nature, holiness, and covenant faithfulness - the sole engine of salvation and the ultimate object of worship. Psalm 54:1, 6 (KJV) - "Save me, O God, by thy name ... I will praise thy name, O LORD; for it is good."

question: What desperate longing for escape from metropolitan turmoil and persecution is cried in Psalm 55:6-7?
opt1: "And I said, Oh that I had wings like a dove! for then would I fly away, and be at rest. Lo, then would I wander far off, and remain in the wilderness. Selah."
opt2: "And I cried, Oh that I had chariot wheels of fire! for then would I ride over the mountains, and dwell in peace;"
opt3: "And I groaned, Oh that I were hidden in the rocks of Engedi! for then would no enemy pursue my soul;"
opt4: "And I sighed, Oh that I could dwell in the high heavens! for then would I escape the oppression of wicked men;"
correct: "And I said, Oh that I had wings like a dove! for then would I fly away, and be at rest. Lo, then would I wander far off, and remain in the wilderness. Selah."
explanation: Overwhelmed by treason and civic turmoil, David yearns for the swift wings of a dove to flee far into the tranquil solitary wilderness. Psalm 55:6-7 (KJV) - "And I said, Oh that I had wings like a dove! for then would I fly away, and be at rest. Lo, then would I wander far off, and remain in the wilderness. Selah."

question: What judicial confusion does David request upon the conspirators, and what sins filled the city in Psalm 55:9-11?
opt1: "Smite them, O God, with blindness: for Jerusalem is filled with idolaters and profane men;"
opt2: "Destroy, O Lord, and divide their tongues: for I have seen violence and strife in the city ... Wickedness is in the midst thereof: deceit and guile depart not from her streets."
opt3: "Scatter them, O Lord, by the sword: for blood toucheth blood in every market and open square;"
opt4: "Break their counsels, O Almighty: for foreign armies have breached the walls of Zion with fire;"
correct: "Destroy, O Lord, and divide their tongues: for I have seen violence and strife in the city ... Wickedness is in the midst thereof: deceit and guile depart not from her streets."
explanation: David prays for a Babel-like scattering ('divide their tongues') upon the treacherous factions filling Jerusalem with violence, deceit, and strife. Psalm 55:9, 11 (KJV) - "Destroy, O Lord, and divide their tongues: for I have seen violence and strife in the city ... Wickedness is in the midst thereof: deceit and guile depart not from her streets."

question: What intimate relationship made the traitor's reproach uniquely heartbreaking in Psalm 55:12-14?
opt1: "it was my trusted general who led my armies: we fought side by side in the valley of Rephaim;"
opt2: "it was the high priest who anointed my head: we offered sacrifices together before the holy ark;"
opt3: "it was thou, a man mine equal, my guide, and mine acquaintance. We took sweet counsel together, and walked unto the house of God in company."
opt4: "it was my beloved brother from the house of Jesse: we grew up together in the pastures of Bethlehem;"
correct: "it was thou, a man mine equal, my guide, and mine acquaintance. We took sweet counsel together, and walked unto the house of God in company."
explanation: The bitterest sting of Absalom's rebellion was Ahithophel's betrayal - David's peer, counselor, and fellow worshipper in the sanctuary (prefiguring Judas). Psalm 55:13-14 (KJV) - "But it was thou, a man mine equal, my guide, and mine acquaintance. We took sweet counsel together, and walked unto the house of God in company."

question: What Korah-like doom upon the unrepentant conspirators does David invoke in Psalm 55:15?
opt1: "Let fire consume their tents, and let their seed be blotted out from under the heavens;"
opt2: "Let the earth open her mouth and swallow their riches, and let none remember their names;"
opt3: "Let the sword of the Philistines overtake them, and their bodies be cast to the fowls of the air;"
opt4: "Let death seize upon them, and let them go down quick into hell: for wickedness is in their dwellings, and among them."
correct: "Let death seize upon them, and let them go down quick into hell: for wickedness is in their dwellings, and among them."
explanation: 'Go down quick into hell' echoes the fate of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram (Num 16:30-33), descending alive ('quick') into Sheol due to entrenched wickedness. Psalm 55:15 (KJV) - "Let death seize upon them, and let them go down quick into hell: for wickedness is in their dwellings, and among them."

question: What three-part daily rhythm of prayer did David maintain with the assurance of God hearing his voice in Psalm 55:17?
opt1: "Evening, and morning, and at noon, will I pray, and cry aloud: and he shall hear my voice."
opt2: "At sunrise, at the evening sacrifice, and at the midnight watch will I lift up my soul in praise;"
opt3: "Seven times a day do I praise thee, and in the morning watch do I meditate upon thy law;"
opt4: "Day and night without ceasing will I pour out my supplication before the throne of grace;"
correct: "Evening, and morning, and at noon, will I pray, and cry aloud: and he shall hear my voice."
explanation: David established the classic three-hour prayer devotion (evening, morning, and noon) mirrored by Daniel in exile (Dan 6:10). Psalm 55:17 (KJV) - "Evening, and morning, and at noon, will I pray, and cry aloud: and he shall hear my voice."

question: Why do the ungodly fail to fear God according to Psalm 55:19?
opt1: "Because their hearts are hardened by the abundance of their gold and cattle;"
opt2: "Because they have no changes, therefore they fear not God."
opt3: "Because they see not the judgments of heaven, and imagine that the Lord sleepeth;"
opt4: "Because no prophet hath warned them of the coming desolations of the Almighty;"
correct: "Because they have no changes, therefore they fear not God."
explanation: Unbroken earthly prosperity and lack of disruptive trials ('no changes') breed a deadly moral complacency that banishes all fear of God. Psalm 55:19 (KJV) - "God shall hear, and afflict them, even he that abideth of old. Selah. Because they have no changes, therefore they fear not God."

question: What striking gastronomic and surgical metaphors expose the duplicity of the traitor's speech in Psalm 55:21?
opt1: "His lips dripped with sweet honey, yet poison of asps was under his tongue: his breath was like milk, yet his teeth were iron;"
opt2: "He spoke words of peace like running wine, but mischief was in his mind: his greetings were fragrant as myrrh, yet his hands were full of blood;"
opt3: "The words of his mouth were smoother than butter, but war was in his heart: his words were softer than oil, yet were they drawn swords."
opt4: "His counsel seemed pleasant as ripe figs, but treason burned in his bosom: his promises were soft as silk, yet their end was bitter as wormwood;"
correct: "The words of his mouth were smoother than butter, but war was in his heart: his words were softer than oil, yet were they drawn swords."
explanation: The traitor masked lethal hostility beneath silky flattery: smooth as butter and soothing as olive oil outwardly, yet lethal as drawn steel. Psalm 55:21 (KJV) - "The words of his mouth were smoother than butter, but war was in his heart: his words were softer than oil, yet were they drawn swords."

question: What famous promise of divine sustenance and support for the righteous is recorded in Psalm 55:22?
opt1: "Commit thy way unto the God of Jacob, and he will fight for thee: he will break the iron yoke of the oppressor;"
opt2: "Trust in the Almighty with all thine heart, and he shall heal thy sorrow: he will guide thy feet upon a rock;"
opt3: "Wait on the Lord in the day of trouble, and he shall refresh thy soul: he will be a shield on thy right hand;"
opt4: "Cast thy burden upon the LORD, and he shall sustain thee: he shall never suffer the righteous to be moved."
correct: "Cast thy burden upon the LORD, and he shall sustain thee: he shall never suffer the righteous to be moved."
explanation: A cornerstone promise: roll your entire heavy load onto Yahweh, and He will actively uphold you and keep you from being shaken (1 Pet 5:7). Psalm 55:22 (KJV) - "Cast thy burden upon the LORD, and he shall sustain thee: he shall never suffer the righteous to be moved."

question: What lifespan verdict is pronounced upon violent and treacherous men in Psalm 55:23?
opt1: "bloody and deceitful men shall not live out half their days; but I will trust in thee."
opt2: "the workers of iniquity shall wither away before forty years have passed;"
opt3: "violent princes shall be swallowed by Sheol before their youth is ended;"
opt4: "the treacherous rulers shall die in darkness and leave no posterity in the land;"
correct: "bloody and deceitful men shall not live out half their days; but I will trust in thee."
explanation: Divine retributive justice cuts short the days of murderers and traitors (exemplified by Absalom and Ahithophel dying in their prime). Psalm 55:23 (KJV) - "But thou, O God, shalt bring them down into the pit of destruction: bloody and deceitful men shall not live out half their days; but I will trust in thee."

question: What historical rebellion during David's reign matches the internal betrayal and civil distress described in Psalm 55?
opt1: The revolt of Sheba the son of Bichri across the northern tribes of Israel
opt2: The conspiracy of Absalom and the treason of David's premier counselor Ahithophel (2 Samuel 15-17)
opt3: The military insurrection of Adonijah supported by Joab and Abiathar the priest
opt4: The civil war between the house of Saul and the house of David at the pool of Gibeon
correct: The conspiracy of Absalom and the treason of David's premier counselor Ahithophel (2 Samuel 15-17)
explanation: Psalm 55 vividly captures David fleeing Jerusalem barefoot up the Mount of Olives while weeping over Ahithophel's treason (2 Sam 15:30-31). Psalm 55:13-14 (KJV) - "But it was thou, a man mine equal, my guide, and mine acquaintance. We took sweet counsel together, and walked unto the house of God in company."

question: What urgent opening plea depicts enemies seeking to devour David daily in Psalm 56:1-2?
opt1: "Save me, O Lord, from the teeth of the Philistines: for they hunt my life in the streets of Gath;"
opt2: "Be merciful unto me, O God: for man would swallow me up; he fighting daily oppresseth me. Mine enemies would daily swallow me up: for they be many that fight against me, O thou most High."
opt3: "Hearken, O Almighty, unto my cry: for the heathen have compassed me about like wild dogs;"
opt4: "Deliver my soul, O God, from the pit: for violent men have digged a trench for my feet;"
correct: "Be merciful unto me, O God: for man would swallow me up; he fighting daily oppresseth me. Mine enemies would daily swallow me up: for they be many that fight against me, O thou most High."
explanation: David uses the graphic verb sha'aph ('swallow me up / pant after me'), depicting relentless predators snapping at his heels. Psalm 56:1-2 (KJV) - "Be merciful unto me, O God: for man would swallow me up; he fighting daily oppresseth me. Mine enemies would daily swallow me up: for they be many that fight against me, O thou most High."

question: What short, profound spiritual reflex in Psalm 56:3 teaches believers how to conquer terror?
opt1: "When trouble draweth near, I will call upon the rock of my salvation;"
opt2: "In the hour of darkness, I will remember the lovingkindness of the Lord;"
opt3: "What time I am afraid, I will trust in thee."
opt4: "Though enemies surround me, I will hide under the shadow of thy wings;"
correct: "What time I am afraid, I will trust in thee."
explanation: David does not claim immunity to natural fear, but instantly transforms fear into active, deliberate faith in Yahweh. Psalm 56:3 (KJV) - "What time I am afraid, I will trust in thee."

question: What triumphant conclusion regarding mortal man does David reach in Psalm 56:4?
opt1: "In the Almighty I will glory all the day: I will not fear the chariots of the ungodly;"
opt2: "The Lord of hosts is my shield and buckler: mortal kings cannot pluck me out of his hand;"
opt3: "Through his holy covenant I am made strong: the arrows of the heathen shall not pierce my heart;"
opt4: "In God I will praise his word, in God I have put my trust; I will not fear what flesh can do unto me."
correct: "In God I will praise his word, in God I have put my trust; I will not fear what flesh can do unto me."
explanation: Anchored in God's infallible promises ('praise his word'), David views hostile humanity as mere frail, perishable 'flesh' powerless against God. Psalm 56:4 (KJV) - "In God I will praise his word, in God I have put my trust; I will not fear what flesh can do unto me."

question: How do David's adversaries continuously distort his speech and plot against him in Psalm 56:5?
opt1: "Every day they wrest my words: all their thoughts are against me for evil."
opt2: "They mock my prayers with scorn: they devise snares to trap my feet in the dark;"
opt3: "They report false tidings to the king: their tongues are like venomous vipers;"
opt4: "They corrupt my judgments at the gate: their eyes look continually for bloodshed;"
correct: "Every day they wrest my words: all their thoughts are against me for evil."
explanation: The adversaries constantly twist, distort, and weaponize David's words ('wrest my words'), obsessively scheming his ruin. Psalm 56:5 (KJV) - "Every day they wrest my words: all their thoughts are against me for evil."

question: What tender image portrays God meticulously recording David's sorrow and fugitive wanderings in Psalm 56:8?
opt1: "Thou countest my footsteps in the wilderness: thou storest my grief in a golden vial;"
opt2: "Thou tellest my wanderings: put thou my tears into thy bottle: are they not in thy book?"
opt3: "Thou weighest my afflictions in the desert: my sighs are written on the palm of thy hand;"
opt4: "Thou watchest my exile among the heathen: my prayers are preserved before the holy altar;"
correct: "Thou tellest my wanderings: put thou my tears into thy bottle: are they not in thy book?"
explanation: Not a single sorrow is wasted: God numbers David's wanderings, gathers every tear into His skin-bottle (lachrymatory), and enters them in His heavenly book. Psalm 56:8 (KJV) - "Thou tellest my wanderings: put thou my tears into thy bottle: are they not in thy book?"

question: What supreme theological confidence ensures the retreat of David's enemies in Psalm 56:9?
opt1: "When the trumpets sound, the ungodly shall flee: for the host of the Lord campeth around me;"
opt2: "When I lift up the standard, the heathen shall melt: for the oath of David is established;"
opt3: "When I cry unto thee, then shall mine enemies turn back: this I know; for God is for me."
opt4: "When the dawn breaketh, the wicked shall stumble: for the light of his countenance will destroy them;"
correct: "When I cry unto thee, then shall mine enemies turn back: this I know; for God is for me."
explanation: The invincible conviction of faith: 'God is for me' (Ki Elohim li) - guaranteed to route every adversary (the OT root of Romans 8:31). Psalm 56:9 (KJV) - "When I cry unto thee, then shall mine enemies turn back: this I know; for God is for me."

question: For what ultimate purpose has God delivered David's soul from death and his feet from falling in Psalm 56:13?
opt1: "that I may reign upon the throne of Judah in peace?"
opt2: "that I may build a magnificent temple in Jerusalem?"
opt3: "that I may subdue all the borders of the Philistines?"
opt4: "that I may walk before God in the light of the living?"
correct: "that I may walk before God in the light of the living?"
explanation: Deliverance is not for self-glory but for covenant fellowship: walking continually in conscious communion with God in the radiant light of life. Psalm 56:13 (KJV) - "For thou hast delivered my soul from death: wilt not thou deliver my feet from falling, that I may walk before God in the light of the living?"

question: What historical crisis in Philistia is identified in the superscription of Psalm 56?
opt1: When the Philistines took David in Gath (1 Samuel 21:10-15)
opt2: When David struck down the giant Goliath in the Valley of Elah
opt3: When David dwelt at Ziklag and raided the Geshurites and Amalekites
opt4: When the lords of the Philistines refused to let David go to battle at Gilboa
correct: When the Philistines took David in Gath (1 Samuel 21:10-15)
explanation: David was recognized and arrested in Goliath's hometown of Gath, forcing him to feign madness before King Achish. Psalm 56:Title (KJV) - "To the chief Musician upon Jonath-elem-rechokim, Michtam of David, when the Philistines took him in Gath."

question: What is the meaning of the cryptic musical tune 'Jonath-elem-rechokim' in the title of Psalm 56?
opt1: 'The roaring lion of Judah', denoting a triumphant battle anthem of conquest
opt2: 'The silent dove of far-off lands' (or distant terebinths), typifying David as a mute, defenseless, exiled dove among the fierce Philistines
opt3: 'The golden chalice of wine', indicating a joyful thanksgiving tune for the grape harvest
opt4: 'The royal harp of the king', signifying a formal coronation melody
correct: 'The silent dove of far-off lands' (or distant terebinths), typifying David as a mute, defenseless, exiled dove among the fierce Philistines
explanation: 'Jonath-elem-rechokim' means 'the dove of silence of distant places', symbolizing David's helpless, mute exile far from the sanctuary in Gath. Psalm 56:Title (KJV) - "To the chief Musician upon Jonath-elem-rechokim, Michtam of David ..."

question: What is the significance of the repetition in Psalm 56:10: 'In God will I praise his word: in the LORD will I praise his word'?
opt1: It indicates that the psalm was copied twice into the temple liturgy by Ezra the scribe
opt2: It distinguishes between the written law of Moses and oral tradition of the elders
opt3: It magnifies God's word using both the general transcendent title 'Elohim' and the sacred covenant name 'Yahweh', affirming absolute confidence in divine revelation
opt4: It represents a musical antiphonal chant between the high priest and the Levitical choir
correct: It magnifies God's word using both the general transcendent title 'Elohim' and the sacred covenant name 'Yahweh', affirming absolute confidence in divine revelation
explanation: A deliberate parallelism binding together Elohim (the cosmic Creator) and Yahweh (the covenant Redeemer) as the guarantor of His reliable word. Psalm 56:10 (KJV) - "In God will I praise his word: in the LORD will I praise his word."

question: Under what sheltering imagery does David take refuge until destroying perils pass by in Psalm 57:1?
opt1: "Save me, O Lord: for my hope is in thee: yea, in the secret cleft of the rock will I hide, until the wrath be spent;"
opt2: "Preserve me, O Almighty: for I rely upon thy power: yea, behind the shield of faith will I dwell, until the morning break;"
opt3: "Be merciful unto me, O God, be merciful unto me: for my soul trusteth in thee: yea, in the shadow of thy wings will I make my refuge, until these calamities be overpast."
opt4: "Deliver my life, O God of Jacob: for I cry unto thee: yea, within the gates of the sanctuary will I abide, until the wicked perish;"
correct: "Be merciful unto me, O God, be merciful unto me: for my soul trusteth in thee: yea, in the shadow of thy wings will I make my refuge, until these calamities be overpast."
explanation: Like a helpless fledgling nestling safely beneath the mother bird's protective feathers, David shelters under God's wings until storms pass. Psalm 57:1 (KJV) - "Be merciful unto me, O God, be merciful unto me: for my soul trusteth in thee: yea, in the shadow of thy wings will I make my refuge, until these calamities be overpast."

question: What inspiring title does David assign to God in Psalm 57:2 regarding the fulfillment of His divine destiny?
opt1: "unto God that broke the sceptre of the heathen"
opt2: "unto God that led our fathers through the deep"
opt3: "unto God that created the heavens and the earth"
opt4: "unto God that performeth all things for me"
correct: "unto God that performeth all things for me"
explanation: God will not leave His work half-finished; He sovereignly carries through ('performeth' - Hebrew gomer) everything concerning David's life and calling. Psalm 57:2 (KJV) - "I will cry unto God most high; unto God that performeth all things for me."

question: Which twin heavenly emissaries will God send down to accomplish David's rescue in Psalm 57:3?
opt1: "God shall send forth his mercy and his truth."
opt2: "God shall send forth his angels and his thunderbolts"
opt3: "God shall send forth his wrath and his justice"
opt4: "God shall send forth his light and his salvation"
correct: "God shall send forth his mercy and his truth."
explanation: Mercy (hesed) and Truth (emet) are personified as heavenly guards dispatched from the celestial court to guarantee David's safety. Psalm 57:3 (KJV) - "He shall send from heaven, and save me from the reproach of him that would swallow me up. Selah. God shall send forth his mercy and his truth."

question: What ferocious animal and military imagery describes David's predators in the cave in Psalm 57:4?
opt1: "My feet are surrounded by serpents: and I dwell among ravening wolves, whose eyes are burning coals, and their claws iron;"
opt2: "My soul is among lions: and I lie even among them that are set on fire, even the sons of men, whose teeth are spears and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword."
opt3: "My life is encompassed by hunters: and I lodge among archers, whose quivers are full of poison, and their shields brass;"
opt4: "My dwelling is with wild leopards: and I hide among violent men, whose hands are dipped in blood, and their heart stone;"
correct: "My soul is among lions: and I lie even among them that are set on fire, even the sons of men, whose teeth are spears and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword."
explanation: Surrounded by Saul's ferocious men, David likens them to man-eating lions breathing fire, with fangs like spears/arrows and cutting slanderous tongues. Psalm 57:4 (KJV) - "My soul is among lions: and I lie even among them that are set on fire, even the sons of men, whose teeth are spears and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword."

question: What majestic doxological chorus elevates God's glory above the cosmos in Psalm 57:5 and 57:11?
opt1: "Sing praises, ye heavens, unto the King of glory; let the whole earth be filled with his praise;"
opt2: "The Lord reigneth over the nations; let the islands rejoice and give thanks at his remembrance;"
opt3: "Be thou exalted, O God, above the heavens; let thy glory be above all the earth."
opt4: "Great is the Lord and greatly to be praised; his dominion endureth throughout all generations;"
correct: "Be thou exalted, O God, above the heavens; let thy glory be above all the earth."
explanation: David elevates his vision above cave darkness into cosmic adoration: desiring God's renown to transcend the highest heavens and encompass the earth. Psalm 57:5, 11 (KJV) - "Be thou exalted, O God, above the heavens; let thy glory be above all the earth."

question: What poetic justice overtakes David's pursuers in Psalm 57:6?
opt1: "They drew the bow against my life: but their bow broke, and their arrows pierced their own hearts. Selah."
opt2: "They set an ambush around the cave: but a thick darkness fell upon them, and they fled in terror. Selah."
opt3: "They hired false witnesses against me: but their own words convicted them, and they were put to shame. Selah."
opt4: "They have prepared a net for my steps; my soul is bowed down: they have digged a pit before me, into the midst whereof they are fallen themselves. Selah."
correct: "They have prepared a net for my steps; my soul is bowed down: they have digged a pit before me, into the midst whereof they are fallen themselves. Selah."
explanation: Divine irony: the very pit excavated by Saul and his troops to entrap David becomes their own grave. Psalm 57:6 (KJV) - "They have prepared a net for my steps; my soul is bowed down: they have digged a pit before me, into the midst whereof they are fallen themselves. Selah."

question: What resolute spiritual equilibrium does David declare twice in Psalm 57:7?
opt1: "My heart is fixed, O God, my heart is fixed: I will sing and give praise."
opt2: "My soul is at rest, O Lord, my soul is at rest: I will wait on thy salvation;"
opt3: "My faith is established, O Most High, my faith is established: I will walk in thy truth;"
opt4: "My foot standeth firm, O God, my foot standeth firm: I will bless thy name;"
correct: "My heart is fixed, O God, my heart is fixed: I will sing and give praise."
explanation: The Hebrew nakon ('fixed') denotes an unshakable, anchored heart immune to panic, determined to burst into vibrant song and praise. Psalm 57:7 (KJV) - "My heart is fixed, O God, my heart is fixed: I will sing and give praise."

question: What poetic summons to praise awakes the musical instruments and the dawn in Psalm 57:8?
opt1: "Sound the trumpet, O Zion; blow the horn, ye priests: let the morning watch rejoice;"
opt2: "Awake up, my glory; awake, psaltery and harp: I myself will awake early."
opt3: "Arise, O my soul; rejoice, stringed instruments: let the sunrise proclaim his righteousness;"
opt4: "Sing aloud, ye saints; strike the timbrel and lute: let the daybreak bring gladness;"
correct: "Awake up, my glory; awake, psaltery and harp: I myself will awake early."
explanation: David stirs his soul ('my glory'), summons the psaltery (harp/lute), and poetically vows to 'awake the dawn' with enthusiastic morning praises. Psalm 57:8 (KJV) - "Awake up, my glory; awake, psaltery and harp: I myself will awake early."

question: How high do God's mercy and truth reach according to Psalm 57:10?
opt1: "For thy lovingkindness surpasses the highest stars, and thy faithfulness the depths of the sea;"
opt2: "For thy goodness spans from the rising sun, and thy righteousness unto the ends of the world;"
opt3: "For thy mercy is great unto the heavens, and thy truth unto the clouds."
opt4: "For thy grace is deeper than the ocean, and thy mercy higher than the mountains of Lebanon;"
correct: "For thy mercy is great unto the heavens, and thy truth unto the clouds."
explanation: God's covenant mercy (hesed) and truth (emet) are measured by cosmic dimensions, towering to the celestial skies and cloud realms. Psalm 57:10 (KJV) - "For thy mercy is great unto the heavens, and thy truth unto the clouds."

question: What historical circumstance and musical tune instruction are preserved in the superscription of Psalm 57?
opt1: 'Shoshannim' (Lilies), a song of loves, when David was crowned king in Hebron
opt2: 'Mahalath Leannoth', a maskil of David, when he was sick in the palace
opt3: 'Gittith', a psalm of praise, when the ark was brought to Mount Zion
opt4: 'Al-taschith' (Destroy not), Michtam of David, when he fled from Saul in the cave (1 Samuel 22 or 24)
correct: 'Al-taschith' (Destroy not), Michtam of David, when he fled from Saul in the cave (1 Samuel 22 or 24)
explanation: Composed in the dark cavern of Adullam or Engedi, set to 'Al-taschith' ('Do not destroy' - David's memorable command regarding Saul in 1 Sam 26:9). Psalm 57:Title (KJV) - "To the chief Musician, Al-taschith, Michtam of David, when he fled from Saul in the cave."

question: What penetrating indictment of corrupt judges and magistrates opens Psalm 58:1-2?
opt1: "Why sit ye in judgment over the poor, O elders of Israel? do ye consider the law of Moses? Nay, your hands take bribes;"
opt2: "Hear the word of the Lord, ye rulers of Sodom: do ye execute justice in the gates? Behold, ye pervert truth for silver;"
opt3: "Shall the ungodly sit upon the bench of righteousness? do ye vindicate the fatherless? Nay, ye justify the wicked;"
opt4: "Do ye indeed speak righteousness, O congregation? do ye judge uprightly, O ye sons of men? Yea, in heart ye work wickedness; ye weigh the violence of your hands in the earth."
correct: "Do ye indeed speak righteousness, O congregation? do ye judge uprightly, O ye sons of men? Yea, in heart ye work wickedness; ye weigh the violence of your hands in the earth."
explanation: David challenges unjust judicial councils who maintain a facade of equity while deliberately weighing out tyranny and violence with cynical precision. Psalm 58:1-2 (KJV) - "Do ye indeed speak righteousness, O congregation? do ye judge uprightly, O ye sons of men? Yea, in heart ye work wickedness; ye weigh the violence of your hands in the earth."

question: How early in life does the innate moral estrangement and dishonesty of the wicked manifest in Psalm 58:3?
opt1: "The wicked are estranged from the womb: they go astray as soon as they be born, speaking lies."
opt2: "From their youth they practice mischief: they learn deceit from the elders of the gate;"
opt3: "When they reach manhood they turn aside: they forsake the covenant of their fathers;"
opt4: "In the days of their strength they run after idols: they speak vanity against the Most High;"
correct: "The wicked are estranged from the womb: they go astray as soon as they be born, speaking lies."
explanation: Human depravity is innate and congenital: from the very womb, fallen man wanders off the path of truth, spontaneously speaking falsehood. Psalm 58:3 (KJV) - "The wicked are estranged from the womb: they go astray as soon as they be born, speaking lies."

question: What zoological metaphor compares the stubborn malice of corrupt rulers to an uncharmable reptile in Psalm 58:4-5?
opt1: "Their bite is like the bite of a rabid wolf: they are as the wild ass that cannot be tamed by the rider;"
opt2: "Their poison is like the poison of a serpent: they are like the deaf adder that stoppeth her ear; Which will not hearken to the voice of charmers, charming never so wisely."
opt3: "Their deceit is as the venom of a scorpion: they are like the horned viper that striketh the horse in the path;"
opt4: "Their wrath is like a roaring lion: they are as the deaf basilisk that hideth in the clefts of the rocks;"
correct: "Their poison is like the poison of a serpent: they are like the deaf adder that stoppeth her ear; Which will not hearken to the voice of charmers, charming never so wisely."
explanation: Like a willfully deaf cobra (pethen) that stops her ears against the most skilled snake-charmer, corrupt magistrates are stubbornly immune to reason and conscience. Psalm 58:4-5 (KJV) - "Their poison is like the poison of a serpent: they are like the deaf adder that stoppeth her ear; Which will not hearken to the voice of charmers, charming never so wisely."

question: What dental imprecation asks God to neutralize the predatory power of tyrants in Psalm 58:6?
opt1: "Shatter their iron jaws, O Lord: pull out the fangs of the devouring wolves;"
opt2: "Break the weapons of their warfare, O God: strip the claws from the beasts of the field;"
opt3: "Break their teeth, O God, in their mouth: break out the great teeth of the young lions, O LORD."
opt4: "Cut out their blasphemous tongues, O Lord: break the arms of the ungodly princes;"
correct: "Break their teeth, O God, in their mouth: break out the great teeth of the young lions, O LORD."
explanation: Depicting oppressors as voracious young lions, David prays that God will shatter their biting fangs, rendering them completely incapable of tearing innocent prey. Psalm 58:6 (KJV) - "Break their teeth, O God, in their mouth: break out the great teeth of the young lions, O LORD."

question: What two vivid natural similes depict the rapid disappearance of the ungodly in Psalm 58:7-8?
opt1: "Let them vanish like morning mist ... As dry stubble before the flames, let them be consumed: like leaves driven by the autumn wind;"
opt2: "Let them be scattered like sea foam ... As melting wax before the furnace, let them dissolve: like a shadow that declineth;"
opt3: "Let them dry up like summer brooks ... As grass upon the housetops, let them wither: like chaff swept away by the storm;"
opt4: "Let them melt away as waters which run continually ... As a snail which melteth, let every one of them pass away: like the untimely birth of a woman, that they may not see the sun."
correct: "Let them melt away as waters which run continually ... As a snail which melteth, let every one of them pass away: like the untimely birth of a woman, that they may not see the sun."
explanation: David piles up vivid similes of futility: vanishing runoff flash-floods, a snail dissolving away in its own slime trail, and a stillborn miscarriage that never gazes upon sunlight. Psalm 58:7-8 (KJV) - "Let them melt away as waters which run continually: when he bendeth his bow to shoot his arrows, let them be as cut in pieces. As a snail which melteth, let every one of them pass away: like the untimely birth of a woman, that they may not see the sun."

question: What culinary imagery depicts the suddenness of divine judgment sweeping away oppressors in Psalm 58:9?
opt1: "Before your pots can feel the thorns, he shall take them away as with a whirlwind, both living, and in his wrath."
opt2: "Before the wine can ferment in the vats, the tempest shall shatter the earthen vessels;"
opt3: "Before the harvest can be gathered into the barn, the east wind shall burn the sheaves;"
opt4: "Before the bread can bake upon the hearth, the fury of the Lord shall overturn the oven;"
correct: "Before your pots can feel the thorns, he shall take them away as with a whirlwind, both living, and in his wrath."
explanation: In nomadic camping, thorn twigs ignite instantly under cooking pots; but before the pot can even feel the heat, God's whirlwind sweeps everything away in a flash. Psalm 58:9 (KJV) - "Before your pots can feel the thorns, he shall take them away as with a whirlwind, both living, and in his wrath."

question: How is the ultimate triumph and moral vindication of the righteous described in Psalm 58:10?
opt1: "The saints shall shout aloud when the pit swalloweth the ungodly: they shall dance upon the ruins of Babylon;"
opt2: "The righteous shall rejoice when he seeth the vengeance: he shall wash his feet in the blood of the wicked."
opt3: "The people of God shall give thanks when the proud are humbled: they shall blow the silver trumpets in Zion;"
opt4: "The congregation of Israel shall triumph over the heathen: they shall set their crowns upon the heads of their children;"
correct: "The righteous shall rejoice when he seeth the vengeance: he shall wash his feet in the blood of the wicked."
explanation: Ancient battlefield imagery of absolute victory: the righteous rejoice not in personal spite, but in the triumphant overthrow of evil and vindication of divine justice. Psalm 58:10 (KJV) - "The righteous shall rejoice when he seeth the vengeance: he shall wash his feet in the blood of the wicked."

question: What universal conclusion will humanity proclaim when God executes righteous judgment in Psalm 58:11?
opt1: "And all flesh shall confess, The Lord our God is holy: there is no king like unto our King;"
opt2: "So that kings shall tremble, saying, The law of the Most High endureth: his judgments are true and righteous;"
opt3: "So that a man shall say, Verily there is a reward for the righteous: verily he is a God that judgeth in the earth."
opt4: "And the nations shall declare, Salvation belongeth unto Yahweh: his throne is established for ever;"
correct: "So that a man shall say, Verily there is a reward for the righteous: verily he is a God that judgeth in the earth."
explanation: The ultimate vindication of providence: observer humanity is forced to concede that living righteously is rewarded, and God is not an idle spectator but an active terrestrial Judge. Psalm 58:11 (KJV) - "So that a man shall say, Verily there is a reward for the righteous: verily he is a God that judgeth in the earth."

question: To what tune is Psalm 58 set according to its superscription, sharing it with Psalms 57 and 59?
opt1: 'Muth-labben' (Death of the Son), a psalm of David
opt2: 'Aijeleth Shahar' (The Hind of the Dawn), a song of praise
opt3: 'Sheminith' (Upon the Eighth), for the chief musician
opt4: 'Al-taschith' (Destroy not), Michtam of David
correct: 'Al-taschith' (Destroy not), Michtam of David
explanation: Psalm 58 is the second of four consecutive 'Al-taschith' ('Destroy not') psalms (Psalms 57, 58, 59, 75). Psalm 58:Title (KJV) - "To the chief Musician, Al-taschith, Michtam of David."

question: What specific class of people is addressed by the Hebrew word 'elem' / 'congregation' (or silent ones / mighty rulers) in Psalm 58:1?
opt1: Civil judges, rulers, and judicial authorities appointed to administer equity in the land
opt2: The Levitical priests offering sacrifices in the sanctuary
opt3: The false prophets prophesying peace in the streets of Jerusalem
opt4: The merchant traders bartering goods at the seaports of Tyre
correct: Civil judges, rulers, and judicial authorities appointed to administer equity in the land
explanation: Psalm 58 is a judicial prophecy exposing the sham trials and institutional corruption of civil magistrates who fail to govern with uprightness. Psalm 58:1 (KJV) - "Do ye indeed speak righteousness, O congregation? do ye judge uprightly, O ye sons of men?"

question: What twin pleas for rescue from murderous assassins open Psalm 59:1-2?
opt1: "Deliver me from mine enemies, O my God: defend me from them that rise up against me. Deliver me from the workers of iniquity, and save me from bloody men."
opt2: "Preserve my soul, O Lord, from the sword: protect me from the snares of Saul;"
opt3: "Hear my voice, O Most High, in the night watch: hide me from the captains of the host;"
opt4: "Deliver my life from the pit of death, O God of Jacob: break the power of the violent;"
correct: "Deliver me from mine enemies, O my God: defend me from them that rise up against me. Deliver me from the workers of iniquity, and save me from bloody men."
explanation: David cries to Elohim for defense against bloodthirsty henchmen dispatched by Saul to stake out his house and execute him. Psalm 59:1-2 (KJV) - "Deliver me from mine enemies, O my God: defend me from them that rise up against me. Deliver me from the workers of iniquity, and save me from bloody men."

question: What protest of innocence regarding the cause of this deadly siege does David voice in Psalm 59:3-4?
opt1: "they compass my dwelling about with spears: yet have I offered bullocks and walked in the statutes of Moses;"
opt2: "the mighty are gathered against me; not for my transgression, nor for my sin, O LORD. They run and prepare themselves without my fault: awake to help me, and behold."
opt3: "they sharpen their swords against my neck: though I served the king with all my heart and harmed no man;"
opt4: "they lay traps for my footsteps in the darkness: seeing I have not coveted the royal crown of Israel;"
correct: "the mighty are gathered against me; not for my transgression, nor for my sin, O LORD. They run and prepare themselves without my fault: awake to help me, and behold."
explanation: David maintains an unblemished conscience: the murderous plot was completely unprovoked by any crime or rebellion on his part. Psalm 59:3-4 (KJV) - "For, lo, they lie in wait for my soul: the mighty are gathered against me; not for my transgression, nor for my sin, O LORD. They run and prepare themselves without my fault: awake to help me, and behold."

question: What canine metaphor portrays the nocturnal prowling of Saul's assassins around the city in Psalm 59:6 and 59:14?
opt1: "They gather at dusk: they howl like hungry jackals, and compass the gates of Zion;"
opt2: "They lurk in the shadows: they growl like ravenous wolves, and watch every door in Jerusalem;"
opt3: "They return at evening: they make a noise like a dog, and go round about the city."
opt4: "They prowl through the streets: they bark like wild foxes, and wait for the morning light;"
correct: "They return at evening: they make a noise like a dog, and go round about the city."
explanation: David compares his stalkers to filthy, snarling, stray scavenger dogs roaming ancient city alleys searching for scraps to devour. Psalm 59:6, 14 (KJV) - "They return at evening: they make a noise like a dog, and go round about the city."

question: What insolent words and practical atheism characterize the assassins' speech in Psalm 59:7?
opt1: "Lo, they boast of their strength: their mouth is full of cursing: for they say, The king hath decreed it;"
opt2: "Behold, they utter blasphemies against the sanctuary: for they say, God hath forsaken the son of Jesse;"
opt3: "They whisper lies in every corner: their lips drip with poison: for they say, None shall deliver him from our hand;"
opt4: "Behold, they belch out with their mouth: swords are in their lips: for who, say they, doth hear?"
correct: "Behold, they belch out with their mouth: swords are in their lips: for who, say they, doth hear?"
explanation: Their murderous words spout forth ('belch out') like sharp blades, arrogantly assuming that no divine Judge hears their conspiracy. Psalm 59:7 (KJV) - "Behold, they belch out with their mouth: swords are in their lips: for who, say they, doth hear?"

question: How does the sovereign LORD react to the raging plots of these bloodthirsty pursuers in Psalm 59:8?
opt1: "But thou, O LORD, shalt laugh at them; thou shalt have all the heathen in derision."
opt2: "The Lord of hosts shall blow with his breath, and scatter them like dry stubble;"
opt3: "The Almighty shall stretch forth his hand, and smite their leaders with sudden blindness;"
opt4: "God shall send his angels from heaven, and overturn their war chariots in the night;"
correct: "But thou, O LORD, shalt laugh at them; thou shalt have all the heathen in derision."
explanation: Total theological serenity: while David is besieged, Yahweh sits enthroned laughing in derision at the laughable impotence of human malice. Psalm 59:8 (KJV) - "But thou, O LORD, shalt laugh at them; thou shalt have all the heathen in derision."

question: What repeated fortress confession forms the reassuring refrain in Psalm 59:9 and 59:17?
opt1: "for the Lord of hosts is my shield and my exceeding great reward for ever;"
opt2: "for the rock of Jacob is an unassailable tower, and his truth shall preserve my life;"
opt3: "for God is my defence ... Unto thee, O my strength, will I sing: for God is my defence, and the God of my mercy."
opt4: "for the Holy One of Israel is my refuge, and under his wings will I find rest;"
correct: "for God is my defence ... Unto thee, O my strength, will I sing: for God is my defence, and the God of my mercy."
explanation: David finds absolute security in God as his misgav (high unassailable fortress/defense) and the personal source of steadfast covenant mercy. Psalm 59:9, 17 (KJV) - "Because of his strength will I wait upon thee: for God is my defence ... Unto thee, O my strength, will I sing: for God is my defence, and the God of my mercy."

question: What striking pedagogical reason does David give for asking God NOT to slay his enemies instantaneously in Psalm 59:11?
opt1: "Destroy them not at once, lest the land become desolate and wild beasts multiply against us;"
opt2: "Smite them not with the sword, lest their children rise up in vengeance against the house of Judah;"
opt3: "Put them not to death, lest the heathen say that the God of Israel delighteth in blood;"
opt4: "Slay them not, lest my people forget: scatter them by thy power; and bring them down, O Lord our shield."
correct: "Slay them not, lest my people forget: scatter them by thy power; and bring them down, O Lord our shield."
explanation: A sudden massacre is soon forgotten; David prays that God will scatter and reduce them to wandering vagabonds as a lasting visual lesson in divine justice. Psalm 59:11 (KJV) - "Slay them not, lest my people forget: scatter them by thy power; and bring them down, O Lord our shield."

question: What global testimony of divine sovereignty will be demonstrated by the judgment of the wicked in Psalm 59:13?
opt1: "and let them know that God ruleth in Jacob unto the ends of the earth. Selah."
opt2: "that all the families of the nations may confess that the Lord alone is God. Selah."
opt3: "so that the kings of the world may fear the name of Yahweh in Jerusalem. Selah."
opt4: "that every tribe may behold the salvation of our God and give glory in the sanctuary. Selah."
correct: "and let them know that God ruleth in Jacob unto the ends of the earth. Selah."
explanation: The consuming judgment reveals that God is not merely a localized tribal deity, but cosmic King ruling over Jacob and extending to the ends of the globe. Psalm 59:13 (KJV) - "Consume them in wrath, consume them, that they may not be: and let them know that God ruleth in Jacob unto the ends of the earth. Selah."

question: What joyful contrast transforms David's morning after a fearful night of canine prowlers in Psalm 59:16?
opt1: "And when the sun ariseth, I will offer burnt offerings in the temple: for the snare is broken and I am delivered;"
opt2: "But I will sing of thy power; yea, I will sing aloud of thy mercy in the morning: for thou hast been my defence and refuge in the day of my trouble."
opt3: "So shall my lips rejoice at daybreak, and I will sound the silver trumpets: for the Lord hath broken the teeth of the ungodly;"
opt4: "Yet in the morning will I praise thy name before the congregation: for thou hast turned my sorrow into a dance of joy;"
correct: "But I will sing of thy power; yea, I will sing aloud of thy mercy in the morning: for thou hast been my defence and refuge in the day of my trouble."
explanation: While his foes spent the night snarling like scavengers, David greets the morning dawn singing aloud of God's fortress power and covenant mercy. Psalm 59:16 (KJV) - "But I will sing of thy power; yea, I will sing aloud of thy mercy in the morning: for thou hast been my defence and refuge in the day of my trouble."

question: What specific historical incident recorded in 1 Samuel 19 is named in the superscription of Psalm 59?
opt1: When Saul threw a javelin to pin David to the wall while he played the harp
opt2: When Saul pursued David with three thousand men to the rocks of the wild goats
opt3: When Saul sent, and they watched the house to kill him (1 Samuel 19:11)
opt4: When Saul visited the witch of Endor on the eve of the battle of Mount Gilboa
correct: When Saul sent, and they watched the house to kill him (1 Samuel 19:11)
explanation: Michal warned David and helped him escape through a window when Saul's hit squad staked out their house to assassinate him in the morning (1 Sam 19:11-18). Psalm 59:Title (KJV) - "To the chief Musician, Al-taschith, Michtam of David; when Saul sent, and they watched the house to kill him."

question: What national lament over military defeat and divine estrangement opens Psalm 60:1-2?
opt1: "Why hast thou forsaken thy flock, O Lord? our armies have fallen before Edom: arise and build Zion;"
opt2: "O God, thou hast cast us off, thou hast scattered us, thou hast been displeased; O turn thyself to us again. Thou hast made the earth to tremble; thou hast broken it: heal the breaches thereof; for it shaketh."
opt3: "How long, O God, wilt thou smoke against the sheep of thy pasture? our gates are burned with fire: heal our wounds;"
opt4: "Turn us again, O God of hosts, and cause thy face to shine: for our captains have turned back from the battle;"
correct: "O God, thou hast cast us off, thou hast scattered us, thou hast been displeased; O turn thyself to us again. Thou hast made the earth to tremble; thou hast broken it: heal the breaches thereof; for it shaketh."
explanation: Composed after a terrifying setback, Israel confesses that military defeat felt like a seismic earthquake splintering the land because God was displeased. Psalm 60:1-2 (KJV) - "O God, thou hast cast us off, thou hast scattered us, thou hast been displeased; O turn thyself to us again. Thou hast made the earth to tremble; thou hast broken it: heal the breaches thereof; for it shaketh."

question: What striking beverage metaphor depicts the staggering trauma inflicted upon the nation in Psalm 60:3?
opt1: "Thou hast fed us with the bread of tears, and given us plenteous weeping to drink;"
opt2: "Thou hast poured out the bitter cup of gall, and made our priests drink the waters of strife;"
opt3: "Thou hast filled our chalice with the wrath of the heathen, and made our princes stagger in darkness;"
opt4: "Thou hast shewed thy people hard things: thou hast made us to drink the wine of astonishment."
correct: "Thou hast shewed thy people hard things: thou hast made us to drink the wine of astonishment."
explanation: 'The wine of astonishment' (yayin tarelah - reeling wine / intoxicating cup of stupor) portrays the blinding, disorienting shock of military disaster. Psalm 60:3 (KJV) - "Thou hast shewed thy people hard things: thou hast made us to drink the wine of astonishment."

question: What military rallying standard has God unfurled for His faithful people in Psalm 60:4?
opt1: "Thou hast given a banner to them that fear thee, that it may be displayed because of the truth. Selah."
opt2: "Thou hast lifted up a golden ensign on Mount Zion, that all tribes may rally to the battle;"
opt3: "Thou hast set up a shield of salvation before thy host, that the Philistines may be put to flight;"
opt4: "Thou hast raised the horn of David in Jerusalem, that the kings may see thy righteous power;"
correct: "Thou hast given a banner to them that fear thee, that it may be displayed because of the truth. Selah."
explanation: God provides a rallying banner (nes) to gather His God-fearing army, unfurled not for carnal empire but for the defense and vindication of divine truth. Psalm 60:4 (KJV) - "Thou hast given a banner to them that fear thee, that it may be displayed because of the truth. Selah."

question: What divine oracle in the sanctuary promises territorial apportionment across the Jordan in Psalm 60:6?
opt1: "The Lord hath decreed from Zion: I will march through Canaan, and give the inheritance of Jacob unto my anointed;"
opt2: "God hath spoken in his holiness; I will rejoice, I will divide Shechem, and mete out the valley of Succoth."
opt3: "The Almighty hath sworn by his name: I will conquer the cities of Ephraim, and establish my tabernacle in Shiloh;"
opt4: "God hath declared by his prophets: I will subdue the borders of the Amorites, and distribute their vineyards;"
correct: "God hath spoken in his holiness; I will rejoice, I will divide Shechem, and mete out the valley of Succoth."
explanation: Speaking from His sanctuary, God acts as sovereign Landlord: measuring out Shechem (west of Jordan) and Succoth (east of Jordan) as His rightful domain. Psalm 60:6 (KJV) - "God hath spoken in his holiness; I will rejoice, I will divide Shechem, and mete out the valley of Succoth."

question: How are the key tribes of Israel designated in God's imperial administration in Psalm 60:7?
opt1: "Benjamin is mine, and Dan is mine; Zebulun is my battle sword; Levi is my high priest;"
opt2: "Reuben is mine, and Gad is mine; Issachar is the shield of my salvation; Naphtali is my royal sceptre;"
opt3: "Gilead is mine, and Manasseh is mine; Ephraim also is the strength of mine head; Judah is my lawgiver;"
opt4: "Asher is mine, and Simeon is mine; Joseph is the crown of my host; David is my eternal prince;"
correct: "Gilead is mine, and Manasseh is mine; Ephraim also is the strength of mine head; Judah is my lawgiver;"
explanation: God claims the Transjordan tribes (Gilead, Manasseh), designates northern powerhouse Ephraim as His warrior helmet ('strength of mine head'), and royal Judah as His legislative sceptre ('my lawgiver' - Gen 49:10). Psalm 60:7 (KJV) - "Gilead is mine, and Manasseh is mine; Ephraim also is the strength of mine head; Judah is my lawgiver;"

question: What three vivid household idioms depict the subjugation of Israel's historic surrounding enemies in Psalm 60:8?
opt1: "Ammon is my footstool; over Syria will I brandish my sword: Tyre, bow down before my throne;"
opt2: "Moab is my servant; over Edom will I break my iron rod: Egypt, bring tribute unto my sanctuary;"
opt3: "Amalek is my prey; over Babylon will I pour out my fury: Assyria, tremble at the sound of my chariot;"
opt4: "Moab is my washpot; over Edom will I cast out my shoe: Philistia, triumph thou because of me."
correct: "Moab is my washpot; over Edom will I cast out my shoe: Philistia, triumph thou because of me."
explanation: Extreme domestic indignities of conquest: Moab is reduced to a foot-washing basin; Edom receives the master's discarded sandal as a sign of ownership; Philistia must shout ironical homage. Psalm 60:8 (KJV) - "Moab is my washpot; over Edom will I cast out my shoe: Philistia, triumph thou because of me."

question: What strategic challenge confronts David regarding the formidable fortified city of Edom in Psalm 60:9?
opt1: "Who will bring me into the strong city? who will lead me into Edom?"
opt2: "Who shall scale the high ramparts of Bozrah? who will overthrow the rock dwellings of Teman?"
opt3: "How shall our armies breach the clefts of Petra? who can guide our footsteps through the desert?"
opt4: "Who will deliver the king of Edom into our hand? who shall conquer the mountain of Seir?"
correct: "Who will bring me into the strong city? who will lead me into Edom?"
explanation: The 'strong city' refers to Petra (Sela) or Bozrah, the almost impregnable rock-hewn fortress of Edom nestled in treacherous cliffs. Psalm 60:9 (KJV) - "Who will bring me into the strong city? who will lead me into Edom?"

question: What fundamental axiom regarding human help and carnal alliances is confessed in Psalm 60:11?
opt1: "Deliver us from the sword: for horses and chariots are deceitful in battle;"
opt2: "Give us help from trouble: for vain is the help of man."
opt3: "Save us, O Lord: for treaties with the heathen bring only sorrow and snare;"
opt4: "Plead our cause: for the wisdom of princes cannot deliver in the day of wrath;"
correct: "Give us help from trouble: for vain is the help of man."
explanation: David renounces all earthly reliance: human armies, alliances, and strategies are utter vanity (shav) without God's sovereign intervention. Psalm 60:11 (KJV) - "Give us help from trouble: for vain is the help of man."

question: What ringing climax of triumphant faith and victorious warfare concludes Psalm 60:12?
opt1: "In the Lord of hosts we shall conquer: for his right hand shall scatter the pride of Seir;"
opt2: "By the power of the Almighty we shall inherit the land: for he hath broken the bow of the Philistines;"
opt3: "Through God we shall do valiantly: for he it is that shall tread down our enemies."
opt4: "The armies of Israel shall shout for joy: for the God of Jacob hath crowned our heads with victory;"
correct: "Through God we shall do valiantly: for he it is that shall tread down our enemies."
explanation: The ultimate battle anthem: human valor is effective only through God ('Through God we shall do valiantly'), who personally tramples every adversary beneath His feet. Psalm 60:12 (KJV) - "Through God we shall do valiantly: for he it is that shall tread down our enemies."

question: What complex multi-front military campaign is documented in the detailed historical title of Psalm 60?

explanation: While David fought the Arameans in the north, Edom attacked the south; Joab made a forced march south and routed Edom in the Valley of Salt. Psalm 60:Title (KJV) - "To the chief Musician upon Shushan-eduth, Michtam of David, to teach; when he strove with Aram-naharaim and with Aram-zobah, when Joab returned, and smote of Edom in the valley of salt twelve thousand."

question: From what distant state and in what emotional condition does the psalmist cry to God in Psalm 61:2?
opt1: "From the end of the earth will I cry unto thee, when my heart is overwhelmed: lead me to the rock that is higher than I."
opt2: "From the depths of the pit will I call upon thy name, when my soul is faint: set my feet upon the holy mountain of Zion;"
opt3: "Out of the valley of darkness will I lift up my voice, when my spirit is troubled: hide me in the secret place of the Most High;"
opt4: "From the borders of the heathen will I seek thy face, when my strength faileth: bring me unto the river of living waters;"
correct: "From the end of the earth will I cry unto thee, when my heart is overwhelmed: lead me to the rock that is higher than I."
explanation: Even in remote exile and feeling utterly overwhelmed, David looks beyond mortal limitations to Yahweh, praying to be lifted onto a supernatural rock fortress higher than himself. Psalm 61:2 (KJV) - "From the end of the earth will I cry unto thee, when my heart is overwhelmed: lead me to the rock that is higher than I."

question: What two protective defensive structures has God provided against the adversary according to Psalm 61:3?
opt1: "For thou art a shield of brass and an iron wall against the oppressor;"
opt2: "For thou hast been a shelter for me, and a strong tower from the enemy."
opt3: "For thou hast built a fortress in the desert and a hiding place from the sword;"
opt4: "For thou art my buckler in battle and a high wall against the heathen host;"
correct: "For thou hast been a shelter for me, and a strong tower from the enemy."
explanation: David recounts God's proven track record: He has served as both a protective shelter (machseh) and an unassailable elevated watchtower (migdal-oz) against attacking foes. Psalm 61:3 (KJV) - "For thou hast been a shelter for me, and a strong tower from the enemy."

question: What perpetual desire for sacred fellowship and divine protection is expressed in Psalm 61:4?
opt1: "I will dwell in the courts of Jerusalem all my days: I will rejoice under the shadow of the altar. Selah."
opt2: "I will worship before the ark of the covenant: I will find safety behind the shields of the sanctuary. Selah."
opt3: "I will abide in thy tabernacle for ever: I will trust in the covert of thy wings. Selah."
opt4: "I will offer sacrifices in Zion morning and evening: I will take refuge in the holy place of the Most High. Selah."
correct: "I will abide in thy tabernacle for ever: I will trust in the covert of thy wings. Selah."
explanation: David yearns for uninterrupted eternal communion in God's tabernacle, sheltering securely beneath the wings of the cherubim over the mercy seat. Psalm 61:4 (KJV) - "I will abide in thy tabernacle for ever: I will trust in the covert of thy wings. Selah."

question: What heritage does God bestow upon the psalmist after hearing his solemn vows in Psalm 61:5?
opt1: "thou hast given me the royal sceptre over the twelve tribes of Israel"
opt2: "thou hast granted me the wealth of the nations and length of days"
opt3: "thou hast established my throne above the mountains of Judah"
opt4: "thou hast given me the heritage of those that fear thy name."
correct: "thou hast given me the heritage of those that fear thy name."
explanation: The ultimate covenant treasure: sharing in the spiritual portion, promises, and eternal inheritance reserved for all who revere Yahweh's Name. Psalm 61:5 (KJV) - "For thou, O God, hast heard my vows: thou hast given me the heritage of those that fear thy name."

question: Which twin divine guardians does the psalmist ask God to prepare to preserve the eternal King in Psalm 61:7?
opt1: "O prepare mercy and truth, which may preserve him."
opt2: "O send forth righteousness and judgment, which may defend his crown"
opt3: "O commission thy angels and hosts, which may fight for his kingdom"
opt4: "O establish peace and salvation, which may surround his throne"
correct: "O prepare mercy and truth, which may preserve him."
explanation: Mercy (hesed) and Truth (emet) are personified as heavenly royal bodyguards dispatched to preserve the King on His throne forever. Psalm 61:7 (KJV) - "He shall abide before God for ever: O prepare mercy and truth, which may preserve him."

question: What daily commitment to worship and obedience concludes Psalm 61:8?
opt1: "Therefore will I offer bullocks upon thine altar, and bless thy holy law day and night;"

opt3: "And I will sound the silver trumpet in Zion, and proclaim thy righteousness to all generations;"
opt4: "So shall my tongue declare thy salvation, and my hands minister in thy sanctuary continually;"
correct: "So will I sing praise unto thy name for ever, that I may daily perform my vows."
explanation: Gratitude translates into continuous action: perpetual praise coupled with faithful daily execution of sacred covenant vows. Psalm 61:8 (KJV) - "So will I sing praise unto thy name for ever, that I may daily perform my vows."

question: What profound spiritual truth is conveyed by the phrase 'the rock that is higher than I' in Psalm 61:2?
opt1: David was looking for a high mountain peak in the desert of Paran to hide from Saul's scouts
opt2: It refers to the stone altar erected by Solomon on Mount Moriah
opt3: Human self-reliance is completely inadequate; the soul requires a divine refuge whose elevation, stability, and security far exceed mortal capabilities

correct: Human self-reliance is completely inadequate; the soul requires a divine refuge whose elevation, stability, and security far exceed mortal capabilities
explanation: When heart and mind are overwhelmed, true peace is found only in a refuge inaccessible to human self-effort - God Himself, the transcendent Rock of Ages. Psalm 61:2 (KJV) - "From the end of the earth will I cry unto thee, when my heart is overwhelmed: lead me to the rock that is higher than I."

question: What musical instrument direction is specified in the superscription of Psalm 61?

question: What dual imagery of sacred shelter is joined in Psalm 61:4?
opt1: The architectural sanctuary ('thy tabernacle') and the maternal avian shelter ('the covert of thy wings')
opt2: The cedar palace of Lebanon and the bronze battlements of Zion

opt4: The high tower of David and the iron chariot of the hosts
correct: The architectural sanctuary ('thy tabernacle') and the maternal avian shelter ('the covert of thy wings')
explanation: David binds together the public sanctuary of worship ('tabernacle') with the tender, intimate imagery of sheltering under God's wings like a protected fledgling. Psalm 61:4 (KJV) - "I will abide in thy tabernacle for ever: I will trust in the covert of thy wings. Selah."

question: How do verses 6 and 7 ('Thou wilt prolong the king's life ... He shall abide before God for ever') point forward prophetically in Christian theology?
opt1: They predict that King Solomon would live to be two hundred years old
