correct: They find their ultimate fulfillment in the resurrected, eternal Messianic King, Jesus Christ, who reigns before God forever (Luke 1:32-33; Hebrews 7:25)
explanation: David's own earthly life ended at age seventy; the promise of an eternal lifespan and perpetual abiding before God finds its true reality only in the risen Christ. Psalm 61:6-7 (KJV) - "Thou wilt prolong the king's life: and his years as many generations. He shall abide before God for ever: O prepare mercy and truth, which may preserve him."

question: What silent, patient posture of soul opens Psalm 62:1-2?
opt1: "In the morning will I cry unto the Lord: for he is my deliverer in the day of evil; I shall stand fast;"
opt2: "Truly my soul waiteth upon God: from him cometh my salvation. He only is my rock and my salvation; he is my defence; I shall not be greatly moved."
opt3: "My heart rejoiceth in the Almighty: from the heavens he sendeth his help; my horn is exalted on high;"
opt4: "Verily the Lord is my shepherd: I shall not lack any good thing; he maketh me to lie down in peace;"
correct: "Truly my soul waiteth upon God: from him cometh my salvation. He only is my rock and my salvation; he is my defence; I shall not be greatly moved."
explanation: The Hebrew dumiyyah denotes silent, restful waiting in total surrender: God alone is the exclusive Rock, Fortress, and Author of salvation. Psalm 62:1-2 (KJV) - "Truly my soul waiteth upon God: from him cometh my salvation. He only is my rock and my salvation; he is my defence; I shall not be greatly moved."

question: What architectural metaphors describe the impending doom of conspiring adversaries in Psalm 62:3?
opt1: "as broken pillars of clay shall ye crumble, and as unmortared stones"

correct: "as a bowing wall shall ye be, and as a tottering fence."

Psalm 62:3 (KJV) - "How long will ye imagine mischief against a man? ye shall be slain all of you: as a bowing wall shall ye be, and as a tottering fence."

question: What deceitful duplicity marks the speech and internal intentions of David's enemies in Psalm 62:4?

correct: "They only consult to cast him down from his excellency: they delight in lies: they bless with their mouth, but they curse inwardly. Selah."
explanation: Total hypocrisy: the rebels mask their treasonous objective (deposing David from royal dignity) beneath polite verbal benedictions while harboring venomous curses inwardly. Psalm 62:4 (KJV) - "They only consult to cast him down from his excellency: they delight in lies: they bless with their mouth, but they curse inwardly. Selah."

question: How does David's confession of stability in Psalm 62:6 advance beyond verse 2?

opt3: In verse 2 he spoke of personal salvation, but in verse 6 he included the entire nation of Israel
opt4: In verse 2 he waited in silence, but in verse 6 he commanded the priests to blow the silver trumpets
correct: In verse 2 he declared 'I shall not be greatly moved', but in verse 6 his faith solidifies to an absolute: 'I shall not be moved'
explanation: A glorious maturation of faith: preaching to his own soul removes all qualifying doubt, elevating confidence from 'not greatly moved' to unshakeable, absolute stability. Psalm 62:2, 6 (KJV) - "I shall not be greatly moved ... He only is my rock and my salvation: he is my defence; I shall not be moved."

question: What universal pastoral invitation is extended to the covenant congregation in Psalm 62:8?

explanation: David invites all people to unreserved trust under every circumstance, pouring out the innermost contents of their heart before God as an unassailable refuge. Psalm 62:8 (KJV) - "Trust in him at all times; ye people, pour out your heart before him: God is a refuge for us. Selah."

question: What verdict does divine balance scales render concerning all classes of mortal humanity in Psalm 62:9?

correct: "Surely men of low degree are vanity, and men of high degree are a lie: to be laid in the balance, they are altogether lighter than vanity."
explanation: Social rank offers zero substance: the commoner is mere vapor ('vanity') and the aristocrat an illusion ('a lie'); placed on God's balance scales, humanity weighs less than a breath. Psalm 62:9 (KJV) - "Surely men of low degree are vanity, and men of high degree are a lie: to be laid in the balance, they are altogether lighter than vanity."

question: What warning is issued regarding extortion, crime, and the accumulation of wealth in Psalm 62:10?

explanation: A vital biblical financial principle: do not turn to unlawful gain, and if legitimate wealth multiplies, never allow the affections of the heart to anchor upon it. Psalm 62:10 (KJV) - "Trust not in oppression, and become not vain in robbery: if riches increase, set not your heart upon them."

question: What numerical formula establishes that ultimate power belongs exclusively to God in Psalm 62:11?

correct: "God hath spoken once; twice have I heard this; that power belongeth unto God."
explanation: The graded numerical idiom ('once ... twice') emphasizes the settled, immutable certainty of divine revelation: omnipotent power belongs solely to Yahweh. Psalm 62:11 (KJV) - "God hath spoken once; twice have I heard this; that power belongeth unto God."

question: Which two complementary divine attributes balance each other in Psalm 62:11-12?

Psalm 62:11-12 (KJV) - "that power belongeth unto God. Also unto thee, O Lord, belongeth mercy: for thou renderest to every man according to his work."

question: What intense personal thirst and longing for God in a barren wilderness opens Psalm 63:1?

Psalm 63:1 (KJV) - "O God, thou art my God; early will I seek thee: my soul thirsteth for thee, my flesh longeth for thee in a dry and thirsty land, where no water is;"

question: What specific sanctuary recollection fuels David's desert devotion in Psalm 63:2?

question: What supreme theological valuation of God's covenant love is proclaimed in Psalm 63:3?
opt1: "Because thy lovingkindness is better than life, my lips shall praise thee."
opt2: "Because thy mercy endureth for ever, my tongue shall declare thy righteousness"
opt3: "Because thy salvation is more precious than rubies, my soul shall magnify thy name"

explanation: Physical life is precious, but God's hesed (covenant lovingkindness) is infinitely superior; without God's love, biological existence is meaningless. Psalm 63:3 (KJV) - "Because thy lovingkindness is better than life, my lips shall praise thee."

question: What lifelong liturgical vows and physical prayer posture are described in Psalm 63:4?

correct: "Thus will I bless thee while I live: I will lift up my hands in thy name."
explanation: Praise is not a transient mood but a lifelong vocation, marked by the ancient posture of lifted hands expressing expectant surrender and adoration. Psalm 63:4 (KJV) - "Thus will I bless thee while I live: I will lift up my hands in thy name."

question: What banquet metaphor depicts the profound satisfaction of David's soul in Psalm 63:5?

question: When does David meditate upon God during the quiet hours of rest in Psalm 63:6?

question: What harmonious partnership between human exertion and divine preservation is captured in Psalm 63:8?

question: How will the king and liars be contrasted in the conclusion of Psalm 63:11?

question: What lethal military weaponry metaphors describe the weaponized slander of the wicked in Psalm 64:3?

opt3: "That they may swallow up the innocent at the gates: deceitfully do they murder without shame;"
opt4: "That they may destroy the seed of the king: secretly do they lay snares in the night watch;"
correct: "That they may shoot in secret at the perfect: suddenly do they shoot at him, and fear not."
explanation: Cowardly ambush: concealed snipers targeting the morally blameless ('the perfect'), launching sudden ambush assaults with zero reverence or fear of God. Psalm 64:4 (KJV) - "That they may shoot in secret at the perfect: suddenly do they shoot at him, and fear not."

question: What arrogant assumption of invisibility emboldens the conspirators in Psalm 64:5?
opt1: "They take counsel together against the Lord: they boast in their chariots, saying, None can resist us;"
opt2: "They bind themselves with an oath: they dig trenches in the dark, saying, The king knoweth not;"
opt3: "They encourage themselves in an evil matter: they commune of laying snares privily; they say, Who shall see them?"
opt4: "They assemble in the chambers of secrecy: they forge lies, saying, God hath forsaken the earth;"
correct: "They encourage themselves in an evil matter: they commune of laying snares privily; they say, Who shall see them?"
explanation: Operating in moral delusion, the conspirators convince themselves that their covert operations and concealed traps are hidden from divine omniscience ('Who shall see them?'). Psalm 64:5 (KJV) - "They encourage themselves in an evil matter: they commune of laying snares privily; they say, Who shall see them?"

question: What dark assessment of human depravity and corrupt scheming is articulated in Psalm 64:6?
opt1: "They invent new devices of cruelty: their minds are filled with darkness, and their hands run to blood;"
opt2: "They study the ruin of the poor: their imagination is wholly corrupted, and their conscience is seared;"
opt3: "They multiply treachery against the covenant: their understanding is blind, and their paths crooked;"
opt4: "They search out iniquities; they accomplish a diligent search: both the inward thought of every one of them, and the heart, is deep."
correct: "They search out iniquities; they accomplish a diligent search: both the inward thought of every one of them, and the heart, is deep."
explanation: Human wicked ingenuity exhausts itself in devious research, revealing the unfathomable, labyrinthine depths of the fallen human heart (Jer 17:9). Psalm 64:6 (KJV) - "They search out iniquities; they accomplish a diligent search: both the inward thought of every one of them, and the heart, is deep."

question: What divine counter-attack shatters the covert archers in Psalm 64:7?
opt1: "But God shall shoot at them with an arrow; suddenly shall they be wounded."
opt2: "And the Lord shall strike them with lightning; instantly shall their bows be broken;"
opt3: "For the Almighty will send an angel against them; in a moment shall they be consumed;"
opt4: "Yet God will overturn their secret mounds; their chariots shall sink in the deep pit;"
correct: "But God shall shoot at them with an arrow; suddenly shall they be wounded."
explanation: Divine poetic justice: while human snipers shot 'suddenly' at the blameless (v. 4), God Himself draws His bow, wounding them 'suddenly' with an unerring heavenly arrow. Psalm 64:7 (KJV) - "But God shall shoot at them with an arrow; suddenly shall they be wounded."

question: What boomerang effect turns the conspirators' own weapon against themselves in Psalm 64:8?
opt1: "And their own swords shall pierce their hearts: all their captains shall perish in shame;"
opt2: "So they shall make their own tongue to fall upon themselves: all that see them shall flee away."
opt3: "So their secret nets shall entangle their own feet: all their wealth shall be plundered;"
opt4: "Thus their false oaths shall condemn them before the elders: the whole assembly shall stone them;"
correct: "So they shall make their own tongue to fall upon themselves: all that see them shall flee away."
explanation: The slanderous words they hurled at others collapse back upon their own heads, destroying their reputation and causing horrified onlookers to flee. Psalm 64:8 (KJV) - "So they shall make their own tongue to fall upon themselves: all that see them shall flee away."

question: What global impact does this divine judgment produce upon observer humanity in Psalm 64:9?
opt1: "And the nations shall bring tribute to Zion, and glorify the Lord of hosts in his holy mountain;"
opt2: "So all flesh shall confess the power of the Almighty, and turn away from the idols of the heathen;"
opt3: "And all men shall fear, and shall declare the work of God; for they shall wisely consider of his doing."
opt4: "Then shall the kings of the earth be humbled, and lay their hands upon their mouths in silence;"
correct: "And all men shall fear, and shall declare the work of God; for they shall wisely consider of his doing."
explanation: God's righteous retribution inspires universal holy awe, compelling observers to thoughtfully analyze and proclaim the undeniable handiwork of God. Psalm 64:9 (KJV) - "And all men shall fear, and shall declare the work of God; for they shall wisely consider of his doing."

question: What joyful climax concludes Psalm 64:10?
opt1: "The saints shall rejoice in his temple, and offer whole burnt offerings; and Israel shall dwell in safety;"
opt2: "The anointed of the Lord shall be exalted, and his enemies put to shame; and the poor shall sing for joy;"
opt3: "The congregation of Jacob shall triumph, and bless his holy name; and righteousness shall reign for ever;"
opt4: "The righteous shall be glad in the LORD, and shall trust in him; and all the upright in heart shall glory."
correct: "The righteous shall be glad in the LORD, and shall trust in him; and all the upright in heart shall glory."
explanation: The psalm culminates in serene spiritual triumph: vindicated saints find their overflowing joy, absolute trust, and highest boast in Yahweh. Psalm 64:10 (KJV) - "The righteous shall be glad in the LORD, and shall trust in him; and all the upright in heart shall glory."

question: What literary motif contrasts human plotting in verse 4 with divine retribution in verse 7?
opt1: The word 'suddenly' (Hebrew pith'om) - the wicked shot suddenly at the blameless (v. 4), so God shoots His arrow suddenly at them (v. 7)
opt2: The motif of 'the morning watch' versus 'the evening shadow'
opt3: The contrast between 'the horn of David' and 'the crown of Saul'
opt4: The symbol of 'the green olive tree' versus 'the dry stubble'
correct: The word 'suddenly' (Hebrew pith'om) - the wicked shot suddenly at the blameless (v. 4), so God shoots His arrow suddenly at them (v. 7)
explanation: A deliberate structural parallelism: the wicked imagine their 'sudden' ambush gives them an unfair advantage, but God's 'sudden' arrow executes swift retributive justice. Psalm 64:4, 7 (KJV) - "suddenly do they shoot at him ... suddenly shall they be wounded."

question: What expectant worship in Zion and divine title regarding prayer open Psalm 65:1-2?
opt1: "Praise waiteth for thee, O God, in Sion: and unto thee shall the vow be performed. O thou that hearest prayer, unto thee shall all flesh come."
opt2: "Rejoice in the Lord, O ye righteous, in Jerusalem: pay your vows before the holy ark: O thou that rulest heaven;"
opt3: "Great is the Almighty in Mount Moriah: sound the silver trumpets in his courts: O thou that forgivest iniquity;"
opt4: "Bless the Lord, O my soul, in the sanctuary: offer sacrifices of thanksgiving: O thou that dwellest between cherubim;"
correct: "Praise waiteth for thee, O God, in Sion: and unto thee shall the vow be performed. O thou that hearest prayer, unto thee shall all flesh come."
explanation: Worship waits in reverent expectation in Zion; God is uniquely addressed by the majestic universal title 'O thou that hearest prayer', drawing all humanity unto Himself. Psalm 65:1-2 (KJV) - "Praise waiteth for thee, O God, in Sion: and unto thee shall the vow be performed. O thou that hearest prayer, unto thee shall all flesh come."

question: What gracious divine atonement resolves the overwhelming burden of human sin in Psalm 65:3?
opt1: "Our sins are multiplied like the sand of the sea: yet according to thy mercy remember us;"
opt2: "Iniquities prevail against me: as for our transgressions, thou shalt purge them away."
opt3: "My transgressions are ever before my face: but with the blood of bullocks wash my soul;"
opt4: "Iniquity hath compassed my steps about: but by thy righteousness blot out our debt;"
correct: "Iniquities prevail against me: as for our transgressions, thou shalt purge them away."
explanation: Human moral failure is confessed with total candor ('Iniquities prevail against me'), met immediately by sovereign expiation: God Himself purges/atones for them (Hebrew tekapperem). Psalm 65:3 (KJV) - "Iniquities prevail against me: as for our transgressions, thou shalt purge them away."

question: What beatitude of sovereign election and temple dwelling is pronounced in Psalm 65:4?
opt1: "Blessed are they that keep thy commandments, and walk in the light of thy sanctuary: they shall inherit the land;"
opt2: "Blessed is the nation whose God is the Lord, and the people whom he hath chosen: they shall behold his glory;"
opt3: "Blessed is the man whom thou choosest, and causest to approach unto thee, that he may dwell in thy courts: we shall be satisfied with the goodness of thy house, even of thy holy temple."
opt4: "Blessed are the pure in heart that stand before the altar: they shall be filled with the fatness of Zion;"
correct: "Blessed is the man whom thou choosest, and causest to approach unto thee, that he may dwell in thy courts: we shall be satisfied with the goodness of thy house, even of thy holy temple."
explanation: Supreme covenant blessedness: divine initiative chooses and draws the believer into intimate fellowship, finding complete soul-satisfaction in the goodness of God's house. Psalm 65:4 (KJV) - "Blessed is the man whom thou choosest, and causest to approach unto thee, that he may dwell in thy courts: we shall be satisfied with the goodness of thy house, even of thy holy temple."

question: How does God answer His people, and of whom is He the confidence across the globe in Psalm 65:5?
opt1: "With mighty wonders of old wilt thou deliver us, O King of Israel; who art the hope of all the tribes of Jacob;"
opt2: "In great mercy and lovingkindness wilt thou hear our cry; who art the shield of all nations under heaven;"
opt3: "Through fire and tempest wilt thou plead our cause; who art the refuge of the righteous from generation to generation;"
opt4: "By terrible things in righteousness wilt thou answer us, O God of our salvation; who art the confidence of all the ends of the earth, and of them that are afar off upon the sea:"
correct: "By terrible things in righteousness wilt thou answer us, O God of our salvation; who art the confidence of all the ends of the earth, and of them that are afar off upon the sea:"
explanation: God answers prayer through awesome ('terrible') righteous deeds, standing as the sole reliable anchor of hope for distant continents and remote ocean voyagers alike. Psalm 65:5 (KJV) - "By terrible things in righteousness wilt thou answer us, O God of our salvation; who art the confidence of all the ends of the earth, and of them that are afar off upon the sea:"

question: What geological and sociological chaos does God sovereignly calm in Psalm 65:6-7?
opt1: "Which by his strength setteth fast the mountains; being girded with power: Which stilleth the noise of the seas, the noise of their waves, and the tumult of the people."
opt2: "Which founded the earth upon the waters: and broke the pride of the kings of the heathen;"
opt3: "Which melteth the hills like wax at his presence: and scattereth the war chariots of the ungodly;"
opt4: "Which commandeth the storm to cease: and delivereth his chosen from the rebellion of the nations;"
correct: "Which by his strength setteth fast the mountains; being girded with power: Which stilleth the noise of the seas, the noise of their waves, and the tumult of the people."
explanation: God's omnipotence anchors immovable mountain ranges, stills roaring oceanic tsunamis, and subdues the turbulent, raging rebellions of human populations. Psalm 65:6-7 (KJV) - "Which by his strength setteth fast the mountains; being girded with power: Which stilleth the noise of the seas, the noise of their waves, and the tumult of the people."

question: What celestial boundary times does God cause to rejoice in Psalm 65:8?
opt1: "thou crownest the sunrise and sunset with golden splendor"
opt2: "thou makest the outgoings of the morning and evening to rejoice."
opt3: "thou commandest the noon day and midnight watch to praise thy name"
opt4: "thou causest the stars of the dawn and the moon of the night to sing"
correct: "thou makest the outgoings of the morning and evening to rejoice."
explanation: The gates of day and night - morning dawn and evening dusk ('the outgoings') - erupt in joyous cosmic celebration before their Creator. Psalm 65:8 (KJV) - "They also that dwell in the uttermost parts are afraid at thy tokens: thou makest the outgoings of the morning and evening to rejoice."

question: With what inexhaustible heavenly reservoir does God enrich the agricultural earth in Psalm 65:9?
opt1: "thou waterest it with the dew of Hermon and the sweet springs of Lebanon: thou givest bread in abundance"
opt2: "thou pourest out the rain of heaven from golden clouds: thou blessest the harvest of wheat and barley"
opt3: "thou greatly enrichest it with the river of God, which is full of water: thou preparest them corn, when thou hast so provided for it."
opt4: "thou openest the windows of the sky with living streams: thou multipliest the sheaves in the barn"
correct: "thou greatly enrichest it with the river of God, which is full of water: thou preparest them corn, when thou hast so provided for it."
explanation: Unlike terrestrial streams that dry up in summer drought, 'the river of God' (the inexhaustible heavenly clouds) is perpetually brimful of water, guaranteeing fruitful grain harvests. Psalm 65:9 (KJV) - "Thou visitest the earth, and waterest it: thou greatly enrichest it with the river of God, which is full of water: thou preparest them corn, when thou hast so provided for it."

question: What fourfold tender agricultural care does God bestow upon farmland in Psalm 65:10?
opt1: "Thou breakest the clods with rain: thou levelest the soil: thou plantest the seed: thou protectest the vine;"
opt2: "Thou sendest the former and the latter rain: thou enricher the loam: thou warmeth the ground: thou multipliest the crop;"
opt3: "Thou plowest the ground in season: thou scatterest the dew: thou ripenest the corn: thou crownest the vineyard;"
opt4: "Thou waterest the ridges thereof abundantly: thou settlest the furrows thereof: thou makest it soft with showers: thou blessest the springing thereof."
correct: "Thou waterest the ridges thereof abundantly: thou settlest the furrows thereof: thou makest it soft with showers: thou blessest the springing thereof."
explanation: A master portrait of divine husbandry: soaking plowed ridges, leveling dry furrows, softening hardened topsoil with gentle showers, and blessing the sprouting shoots. Psalm 65:10 (KJV) - "Thou waterest the ridges thereof abundantly: thou settlest the furrows thereof: thou makest it soft with showers: thou blessest the springing thereof."

question: What crowning splendor and abundance of divine harvest paths is depicted in Psalm 65:11?
opt1: "Thou crownest the year with thy goodness; and thy paths drop fatness."
opt2: "Thou fillest the autumn with thy bounty; and thy clouds drop sweet wine"
opt3: "Thou blessest the season with thy righteousness; and the earth overflows with oil"
opt4: "Thou satisfiest the land with thy lovingkindness; and thy footsteps bring peace"
correct: "Thou crownest the year with thy goodness; and thy paths drop fatness."
explanation: The harvest season is crowned with divine beneficence; wherever God's chariot-wheels pass ('thy paths'), the land overflows with dripping fertility and abundance ('fatness'). Psalm 65:11 (KJV) - "Thou crownest the year with thy goodness; and thy paths drop fatness."

question: How is non-human creation poetically animated in rejoicing at the harvest in Psalm 65:13?
opt1: "The meadows are filled with cattle; the orchards blossom with pomegranates; they dance before the Lord"
opt2: "The pastures are clothed with flocks; the valleys also are covered over with corn; they shout for joy, they also sing."
opt3: "The hills are covered with olive trees; the plains overflow with golden sheaves; they magnify the Creator"
opt4: "The wilderness rejoiceth like a garden; the brooks flow with sweet honey; they praise the God of Jacob"
correct: "The pastures are clothed with flocks; the valleys also are covered over with corn; they shout for joy, they also sing."
explanation: A breathtaking personification of creation: grasslands don flocks of sheep like royal robes, valleys carpet themselves in golden grain, joining in a jubilant shout and song of praise. Psalm 65:13 (KJV) - "The pastures are clothed with flocks; the valleys also are covered over with corn; they shout for joy, they also sing."

question: What universal summons to praise God's glorious Name opens Psalm 66:1-2?
opt1: "O praise the Lord, all ye nations: extol his holiness in the sanctuary: give him the glory due unto his name;"
opt2: "Make a joyful noise unto God, all ye lands: Sing forth the honour of his name: make his praise glorious."
opt3: "Clap your hands, all ye people: shout unto the King of glory: sound the trumpets of his salvation;"
opt4: "Rejoice in the Almighty, all ye tribes: magnify his power across the earth: declare his wonderful works;"
correct: "Make a joyful noise unto God, all ye lands: Sing forth the honour of his name: make his praise glorious."
explanation: Global evangelistic summons: all nations and continents are commanded to break forth in joyful acclaim, celebrating the honor of God's Name with splendid, glorious praise. Psalm 66:1-2 (KJV) - "Make a joyful noise unto God, all ye lands: Sing forth the honour of his name: make his praise glorious."

question: How do enemies react to the overwhelming display of God's power in Psalm 66:3?
opt1: "in the presence of thy holiness shall the proud kings fall down in the dust"
opt2: "before the brightness of thy lightning shall the armies of the heathen be consumed"
opt3: "through the greatness of thy power shall thine enemies submit themselves unto thee."
opt4: "at the sound of thy chariot wheels shall the ungodly flee into the mountains"
correct: "through the greatness of thy power shall thine enemies submit themselves unto thee."
explanation: The Hebrew yikhachashu ('submit themselves') implies a feigned, cringe-like subjection: God's sheer omnipotence compels even hostile rebels to reluctantly yield outward homage. Psalm 66:3 (KJV) - "Say unto God, How terrible art thou in thy works! through the greatness of thy power shall thine enemies submit themselves unto thee."

question: What two monumental historical water-crossing miracles are celebrated in Psalm 66:6?
opt1: "He divided the waters of the Red Sea: he brought forth living streams from the flinty rock in Horeb;"
opt2: "He made a pathway through the great deep: he dried up the springs of Jordan before the ark of the covenant;"
opt3: "He held back the waves of the ocean: he guided the children of Israel through the wilderness of waters;"
opt4: "He turned the sea into dry land: they went through the flood on foot: there did we rejoice in him."
correct: "He turned the sea into dry land: they went through the flood on foot: there did we rejoice in him."
explanation: Israel celebrates the Red Sea crossing (Exodus 14) and the Jordan River crossing ('the flood', Joshua 3), marching across dry seabed and riverbeds on foot with jubilant joy. Psalm 66:6 (KJV) - "He turned the sea into dry land: they went through the flood on foot: there did we rejoice in him."

question: What ongoing preservation of physical life and footing does God grant His people in Psalm 66:9?
opt1: "Which holdeth our soul in life, and suffereth not our feet to be moved."
opt2: "Who delivereth our steps from the pit, and compasseth our path with angels of salvation"
opt3: "Which keepeth our breath in his hand, and planteth our feet upon the rock of ages"
opt4: "Who protecteth our heads in the battle, and leadeth our steps into the garden of peace"
correct: "Which holdeth our soul in life, and suffereth not our feet to be moved."
explanation: Yahweh continuously maintains the vital spark of life in our souls and keeps our feet from slipping into disaster amidst perilous trials. Psalm 66:9 (KJV) - "Which holdeth our soul in life, and suffereth not our feet to be moved."

question: What metallurgical metaphor describes the severe purifying trials inflicted upon God's people in Psalm 66:10?
opt1: "For thou hast placed us in the furnace of affliction: thou hast purged our dross like refined gold"
opt2: "For thou, O God, hast proved us: thou hast tried us, as silver is tried."
opt3: "For thou hast weighed our spirits in the balance: thou hast hammered our faith upon the anvil"
opt4: "For thou hast sifted us like wheat in the sieve: thou hast cleansed our souls from all impurities"
correct: "For thou, O God, hast proved us: thou hast tried us, as silver is tried."
explanation: Covenant testing is not destructive but refining: God smelts His saints in the crucible of adversity to purge away dross, exactly like silver in the silversmith's fire. Psalm 66:10 (KJV) - "For thou, O God, hast proved us: thou hast tried us, as silver is tried."

question: What terrifying ordeals did Israel pass through before God brought them into ultimate abundance in Psalm 66:12?
opt1: "Thou hast delivered us into the hand of cruel tyrants; we wandered through drought and plague: yet thou gavest us milk and honey;"
opt2: "Thou hast broken our bows before the enemy; we drank the cup of trembling: but thou crownedst our heads with oil;"
opt3: "Thou hast caused men to ride over our heads; we went through fire and through water: but thou broughtest us out into a wealthy place."
opt4: "Thou hast laid our bodies in chains of brass; we passed through the iron furnace: but thou establishedst our feet in Zion;"
correct: "Thou hast caused men to ride over our heads; we went through fire and through water: but thou broughtest us out into a wealthy place."
explanation: Extreme subjugation (foes riding over their necks) and elemental peril ('fire and water') culminated in God bringing them into a 'wealthy place' (revayah - a spacious, overflowing land of abundance). Psalm 66:12 (KJV) - "Thou hast caused men to ride over our heads; we went through fire and through water: but thou broughtest us out into a wealthy place."

question: When did the psalmist make the sacred vows that he now brings into God's house in Psalm 66:13-14?
opt1: "Which I swore in the presence of the elders, in the day of the solemn feast"
opt2: "Which my heart conceived in the quiet night, while meditating on the law of Moses"
opt3: "Which I promised before the high priest, when the horn of oil anointed my head"
opt4: "Which my lips have uttered, and my mouth hath spoken, when I was in trouble."
correct: "Which my lips have uttered, and my mouth hath spoken, when I was in trouble."
explanation: True spiritual integrity does not forget crisis vows: promises made in the agonizing crucible of trouble are faithfully executed in the sanctuary during the hour of deliverance. Psalm 66:14 (KJV) - "Which my lips have uttered, and my mouth hath spoken, when I was in trouble."

question: What personal evangelistic invitation to fellow God-fearers is issued in Psalm 66:16?
opt1: "Come and hear, all ye that fear God, and I will declare what he hath done for my soul."
opt2: "Draw near, all ye tribes of Jacob, and listen to the testimony of my lips before the holy ark;"
opt3: "Assemble, ye righteous elders, and behold how the Almighty hath broken the teeth of the ungodly;"
opt4: "Gather together, all ye saints of Zion, and hear the praises which my mouth shall utter;"
correct: "Come and hear, all ye that fear God, and I will declare what he hath done for my soul."
explanation: Personal testimony: having celebrated national history, the psalmist calls all reverent believers to hear his firsthand, personal experience of God's saving grace. Psalm 66:16 (KJV) - "Come and hear, all ye that fear God, and I will declare what he hath done for my soul."

question: What indispensable condition of heart determines whether the Lord will hear human prayer in Psalm 66:18?
opt1: "If I offer sacrifices without the blood of lambs, the Almighty will reject my petition;"
opt2: "If I regard iniquity in my heart, the Lord will not hear me:"
opt3: "If my hands are defiled with unwashed dust, the Holy One will turn away his face;"
opt4: "If I forget the fast days of the sanctuary, the God of Israel will keep silence;"
correct: "If I regard iniquity in my heart, the Lord will not hear me:"
explanation: A foundational axiom of prayer: 'regarding' (cherishing, harboring, entertaining) unrepentant sin in the heart creates an impenetrable barrier that stops prayer from reaching God. Psalm 66:18 (KJV) - "If I regard iniquity in my heart, the Lord will not hear me:"

question: What joyful doxology celebrating answered prayer and steadfast mercy concludes Psalm 66:20?
opt1: "Praise the Lord of hosts, who hath delivered my soul from death, and my feet from falling;"
opt2: "Glory be to the King of Zion, who hath broken the snare of the fowler, and established my steps;"
opt3: "Blessed be God, which hath not turned away my prayer, nor his mercy from me."
opt4: "Exalted be the God of our salvation, who hath crowned his servant with peace, and satisfied my desire;"
correct: "Blessed be God, which hath not turned away my prayer, nor his mercy from me."
explanation: The psalm closes with exuberant thanksgiving that God did not dismiss the believer's prayer nor withhold His steadfast covenant mercy (hesed). Psalm 66:20 (KJV) - "Blessed be God, which hath not turned away my prayer, nor his mercy from me."

question: What adaptation of the Aaronic blessing with a global missional focus opens Psalm 67:1-2?
opt1: "The Lord bless thee and keep thee from all evil: that thy kingdom may be established in Zion, and thy seed possess the gates of their enemies. Selah;"
opt2: "The Lord make his face shine upon his holy temple: that the heathen may fear his great name, and bring silver from the ends of the world. Selah;"
opt3: "God be merciful unto us, and bless us; and cause his face to shine upon us; Selah. That thy way may be known upon earth, thy saving health among all nations."
opt4: "God be gracious unto the seed of Jacob, and grant peace: that thy law may be written in the hearts of all the families of the earth. Selah;"
correct: "God be merciful unto us, and bless us; and cause his face to shine upon us; Selah. That thy way may be known upon earth, thy saving health among all nations."
explanation: Israel seeks divine favor and the shining of God's countenance not for selfish isolation, but so that God's redemptive way and 'saving health' (salvation) will reach every ethnic group across the globe. Psalm 67:1-2 (KJV) - "God be merciful unto us, and bless us; and cause his face to shine upon us; Selah. That thy way may be known upon earth, thy saving health among all nations."

question: What repeated worldwide missionary chorus resounds in Psalm 67:3 and 67:5?
opt1: "Sing unto the Lord a new song; let the ends of the earth rejoice;"
opt2: "Give unto the Lord glory and strength; bow down before his holy footstool;"
opt3: "Magnify the God of Abraham; proclaim his wondrous salvation to the heathen;"
opt4: "Let the people praise thee, O God; let all the people praise thee."
correct: "Let the people praise thee, O God; let all the people praise thee."
explanation: The heartbeat of biblical missions: the psalm repeats this universal refrain verbatim twice, desiring all ethnic peoples (amim) to unite in worshipping the one true God. Psalm 67:3, 5 (KJV) - "Let the people praise thee, O God; let all the people praise thee."

question: Why are the nations summoned to be glad and sing for joy in Psalm 67:4?
opt1: "for thou shalt judge the people righteously, and govern the nations upon earth. Selah."
opt2: "because thou hast broken the iron chariots of the heathen, and given their lands to the righteous. Selah."
opt3: "for thou hast poured out plentiful rain from heaven, and satisfied the poor with bread. Selah."
opt4: "seeing that the kingdom of David is exalted above all hills, and peace floweth like a river. Selah."
correct: "for thou shalt judge the people righteously, and govern the nations upon earth. Selah."
explanation: Pagan nations rejoice because God's kingdom replaces corrupt human tyranny with perfectly impartial justice and loving divine pastoral guidance. Psalm 67:4 (KJV) - "O let the nations be glad and sing for joy: for thou shalt judge the people righteously, and govern the nations upon earth. Selah."

question: What agricultural harvest blessing leads to universal reverence in Psalm 67:6-7?
opt1: "Then shall the valleys overflow with corn; and the mountains drop sweet wine: and all kings shall fall down in Zion;"
opt2: "Then shall the earth yield her increase; and God, even our own God, shall bless us. God shall bless us; and all the ends of the earth shall fear him."
opt3: "Then shall our barns be filled with plenty; and the Lord our shield will multiply our flocks: and the heathen shall tremble;"
opt4: "And the desert shall blossom as the rose; and the Almighty shall dwell among his people: and the islands shall give thanks;"
correct: "Then shall the earth yield her increase; and God, even our own God, shall bless us. God shall bless us; and all the ends of the earth shall fear him."
explanation: Physical agricultural abundance serves as a tangible pledge of God's favor, inspiring worldwide holy awe and reverence for Yahweh to the ends of the earth. Psalm 67:6-7 (KJV) - "Then shall the earth yield her increase; and God, even our own God, shall bless us. God shall bless us; and all the ends of the earth shall fear him."

question: What ancient Old Testament covenant promise forms the theological foundation of Psalm 67?
opt1: The Davidic Covenant of eternal dynastic kingship in 2 Samuel 7
opt2: The Levitical covenant of salt granted to Phinehas in Numbers 25
opt3: The Abrahamic Covenant (Genesis 12:1-3) - where God promises to bless Abraham's seed so that 'all families of the earth be blessed'
opt4: The covenant of circumcision established with Ishmael in the desert
correct: The Abrahamic Covenant (Genesis 12:1-3) - where God promises to bless Abraham's seed so that 'all families of the earth be blessed'
explanation: Psalm 67 is the definitive OT missionary psalm, reflecting the Abrahamic purpose that God's blessing upon Israel exists to funnel salvation to all Gentiles. Psalm 67:1-2 (KJV) - "God be merciful unto us, and bless us; and cause his face to shine upon us; Selah. That thy way may be known upon earth, thy saving health among all nations."

question: What Hebrew word in Psalm 67:2 is translated in the King James Version as 'saving health'?
opt1: Shalom (peace, welfare)
opt2: Kadosh (holiness, sacredness)
opt3: Rophe (physician, healer)
opt4: Yeshuah (salvation, deliverance, wholeness)
correct: Yeshuah (salvation, deliverance, wholeness)
explanation: Yeshuah denotes comprehensive, dynamic salvation - spiritual rescue, moral restoration, and covenant wholeness (the root of the Name 'Jesus'). Psalm 67:2 (KJV) - "That thy way may be known upon earth, thy saving health among all nations."

question: What intimate personal and national covenant title is ascribed to God in Psalm 67:6?
opt1: "even our own God"
opt2: "the King of the whole earth"
opt3: "the Maker of heaven and dry land"
opt4: "the Horn of our salvation"
correct: "even our own God"
explanation: Elohim Eloheinu ('God, even our own God') expresses the thrilling reality of personal covenant belonging: the cosmic Sovereign belongs intimately to His covenant people. Psalm 67:6 (KJV) - "Then shall the earth yield her increase; and God, even our own God, shall bless us."

question: What musical accompaniment instruction is designated in the superscription of Psalm 67?
opt1: 'upon Gittith' (a vintage tune played on Gittite harps)
opt2: 'on Neginoth' (accompanied by stringed instruments)
opt3: 'upon Shoshannim' (played on lily-shaped trumpets)
opt4: 'upon Alamoth' (sung by high soprano maiden voices)
correct: 'on Neginoth' (accompanied by stringed instruments)
explanation: 'Neginoth' indicates that this radiant hymn of universal missionary praise was arranged for plucked stringed instruments. Psalm 67:Title (KJV) - "To the chief Musician on Neginoth, A Psalm or Song."

question: How is divine global governance depicted in the Hebrew verb 'tanchem' translated 'govern' in Psalm 67:4?
opt1: As an iron-fisted emperor crushing all national borders
opt2: As a distant observer leaving nations to their own fate
opt3: As a benevolent Shepherd leading, guiding, and pasturing the nations of the earth
opt4: As a military conqueror dividing earthly spoils
correct: As a benevolent Shepherd leading, guiding, and pasturing the nations of the earth
explanation: The verb nachah ('govern' / 'lead') carries the pastoral imagery of Psalm 23:3 ('He leadeth me'), portraying God shepherding human nations in truth and equity. Psalm 67:4 (KJV) - "for thou shalt judge the people righteously, and govern the nations upon earth. Selah."

question: In historic Jewish liturgy, during which major agricultural festival was Psalm 67 traditionally chanted?
opt1: Purim, during the reading of the Megillah of Esther
opt2: Hanukkah, at the lighting of the eight sacred lamps
opt3: The Day of Atonement (Yom Kippur), during the evening fast
opt4: The Feast of Weeks (Shavuot / Pentecost) and during the counting of the Omer leading up to the wheat harvest
correct: The Feast of Weeks (Shavuot / Pentecost) and during the counting of the Omer leading up to the wheat harvest
explanation: Because of its seven verses and prominent harvest imagery (v. 6), Psalm 67 became the central liturgy for Shavuot and the 49-day counting of the Omer. Psalm 67:6 (KJV) - "Then shall the earth yield her increase; and God, even our own God, shall bless us."

question: What historic Ark-procession battle cry opens Psalm 68:1-2?
opt1: "Arise, O Lord, into thy rest; thou, and the ark of thy strength: let thy priests be clothed with righteousness;"
opt2: "Rise up, O God of hosts, and defend Zion: let the kings of the heathen melt like morning mist before thy face;"
opt3: "Gird thy sword upon thy thigh, O Most Mighty: march through the wilderness, and consume the armies of the ungodly;"
opt4: "Let God arise, let his enemies be scattered: let them also that hate him flee before him. As smoke is driven away, so drive them away: as wax melteth before the fire, so let the wicked perish at the presence of God."
correct: "Let God arise, let his enemies be scattered: let them also that hate him flee before him. As smoke is driven away, so drive them away: as wax melteth before the fire, so let the wicked perish at the presence of God."
explanation: David opens this monumental triumphal procession quoting the ancient marching invocation of Moses when the Ark set forward in the wilderness (Num 10:35). Psalm 68:1-2 (KJV) - "Let God arise, let his enemies be scattered: let them also that hate him flee before him. As smoke is driven away, so drive them away: as wax melteth before the fire, so let the wicked perish at the presence of God."

question: By what sacred abbreviated covenant Name is God to be extolled as He rides upon the heavens in Psalm 68:4?
opt1: "by his name JAH, and rejoice before him."
opt2: "by his name ELOHIM, and bow down at his footstool"
opt3: "by his name SHADDAI, and worship in the beauty of holiness"
opt4: "by his name ADONAI, and sing praises unto his throne"
correct: "by his name JAH, and rejoice before him."
explanation: JAH (Yah) is the poetic contraction of Yahweh (the self-existent covenant Redeemer), riding majestically across the heavenly expanse. Psalm 68:4 (KJV) - "Sing unto God, sing praises to his name: extol him that rideth upon the heavens by his name JAH, and rejoice before him."

question: How does God manifest His tender compassion toward the lonely and socially vulnerable in Psalm 68:5-6?
opt1: "A shelter for the afflicted, and a healer of the brokenhearted: he satisfieth the poor with bread, and freeth the captive;"
opt2: "A father of the fatherless, and a judge of the widows, is God in his holy habitation. God setteth the solitary in families: he bringeth out those which are bound with chains: but the rebellious dwell in a dry land."
opt3: "A helper of the needy, and a shield for the stranger: he gathereth the outcasts of Israel into Jerusalem;"
opt4: "A deliverer of the oppressed, and an avenger of the innocent: he planteth the humble in a fertile land;"
correct: "A father of the fatherless, and a judge of the widows, is God in his holy habitation. God setteth the solitary in families: he bringeth out those which are bound with chains: but the rebellious dwell in a dry land."
explanation: From His celestial sanctuary, the omnipotent Sovereign personally defends orphans and widows, adopts the isolated into loving families, and liberates prisoners. Psalm 68:5-6 (KJV) - "A father of the fatherless, and a judge of the widows, is God in his holy habitation. God setteth the solitary in families: he bringeth out those which are bound with chains: but the rebellious dwell in a dry land."

question: What vast company of heralds publishes the divine word of military victory in Psalm 68:11-12?
opt1: "The Almighty sounded his trumpet: ten thousand captains shouted the victory: and the elders rejoiced at the gate;"
opt2: "God proclaimed salvation from Zion: the priests blew with silver horns: and the warriors divided the golden crowns;"
opt3: "The Lord gave the word: great was the company of those that published it. Kings of armies did flee apace: and she that tarried at home divided the spoil."
opt4: "The King decreed righteousness from heaven: the hosts of Israel pursued the enemy: and the poor were enriched;"
correct: "The Lord gave the word: great was the company of those that published it. Kings of armies did flee apace: and she that tarried at home divided the spoil."
explanation: When God gives the word, a vast choir of women heralds (Hebrew mebasserot) proclaims the triumph, while women remaining at home divide the battle spoils. Psalm 68:11-12 (KJV) - "The Lord gave the word: great was the company of those that published it. Kings of armies did flee apace: and she that tarried at home divided the spoil."

question: What radiant transformation from soot and misery to glorious beauty is promised in Psalm 68:13?
opt1: "Though ye have wept in the ashes of exile, yet shall ye be clothed in fine linen and crowned with pure gold;"
opt2: "Though ye were bound in the mire of Egypt, yet shall ye soar like eagles with plumage of shining brass;"
opt3: "Though ye wandered in sackcloth, yet shall ye shine like the stars of heaven in royal purple;"
opt4: "Though ye have lien among the pots, yet shall ye be as the wings of a dove covered with silver, and her feathers with yellow gold."
correct: "Though ye have lien among the pots, yet shall ye be as the wings of a dove covered with silver, and her feathers with yellow gold."
explanation: A stunning picture of redemption: wretched slaves crouching among the filthy soot of campfire pots are transformed into shimmering doves with silver wings and golden plumage. Psalm 68:13 (KJV) - "Though ye have lien among the pots, yet shall ye be as the wings of a dove covered with silver, and her feathers with yellow gold."

question: Why does Psalm 68:16 rebuke the towering mountain peaks of Bashan in favor of Mount Zion?
opt1: "Why leap ye, ye high hills? this is the hill which God desireth to dwell in; yea, the LORD will dwell in it for ever."
opt2: "Why boast ye, ye mountains of Lebanon? the rock of Moriah is holy, and the Lord hath established his throne thereon;"
opt3: "Why shake ye, ye peaks of Hermon? the hill of the sanctuary is chosen, and the Almighty shall never depart;"
opt4: "Why envy ye, ye rocks of Seir? the house of David is exalted, and the glory of God shall fill the courts;"
correct: "Why leap ye, ye high hills? this is the hill which God desireth to dwell in; yea, the LORD will dwell in it for ever."
explanation: The lofty, basalt crags of Bashan look down with jealous envy ('Why leap ye with jealousy?'), yet God bypassed the colossal peaks to make humble Mount Zion His eternal dwelling place. Psalm 68:16 (KJV) - "Why leap ye, ye high hills? this is the hill which God desireth to dwell in; yea, the LORD will dwell in it for ever."

question: Which triumphant verse from Psalm 68:18 does the Apostle Paul quote in Ephesians 4:8 concerning the ascension of Christ?
opt1: "The chariots of God are twenty thousand, even thousands of angels: the Lord is among them, as in Sinai, in the holy place;"
opt2: "Thou hast ascended on high, thou hast led captivity captive: thou hast received gifts for men; yea, for the rebellious also, that the LORD God might dwell among them."
opt3: "Blessed be the Lord, who daily loadeth us with benefits, even the God of our salvation. Selah;"
opt4: "He that is our God is the God of salvation; and unto GOD the Lord belong the issues from death;"
correct: "Thou hast ascended on high, thou hast led captivity captive: thou hast received gifts for men; yea, for the rebellious also, that the LORD God might dwell among them."
explanation: Paul applies this verse to Jesus Christ, who conquered sin, death, and demonic powers in His ascension, bestowing spiritual gifts upon His Church (Eph 4:8-11). Psalm 68:18 (KJV) - "Thou hast ascended on high, thou hast led captivity captive: thou hast received gifts for men; yea, for the rebellious also, that the LORD God might dwell among them."

question: What daily divine blessing and authority over mortality are praised in Psalm 68:19-20?
opt1: "Praise the Lord of hosts, who continually compasseth us with favor, even the rock of our strength: he openeth the gates of eternal life;"
opt2: "Exalted be the Almighty, who morning by morning reneweth his mercy: he hath broken the iron cords of the grave;"
opt3: "Blessed be the Lord, who daily loadeth us with benefits, even the God of our salvation. Selah. He that is our God is the God of salvation; and unto GOD the Lord belong the issues from death."
opt4: "Glory be to the King of Zion, who bountifully satisfieth our desire: unto him belongeth victory over the sword;"
correct: "Blessed be the Lord, who daily loadeth us with benefits, even the God of our salvation. Selah. He that is our God is the God of salvation; and unto GOD the Lord belong the issues from death."
explanation: Every single day God loads His saints with His bountiful benefits, and to Yahweh Adonai belong the escapes ('issues') from the gates of death. Psalm 68:19-20 (KJV) - "Blessed be the Lord, who daily loadeth us with benefits, even the God of our salvation. Selah. He that is our God is the God of salvation; and unto GOD the Lord belong the issues from death."

question: What African nations are prophesied to submit and worship God in Psalm 68:31?
opt1: "Kings shall sail from Tyre; the princes of Libya shall bring incense to Jerusalem;"
opt2: "Envoys shall arrive from Cush; the merchant caravans of Sheba shall bow before the Lord;"
opt3: "Captains shall come from Phut; the dwellers of Nubia shall offer bullocks upon the altar;"
opt4: "Princes shall come out of Egypt; Ethiopia shall soon stretch out her hands unto God."
correct: "Princes shall come out of Egypt; Ethiopia shall soon stretch out her hands unto God."
explanation: A magnificent prophecy of Gentile conversion: ancient oppressor Egypt sends princes, and Ethiopia (Cush) rapidly stretches forth her hands in joyful adoration to Yahweh. Psalm 68:31 (KJV) - "Princes shall come out of Egypt; Ethiopia shall soon stretch out her hands unto God."

question: What liturgical order of the celebratory procession into the sanctuary is described in Psalm 68:25?
opt1: "The singers went before, the players on instruments followed after; among them were the damsels playing with timbrels."
opt2: "The priests carrying the ark went before, the warriors followed after; surrounded by elders chanting the law"
opt3: "The high priest in the golden ephod went before, the Levites followed after; with trumpeters sounding fanfares"
opt4: "The king and his princes went before, the choir of Korah followed after; accompanied by players of harps"
correct: "The singers went before, the players on instruments followed after; among them were the damsels playing with timbrels."
explanation: The order of the temple procession: choral vocalists leading the way, instrumentalists following behind, flanked by young maidens playing tambourines (timbrels). Psalm 68:25 (KJV) - "The singers went before, the players on instruments followed after; among them were the damsels playing with timbrels."

question: What desperate oceanic and muddy quagmire metaphors describe the suffering servant in Psalm 69:1-2?
opt1: "Save me, O God; for the waters are come in unto my soul. I sink in deep mire, where there is no standing: I am come into deep waters, where the floods overflow me."
opt2: "Deliver me, O Lord; for the storms of the sea compass me about: I fall into a pit of thorns, where none can help;"
opt3: "Hear my cry, O Almighty; for the torrents of Belial overwhelm my spirit: I wander in the desert without a path;"
opt4: "Rescue my life, O God of Jacob; for the waves of death beat upon my head: I sink into the shadow of the grave;"
correct: "Save me, O God; for the waters are come in unto my soul. I sink in deep mire, where there is no standing: I am come into deep waters, where the floods overflow me."
explanation: A portrait of extreme, suffocating crisis: rising floodwaters choking the throat and quicksand-like mire offering zero foothold, sweeping the soul under. Psalm 69:1-2 (KJV) - "Save me, O God; for the waters are come in unto my soul. I sink in deep mire, where there is no standing: I am come into deep waters, where the floods overflow me."

question: Which phrase from Psalm 69:4 did Jesus apply to Himself in John 15:25 regarding the hostility of His opponents?
opt1: "They that speak against me have laid snares in the gate"
opt2: "They that hate me without a cause are more than the hairs of mine head"
opt3: "They that rejoice at my hurt have sharpened their swords"
opt4: "They that compass my dwelling have mocked my prayer"
correct: "They that hate me without a cause are more than the hairs of mine head"
explanation: In John 15:25, Jesus declares that the irrational, unprovoked hatred of the world fulfilled the prophetic word: 'They hated me without a cause'. Psalm 69:4 (KJV) - "They that hate me without a cause are more than the hairs of mine head: they that would destroy me, being mine enemies wrongfully, are mighty: then I restored that which I took not away."

question: Which verse from Psalm 69:9 is applied to Jesus cleansing the Temple (John 2:17) and His vicarious suffering (Romans 15:3)?
opt1: "Because for thy sake I have borne reproach; shame hath covered my face from the congregation;"
opt2: "I am become a stranger unto my brethren, and an alien unto my mother's children;"
opt3: "For the zeal of thine house hath eaten me up; and the reproaches of them that reproached thee are fallen upon me."
opt4: "When I wept, and chastened my soul with fasting, that was to my reproach;"
correct: "For the zeal of thine house hath eaten me up; and the reproaches of them that reproached thee are fallen upon me."
explanation: Consumed by passionate devotion to God's temple, Jesus bore on Himself the ultimate reproaches and blasphemies hurled against God. Psalm 69:9 (KJV) - "For the zeal of thine house hath eaten me up; and the reproaches of them that reproached thee are fallen upon me."

question: How did societal authorities and public carousers mock the psalmist in Psalm 69:12?
opt1: "The elders of the council condemned my words; and the rabble spat upon my garments"
opt2: "The judges at the bench took bribes against me; and the profane made jests in the market"
opt3: "The rulers of the city plotted my death; and the heathen laughed at my fasting"
opt4: "They that sit in the gate speak against me; and I was the song of the drunkards."
correct: "They that sit in the gate speak against me; and I was the song of the drunkards."
explanation: Ostracized by both upper and lower classes: formal civic leaders at the city gate slandered him, while tavern drunkards composed mocking tavern ballads about his grief. Psalm 69:12 (KJV) - "They that sit in the gate speak against me; and I was the song of the drunkards."

question: What prophetic details regarding Christ's crucifixion torment and thirst are recorded in Psalm 69:20-21?
opt1: "Reproach hath broken my heart; and I am full of heaviness: and I looked for some to take pity, but there was none; and for comforters, but I found none. They gave me also gall for my meat; and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink."
opt2: "Sorrow hath crushed my spirit; and my friends stood afar off: they offered me bitter wine in my agony;"
opt3: "Mine enemies pierced my hands; and there was no man to bind up my wounds: they mocked my thirst with water of gall;"
opt4: "The fury of the oppressor consumed my flesh; and all my disciples fled: they pressed vinegar upon my lips in derision;"
correct: "Reproach hath broken my heart; and I am full of heaviness: and I looked for some to take pity, but there was none; and for comforters, but I found none. They gave me also gall for my meat; and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink."
explanation: A startlingly accurate crucifixion prophecy: dying of a ruptured, broken heart without earthly comforters, given bitter gall and sour wine vinegar to drink (Matt 27:34, 48). Psalm 69:20-21 (KJV) - "Reproach hath broken my heart; and I am full of heaviness: and I looked for some to take pity, but there was none; and for comforters, but I found none. They gave me also gall for my meat; and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink."

question: Which imprecation from Psalm 69:25 is cited by the Apostle Peter in Acts 1:20 concerning the desolate fate of Judas Iscariot?
opt1: "Let them be blotted out of the book of the living, and not be written with the righteous;"
opt2: "Let their habitation be desolate; and let none dwell in their tents."
opt3: "Let their eyes be darkened, that they see not; and make their loins continually to shake;"
opt4: "Pour out thine indignation upon them, and let thy wrathful anger take hold of them;"
correct: "Let their habitation be desolate; and let none dwell in their tents."
explanation: Peter cites Psalm 69:25 to justify replacing Judas after his suicide left his habitation and apostolic office desolate (Acts 1:20). Psalm 69:25 (KJV) - "Let their habitation be desolate; and let none dwell in their tents."

question: What terrifying spiritual erasure is pronounced upon obstinate persecutors in Psalm 69:28?
opt1: "Let their names be cast into outer darkness, and their memorial perish from under heaven;"
opt2: "Let their souls be delivered to the tormentors, and their heritage given to the heathen;"
opt3: "Let them be blotted out of the book of the living, and not be written with the righteous."
opt4: "Let their posterity be cut off in a single generation, and their sepulchres be forgotten;"
correct: "Let them be blotted out of the book of the living, and not be written with the righteous."
explanation: The ultimate spiritual judgment: removal from the divine register of the living, forfeiting all covenant blessings among the righteous. Psalm 69:28 (KJV) - "Let them be blotted out of the book of the living, and not be written with the righteous."

question: What spiritual offering pleases the LORD far better than costly animal sacrifices in Psalm 69:30-31?
opt1: "I will offer a contrite heart and broken spirit: this shall please the Almighty more than the blood of ten thousand rams;"
opt2: "I will pay my vows in the congregation of the saints: this shall be sweeter to the Lord than rivers of olive oil;"
opt3: "I will walk in uprightness and execute judgment at the gate: this shall be accepted above whole burnt offerings;"
opt4: "I will praise the name of God with a song, and will magnify him with thanksgiving. This also shall please the LORD better than an ox or bullock that hath horns and hoofs."
correct: "I will praise the name of God with a song, and will magnify him with thanksgiving. This also shall please the LORD better than an ox or bullock that hath horns and hoofs."
explanation: Inward spiritual thanksgiving and heartfelt sung adoration are prized by God above the ritual slaughter of the most pristine mature bullock possessing horns and split hoofs. Psalm 69:30-31 (KJV) - "I will praise the name of God with a song, and will magnify him with thanksgiving. This also shall please the LORD better than an ox or bullock that hath horns and hoofs."

question: What musical tune instruction appears in the superscription of Psalm 69, shared with Psalm 45?
opt1: 'upon Shoshannim' (Lilies)
opt2: 'upon Gittith' (Winepresses)
opt3: 'upon Mahalath' (Sickness)
opt4: 'upon Muth-labben' (Death of the Son)
correct: 'upon Shoshannim' (Lilies)
explanation: 'Shoshannim' means 'Lilies', signifying a lovely, delicate melody associated with sacred beauty and deep emotional expression. Psalm 69:Title (KJV) - "To the chief Musician upon Shoshannim, A Psalm of David."

question: What prominent place does Psalm 69 hold in the New Testament among all the Psalms?
opt1: It is the only Psalm never quoted by any New Testament author
opt2: It is the second most frequently quoted Psalm in the New Testament (surpassed only by Psalm 110), extensively cited regarding the suffering of Christ
opt3: It is cited exclusively in the Book of Revelation regarding the seven trumpets
opt4: It was recited verbatim by Stephen before his martyrdom in Acts 7
correct: It is the second most frequently quoted Psalm in the New Testament (surpassed only by Psalm 110), extensively cited regarding the suffering of Christ
explanation: Because of its intense Messianic typological depth, Psalm 69 is quoted repeatedly across Matthew, John, Romans, and Acts to explain Jesus' rejection, crucifixion, and enemies. Psalm 69:9 (KJV) - "For the zeal of thine house hath eaten me up; and the reproaches of them that reproached thee are fallen upon me."

question: What urgent opening cry for instantaneous divine intervention begins Psalm 70:1?
opt1: "Bow down thine ear, O Lord, and hear my prayer: make no tarrying in the day of trouble;"
opt2: "Make haste, O God, to deliver me; make haste to help me, O LORD."
opt3: "Hearken, O Almighty, unto my weeping: arise quickly to save my soul from the pit;"
opt4: "Look upon my affliction, O God of Jacob: send help from thy holy sanctuary without delay;"
correct: "Make haste, O God, to deliver me; make haste to help me, O LORD."
explanation: David breathes an emergency SOS: repeating the urgent imperative 'Make haste' twice, pleading for immediate rescue from imminent peril. Psalm 70:1 (KJV) - "Make haste, O God, to deliver me; make haste to help me, O LORD."

question: What three forms of defeat does David pray will overtake his malicious pursuers in Psalm 70:2?
opt1: "Let them be scattered like chaff, broken in battle, and blotted out from under the heavens;"
opt2: "Let their chariots sink in the deep mire, their bows be shattered, and their memory perish;"
opt3: "Let them be ashamed and confounded that seek after my soul: let them be turned backward, and put to confusion, that desire my hurt."
opt4: "Let them be smitten with blindness, fall into their own pit, and be consumed by the wrath of God;"
correct: "Let them be ashamed and confounded that seek after my soul: let them be turned backward, and put to confusion, that desire my hurt."
explanation: David prays that his pursuers will suffer humiliating exposure (ashamed), psychological disorientation (confounded), and sudden retreat (turned backward). Psalm 70:2 (KJV) - "Let them be ashamed and confounded that seek after my soul: let them be turned backward, and put to confusion, that desire my hurt."

question: What malicious gloating interjection characterizes the scornful adversaries in Psalm 70:3?
opt1: "that cry, Where is his God?"
opt2: "that boast, We have swallowed him up"
opt3: "that shout, The crown of David is fallen"
opt4: "that say, Aha, aha."
correct: "that say, Aha, aha."
explanation: 'Aha, aha' (Hebrew he'ach, he'ach) is the mocking cry of schadenfreude - gloating over another's tragedy - which God repays with shameful retreat. Psalm 70:3 (KJV) - "Let them be turned back for a reward of their shame that say, Aha, aha."

question: What continual declaration of worship is commanded for those who love God's salvation in Psalm 70:4?
opt1: "Let all those that seek thee rejoice and be glad in thee: and let such as love thy salvation say continually, Let God be magnified."
opt2: "Let the righteous give thanks in the temple: and let the upright declare for ever, The Lord is holy;"
opt3: "Let the seed of Abraham triumph in Zion: and let the humble proclaim without ceasing, God is our shield;"
opt4: "Let all the saints sing praises upon the harp: and let the redeemed shout aloud, Great is the King of glory;"
correct: "Let all those that seek thee rejoice and be glad in thee: and let such as love thy salvation say continually, Let God be magnified."
explanation: While enemies mock with 'Aha, aha', lovers of God's salvation counter with an endless, joyful anthem of adoration: 'Let God be magnified'. Psalm 70:4 (KJV) - "Let all those that seek thee rejoice and be glad in thee: and let such as love thy salvation say continually, Let God be magnified."

question: What humble self-description and concluding plea frame Psalm 70:5?
opt1: "For I am weary of groaning: arise, O Lord of hosts: thou art my fortress and horn of salvation; delay not;"
opt2: "But I am poor and needy: make haste unto me, O God: thou art my help and my deliverer; O LORD, make no tarrying."
opt3: "Behold, I am weak and afflicted: send forth thy light, O Most High: thou art my rock and shield; fail me not;"
opt4: "Seeing my soul is in deep sorrow: stretch out thine arm, O King: thou art my high tower and savior; hear my cry;"
correct: "But I am poor and needy: make haste unto me, O God: thou art my help and my deliverer; O LORD, make no tarrying."
explanation: David strips away all royal pride, identifying as an impoverished beggar ('poor and needy') totally dependent on God, concluding with 'O LORD, make no tarrying'. Psalm 70:5 (KJV) - "But I am poor and needy: make haste unto me, O God: thou art my help and my deliverer; O LORD, make no tarrying."

question: What remarkable relationship exists between Psalm 70 and Psalm 40 in the biblical Psalter?
opt1: Psalm 70 is the mirror opposite of Psalm 40, composed as a curse against Israel
opt2: Psalm 70 was originally the introduction to Psalm 40 before Ezra's compilation
opt3: Psalm 70 is an almost verbatim excerpt of the final five verses of Psalm 40 (Psalm 40:13-17), detached to serve as an independent emergency prayer
opt4: Psalm 70 was written by Asaph, while Psalm 40 was composed by Moses
correct: Psalm 70 is an almost verbatim excerpt of the final five verses of Psalm 40 (Psalm 40:13-17), detached to serve as an independent emergency prayer
explanation: Psalm 70 reproduces Psalm 40:13-17 with minor variations (predominantly substituting Elohim for Yahweh), providing a standalone pocket-liturgy for sudden crises. Psalm 70:1 (KJV) - "Make haste, O God, to deliver me; make haste to help me, O LORD."

question: What is the liturgical purpose specified by the phrase 'to bring to remembrance' in the title of Psalm 70?
opt1: To remind King Solomon of the promises made to his father David
opt2: A historical commemoration chanted on the anniversary of the Exodus
opt3: A mnemonic poem taught to young Levitical apprentices
opt4: To serve as a memorial prayer accompanying the Azkarah (memorial portion of the grain offering, Lev 2:2) to remind God of His covenant mercy
correct: To serve as a memorial prayer accompanying the Azkarah (memorial portion of the grain offering, Lev 2:2) to remind God of His covenant mercy
explanation: 'Lehazkir' ('to bring to remembrance') links this psalm directly to the altar's memorial sacrifice, presenting the believer's desperate crisis before God's memory. Psalm 70:Title (KJV) - "To the chief Musician, A Psalm of David, to bring to remembrance."

question: What Hebrew imperative is translated 'make haste' in Psalm 70:1 and 70:5?
opt1: Hushah (hurry, hasten quickly)
opt2: Qumah (arise)
opt3: Shama (hear)
opt4: Hoshiah (save now)
correct: Hushah (hurry, hasten quickly)
explanation: The frantic cry hushah reflects an emergency where even a moment's delay could prove fatal, begging God to arrive without pausing. Psalm 70:1, 5 (KJV) - "Make haste, O God, to deliver me ... make haste unto me, O God ... make no tarrying."

question: How does the confession 'thou art my help and my deliverer' in Psalm 70:5 anchor the soul in crisis?
opt1: It claims that David's armies are supported by Egyptian mercenaries
opt2: It confesses that God is not merely one helper among many, but the exclusive Source (Ezri) and Rescuer (Mepalti) of the saint
opt3: It reminds the high priest to offer daily animal sacrifices
opt4: It asserts that angels will fight without human involvement
correct: It confesses that God is not merely one helper among many, but the exclusive Source (Ezri) and Rescuer (Mepalti) of the saint
explanation: Calling God 'my help' (Ezri) and 'my deliverer' (Mepalti) places absolute trust in God's personal character rather than circumstances. Psalm 70:5 (KJV) - "thou art my help and my deliverer; O LORD, make no tarrying."

question: What contrasting vocal responses are juxtaposed in verses 3 and 4 of Psalm 70?
opt1: The weeping of the mourners versus the shouting of the warriors
opt2: The silence of the grave versus the music of the golden harp
opt3: The contemptuous sneer of the ungodly ('Aha, aha') versus the glorious perpetual doxology of the faithful ('Let God be magnified')
opt4: The cursing of the false witnesses versus the blessing of the high priest
correct: The contemptuous sneer of the ungodly ('Aha, aha') versus the glorious perpetual doxology of the faithful ('Let God be magnified')
explanation: A stark poetic contrast between the brief, malicious cackle of persecutors ('Aha, aha') and the eternal, magnificent anthem of the redeemed ('Let God be magnified'). Psalm 70:3-4 (KJV) - "Let them be turned back for a reward of their shame that say, Aha, aha. Let all those that seek thee rejoice and be glad in thee: and let such as love thy salvation say continually, Let God be magnified."

question: What foundational confession of trust and prayer for refuge opens Psalm 71:1-3?
opt1: "I cried unto the Lord in my youth, and he heard my supplication: be thou my shield of defense; for thou art my salvation;"
opt2: "Preserve me, O Almighty, from the snare of the hunter: be thou my hiding place in Zion; for thou hast broken the enemy;"
opt3: "In thee, O LORD, do I put my trust: let me never be put to confusion ... Be thou my strong habitation, whereunto I may continually resort: thou hast given commandment to save me; for thou art my rock and my fortress."
opt4: "Unto thee lift I up mine eyes, O King of Israel: be thou my tower of safety; for thy commandment is light;"
correct: "In thee, O LORD, do I put my trust: let me never be put to confusion ... Be thou my strong habitation, whereunto I may continually resort: thou hast given commandment to save me; for thou art my rock and my fortress."
explanation: The aging psalmist views God as a 'strong habitation' - a home to which he may continually retreat anytime, resting on God's sovereign decree to save him. Psalm 71:1, 3 (KJV) - "In thee, O LORD, do I put my trust: let me never be put to confusion ... Be thou my strong habitation, whereunto I may continually resort: thou hast given commandment to save me; for thou art my rock and my fortress."

question: How does the psalmist describe God's providential care over his entire lifespan in Psalm 71:5-6?
opt1: "For from my childhood hast thou taught me thy law: thou hast sheltered my footsteps from every pit: my tongue shall magnify thee;"
opt2: "For thou gavest me strength in the days of battle: thou didst anoint my head with holy oil: my soul shall bless thy name;"
opt3: "For the covenant of Abraham was upon my flesh: thou broughtest me through the wilderness: my mouth shall show forth thy truth;"
opt4: "For thou art my hope, O Lord GOD: thou art my trust from my youth. By thee have I been holden up from the womb: thou art he that took me out of my mother's bowels: my praise shall be continually of thee."
correct: "For thou art my hope, O Lord GOD: thou art my trust from my youth. By thee have I been holden up from the womb: thou art he that took me out of my mother's bowels: my praise shall be continually of thee."
explanation: Lifelong divine fidelity: God has been the psalmist's personal trust from boyhood, sustaining him from the womb and guiding his infant birth. Psalm 71:5-6 (KJV) - "For thou art my hope, O Lord GOD: thou art my trust from my youth. By thee have I been holden up from the womb: thou art he that took me out of my mother's bowels: my praise shall be continually of thee."

question: What mysterious spectacle has the psalmist become to observers in Psalm 71:7?
opt1: "I am as a wonder unto many; but thou art my strong refuge."
opt2: "I am as a sign of mourning to the tribes of Israel"
opt3: "I am become an outcast among mine own brethren"
opt4: "I am counted as a stranger in the gates of Jerusalem"
correct: "I am as a wonder unto many; but thou art my strong refuge."
explanation: The Hebrew mopheth means a sign, portending wonder or spectacle: onlookers marvelled at how one man could survive such relentless, crushing ordeals, protected solely by God. Psalm 71:7 (KJV) - "I am as a wonder unto many; but thou art my strong refuge."

question: What poignant prayer of the aging believer against abandonment is recorded in Psalm 71:9?
opt1: "Forget me not when my hair is grey; and leave me not to the cruelty of the adversary"
opt2: "Cast me not off in the time of old age; forsake me not when my strength faileth."
opt3: "Remove not thy mercy when my steps are weak; and hide not thy face when mine eyes grow dim"
opt4: "Depart not from my dwelling in the evening of life; and preserve my soul from the fear of death"
correct: "Cast me not off in the time of old age; forsake me not when my strength faileth."
explanation: A classic prayer of aging saints: conscious of failing physical stamina and waning vitality, the believer pleads for God's abiding covenant presence. Psalm 71:9 (KJV) - "Cast me not off in the time of old age; forsake me not when my strength faileth."

question: What opportunistic conspiracy do enemies plot against the vulnerable elder in Psalm 71:10-11?
opt1: "Saying, His strength is gone: let us plunder his house and divide his inheritance;"
opt2: "Saying, The king cannot reign in his infirmity: let us set his crown upon the younger prince;"
opt3: "Saying, God hath forsaken him: persecute and take him; for there is none to deliver him."
opt4: "Saying, He is stricken of the Almighty: let us cast him out of the city gates;"
correct: "Saying, God hath forsaken him: persecute and take him; for there is none to deliver him."
explanation: Cruel adversaries mistake physical aging and weakness for divine abandonment, plotting a predatory strike because they assume God will not intervene. Psalm 71:11 (KJV) - "Saying, God hath forsaken him: persecute and take him; for there is none to deliver him."

question: Why cannot the psalmist fully enumerate God's righteousness and salvation in Psalm 71:15?
opt1: "for my memory faileth in mine old age"
opt2: "for the scroll of the covenant is sealed"
opt3: "for mortal tongue cannot speak the language of angels"
opt4: "for I know not the numbers thereof."
correct: "for I know not the numbers thereof."
explanation: God's saving mercies and righteous deeds are literally infinite, defying human arithmetic and exceeding all computational capacity. Psalm 71:15 (KJV) - "My mouth shall shew forth thy righteousness and thy salvation all the day; for I know not the numbers thereof."

question: What sole moral righteousness will the psalmist mention as he goes forth in Psalm 71:16?
opt1: "I will go in the strength of the Lord GOD: I will make mention of thy righteousness, even of thine only."
opt2: "I will boast of the covenant of David, and the integrity of my hands in the sanctuary"
opt3: "I will declare the statutes of Moses, and my faithful walking before the holy ark"
opt4: "I will proclaim the victories of Israel, and the valor of our captains in battle"
correct: "I will go in the strength of the Lord GOD: I will make mention of thy righteousness, even of thine only."
explanation: Renouncing all self-righteousness, the psalmist relies solely on the power of Adonai Yahweh, exalting God's imputed righteousness alone. Psalm 71:16 (KJV) - "I will go in the strength of the Lord GOD: I will make mention of thy righteousness, even of thine only."

question: What intergenerational mission drives the aging saint's request for preservation in Psalm 71:18?
opt1: "Preserve my life, O Lord, that I may build a house of cedar for the ark of thy covenant"
opt2: "Now also when I am old and greyheaded, O God, forsake me not; until I have shewed thy strength unto this generation, and thy power to every one that is to come."
opt3: "Spare my soul, O Almighty, until I see the children of my sons inherit the land of promise"
opt4: "Hold up my hands, O God of Jacob, until the armies of the heathen are utterly destroyed"
correct: "Now also when I am old and greyheaded, O God, forsake me not; until I have shewed thy strength unto this generation, and thy power to every one that is to come."
explanation: The noble goal of Christian longevity: living long enough to transmit the testimony of God's omnipotence and covenant faithfulness to the next generation and future posterity. Psalm 71:18 (KJV) - "Now also when I am old and greyheaded, O God, forsake me not; until I have shewed thy strength unto this generation, and thy power to every one that is to come."

question: What hope of personal revival and subterranean resurrection is confessed in Psalm 71:20?
opt1: "Though my body fall into the pit, yet shalt thou raise my bones in the morning of Zion"
opt2: "Though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, thy rod and staff shall comfort me"
opt3: "Thou, which hast shewed me great and sore troubles, shalt quicken me again, and shalt bring me up again from the depths of the earth."
opt4: "Even when my flesh rotters in the dust, the breath of the Almighty shall restore my spirit"
correct: "Thou, which hast shewed me great and sore troubles, shalt quicken me again, and shalt bring me up again from the depths of the earth."
explanation: A shining declaration of revival and resurrection: though plunged into the deepest abyss of suffering, God will quicken (revive) the saint and bring him up from subterranean depths. Psalm 71:20 (KJV) - "Thou, which hast shewed me great and sore troubles, shalt quicken me again, and shalt bring me up again from the depths of the earth."

question: What two musical instruments will accompany the psalmist's praise to the 'Holy One of Israel' in Psalm 71:22?
opt1: The silver trumpet and the ram's horn
opt2: The timbrel and the high sounding cymbals
opt3: The ten-stringed lute and the double flute
opt4: The psaltery and the harp
