correct: The psaltery and the harp
explanation: David pairs the plucked stringed psaltery (nevel) and harp (kinnor) to sing praises to Yahweh, using the rare Title 'Holy One of Israel'. Psalm 71:22 (KJV) - "I will also praise thee with the psaltery, even thy truth, O my God: unto thee will I sing with the harp, O thou Holy One of Israel."

question: What opening petition seeks divine justice and righteousness for the royal dynasty in Psalm 72:1-2?
opt1: "Grant wisdom unto the son of David, O Lord, and length of days unto the king: that he may build thy temple;"
opt2: "Establish the throne of Solomon in peace, O God, and his kingdom above the heathen: that he may judge uprightly;"
opt3: "Anoint the king with the horn of salvation, O Most High, and give him victory: that the poor may rejoice;"
opt4: "Give the king thy judgments, O God, and thy righteousness unto the king's son. He shall judge thy people with righteousness, and thy poor with judgment."
correct: "Give the king thy judgments, O God, and thy righteousness unto the king's son. He shall judge thy people with righteousness, and thy poor with judgment."
explanation: A royal prayer for Solomon and ultimately the Messianic Son of David, praying that divine justice and moral equity characterize His administration. Psalm 72:1-2 (KJV) - "Give the king thy judgments, O God, and thy righteousness unto the king's son. He shall judge thy people with righteousness, and thy poor with judgment."

question: How does the King champion the cause of the socially oppressed in Psalm 72:4?
opt1: "He shall judge the poor of the people, he shall save the children of the needy, and shall break in pieces the oppressor."
opt2: "He will distribute bread to the hungry, cloth the fatherless, and banish the unrighteous ruler;"
opt3: "He shall build shelters for the destitute, protect the widow, and overthrow the tables of usurers;"
opt4: "He will plead the cause of the afflicted at the gate, deliver the captive, and destroy the proud;"
correct: "He shall judge the poor of the people, he shall save the children of the needy, and shall break in pieces the oppressor."
explanation: The Messianic King demonstrates His true glory not by pampering elites, but by defending the vulnerable, saving impoverished children, and pulverizing tyrannical oppressors. Psalm 72:4 (KJV) - "He shall judge the poor of the people, he shall save the children of the needy, and shall break in pieces the oppressor."

question: What gentle agricultural simile portrays the refreshing, life-giving descent of the King's reign in Psalm 72:6?
opt1: "His presence shall be as the morning sun upon the fruitful vines: as dew upon the lilies of Sharon"
opt2: "He shall come down like rain upon the mown grass: as showers that water the earth."
opt3: "His words shall drop as honey from the comb: as living streams in the dry desert"
opt4: "His righteousness shall blossom like the olive tree: as the fragrance of Lebanon after the storm"
correct: "He shall come down like rain upon the mown grass: as showers that water the earth."
explanation: Mown meadow grass is freshly clipped and vulnerable to scorching heat; the King's reign descends upon parched humanity like tender soaking rain showers, sparking immediate lush regeneration. Psalm 72:6 (KJV) - "He shall come down like rain upon the mown grass: as showers that water the earth."

question: What global geographic boundaries define the King's universal empire in Psalm 72:8?
opt1: "He shall govern all nations from Dan to Beersheba, and from the Jordan unto the Great Sea"
opt2: "His kingdom shall extend from the river of Egypt to the Euphrates, and over all the islands"
opt3: "He shall have dominion also from sea to sea, and from the river unto the ends of the earth."
opt4: "He shall rule from the mountains of Lebanon to the wilderness of Zin, and unto the ends of heaven"
correct: "He shall have dominion also from sea to sea, and from the river unto the ends of the earth."
explanation: A worldwide Messianic dominion: spanning ocean to ocean and from the river Euphrates to the uttermost peripheries of the globe (prophetically quoted in Zech 9:10). Psalm 72:8 (KJV) - "He shall have dominion also from sea to sea, and from the river unto the ends of the earth."

question: Which international monarchs bring royal tribute and bow before the King in Psalm 72:10-11?
opt1: "The pharaohs of Egypt and the princes of Tyre shall offer gold: the kings of Babylon shall lay down their sceptres;"
opt2: "The rulers of Syria and the lords of the Philistines shall send tribute: the kings of Edom shall bow at his footstool;"
opt3: "The princes of Cush and the merchants of Damascus shall present spices: all empires shall worship before his throne;"
opt4: "The kings of Tarshish and of the isles shall bring presents: the kings of Sheba and Seba shall offer gifts. Yea, all kings shall fall down before him: all nations shall serve him."
correct: "The kings of Tarshish and of the isles shall bring presents: the kings of Sheba and Seba shall offer gifts. Yea, all kings shall fall down before him: all nations shall serve him."
explanation: From the western Mediterranean maritime outposts (Tarshish) to wealthy southern Arabian empires (Sheba and Seba), all global monarchs prostrate before Him (prefiguring the Magi, Matt 2:11). Psalm 72:10-11 (KJV) - "The kings of Tarshish and of the isles shall bring presents: the kings of Sheba and Seba shall offer gifts. Yea, all kings shall fall down before him: all nations shall serve him."

question: How precious is the life and blood of the poor in the King's sight in Psalm 72:14?
opt1: "He shall redeem their soul from deceit and violence: and precious shall their blood be in his sight."
opt2: "He will avenge their affliction upon the oppressor: and their tears shall be gathered in his bottle"
opt3: "He shall preserve their footsteps from the pit: and their names shall be written in gold upon his palace"
opt4: "He will ransom their children from the sword: and their inheritance shall be established for ever"
correct: "He shall redeem their soul from deceit and violence: and precious shall their blood be in his sight."
explanation: Worldly tyrants treat the poor as cheap, expendable cannon fodder; the Messianic King values the life and blood of the humblest needy soul as infinitely precious. Psalm 72:14 (KJV) - "He shall redeem their soul from deceit and violence: and precious shall their blood be in his sight."

question: What miraculous agricultural fertility on mountain summits is envisioned in Psalm 72:16?
opt1: "A single vineyard planted upon the barren hill shall yield ten thousand measures of sweet wine;"
opt2: "There shall be an handful of corn in the earth upon the top of the mountains; the fruit thereof shall shake like Lebanon: and they of the city shall flourish like grass of the earth."
opt3: "The desert mountain shall be terraced with olive trees; and the valleys shall overflow with golden grain;"
opt4: "The stony rocks shall blossom with pomegranates and figs; and the streets of Jerusalem shall be full of rejoicing;"
correct: "There shall be an handful of corn in the earth upon the top of the mountains; the fruit thereof shall shake like Lebanon: and they of the city shall flourish like grass of the earth."
explanation: Hyperbolic supernatural abundance: a mere handful of seed cast on the least fertile terrain (barren rock-tops of mountains) explodes into a harvest waving like the towering cedar forests of Lebanon. Psalm 72:16 (KJV) - "There shall be an handful of corn in the earth upon the top of the mountains; the fruit thereof shall shake like Lebanon: and they of the city shall flourish like grass of the earth."

question: What eternal durability of the King's Name and universal blessing conclude Psalm 72:17?
opt1: "His throne shall outlast the stars of heaven: his crown shall never fade: and the earth shall be full of his fame;"
opt2: "His kingdom shall know no end: his statutes shall govern the nations: and all tribes shall glorify his power;"
opt3: "His name shall endure for ever: his name shall be continued as long as the sun: and men shall be blessed in him: all nations shall call him blessed."
opt4: "His righteousness shall shine throughout all generations: his seed shall inherit the earth: and the righteous shall triumph;"
correct: "His name shall endure for ever: his name shall be continued as long as the sun: and men shall be blessed in him: all nations shall call him blessed."
explanation: The ultimate fulfillment of the Abrahamic covenant: the King's Name endures as long as the sun, and all nations find eternal beatitude and blessing in Him (Gen 22:18). Psalm 72:17 (KJV) - "His name shall endure for ever: his name shall be continued as long as the sun: and men shall be blessed in him: all nations shall call him blessed."

question: What grand doxology concludes Book II of the Psalter in Psalm 72:18-19?
opt1: "Glory be to Yahweh Sabaoth, the Holy One of Jacob: let the heavens declare his praise, and the earth shout for joy; Amen;"
opt2: "Praise the Lord our King from everlasting to everlasting: let all flesh bless his holy sanctuary; Hallelujah, Amen;"
opt3: "Exalted be the God of our salvation throughout all generations: let the congregation of Zion worship; Amen, and Amen;"
opt4: "Blessed be the LORD God, the God of Israel, who only doeth wondrous things. And blessed be his glorious name for ever: and let the whole earth be filled with his glory; Amen, and Amen."
correct: "Blessed be the LORD God, the God of Israel, who only doeth wondrous things. And blessed be his glorious name for ever: and let the whole earth be filled with his glory; Amen, and Amen."
explanation: The solemn concluding doxology of Book II (Psalms 42-72), sealing the royal Messianic vision with a double 'Amen, and Amen' and praying that God's glory fill the entire cosmos. Psalm 72:18-19 (KJV) - "Blessed be the LORD God, the God of Israel, who only doeth wondrous things. And blessed be his glorious name for ever: and let the whole earth be filled with his glory; Amen, and Amen."

question: What historical editorial note marks the conclusion of Book II of the Psalter in Psalm 72:20?
opt1: "The prayers of David the son of Jesse are ended."
opt2: "Thus far are the words of the sweet psalmist of Israel"
opt3: "Here endeth the second book of the psalms of the sanctuary"
opt4: "These are the royal prayers written for Solomon the king"
correct: "The prayers of David the son of Jesse are ended."
explanation: This historic colophon indicates the close of the original Davidic collection that formed the core of Book II of the Psalter. Psalm 72:20 (KJV) - "The prayers of David the son of Jesse are ended."

question: What core theological axiom opens Psalm 73:1, and what near-fatal spiritual crisis followed in verses 2-3?
opt1: "Truly God is good to Israel, even to such as are of a clean heart. But as for me, my feet were almost gone; my steps had well nigh slipped. For I was envious at the foolish, when I saw the prosperity of the wicked."
opt2: "The Lord is righteous in all his ways: yet my heart grew faint within me when the heathen conquered Zion;"
opt3: "Great is the Holy One of Jacob: but my faith was shaken when the righteous fell by the sword;"
opt4: "Verily God judgeth the earth: yet I stumbled in darkness when the ungodly multiplied their gold;"
correct: "Truly God is good to Israel, even to such as are of a clean heart. But as for me, my feet were almost gone; my steps had well nigh slipped. For I was envious at the foolish, when I saw the prosperity of the wicked."
explanation: Opening Book III of the Psalter, Asaph affirms God's goodness to the pure in heart, yet confesses he nearly suffered total apostasy through bitter envy over the worldly prosperity of the wicked. Psalm 73:1-3 (KJV) - "Truly God is good to Israel, even to such as are of a clean heart. But as for me, my feet were almost gone; my steps had well nigh slipped. For I was envious at the foolish, when I saw the prosperity of the wicked."

question: How does Asaph describe the apparent health, peaceful death, and trouble-free existence of the ungodly in Psalm 73:4-5?
opt1: "Their youth fadeth not: their sepulchres are adorned with marble: they taste not the cup of sorrow;"
opt2: "For there are no bands in their death: but their strength is firm. They are not in trouble as other men; neither are they plagued like other men."
opt3: "They lie down in sweet sleep without fear: their cattle multiply: and no pestilence cometh nigh their tent;"
opt4: "Their days are prolonged in honor: they die in peace without pain: neither doth sickness touch their children;"
correct: "For there are no bands in their death: but their strength is firm. They are not in trouble as other men; neither are they plagued like other men."
explanation: The wicked often appear to enjoy robust vitality and die tranquil deaths ('no bands [pains] in their death'), completely insulated from the crushing hardships common to ordinary mortals. Psalm 73:4-5 (KJV) - "For there are no bands in their death: but their strength is firm. They are not in trouble as other men; neither are they plagued like other men."

question: What cosmic arrogance characterizes the speech and strutting blasphemy of the wicked in Psalm 73:8-9?
opt1: "They mock the law of God, and boast in their chariots: they say, The Almighty seeth not in the dark;"
opt2: "Their lips are full of cursing and deceit: they roar like lions against Zion, defying heaven;"
opt3: "They are corrupt, and speak wickedly concerning oppression: they speak loftily. They set their mouth against the heavens, and their tongue walketh through the earth."
opt4: "They blaspheme the holy ark, and plot treason at the gate: their words are sharper than iron swords;"
correct: "They are corrupt, and speak wickedly concerning oppression: they speak loftily. They set their mouth against the heavens, and their tongue walketh through the earth."
explanation: Boundless egotism: their arrogant mouths dictate to heaven itself, while their boastful tongues strut unimpeded across the terrestrial globe. Psalm 73:8-9 (KJV) - "They are corrupt, and speak wickedly concerning oppression: they speak loftily. They set their mouth against the heavens, and their tongue walketh through the earth."

question: What temporary cynical conclusion regarding personal holiness did Asaph entertain in Psalm 73:13-14?
opt1: "Surely my fasting hath been forgotten, and my sacrifices rejected: for the Lord hath cast me off in anger;"
opt2: "Lo, I have walked uprightly for nought, and kept the commandments without reward: for sorrow compasseth my bed;"
opt3: "Behold, my prayers are empty breath, and my tears have brought no deliverer: for the heathen prosper in their sin;"
opt4: "Verily I have cleansed my heart in vain, and washed my hands in innocency. For all the day long have I been plagued, and chastened every morning."
correct: "Verily I have cleansed my heart in vain, and washed my hands in innocency. For all the day long have I been plagued, and chastened every morning."
explanation: Observing wicked men thrive while he suffered constant daily chastening, Asaph was tempted to conclude that pursuing moral purity and ethical innocence was a complete waste of effort. Psalm 73:13-14 (KJV) - "Verily I have cleansed my heart in vain, and washed my hands in innocency. For all the day long have I been plagued, and chastened every morning."

question: What decisive turning point resolved Asaph's agonizing crisis of faith in Psalm 73:16-17?
opt1: "When I thought to know this, it was too painful for me; Until I went into the sanctuary of God; then understood I their end."
opt2: "When I consulted the elders of Israel, they could not answer; until the prophet Nathan revealed the secret;"
opt3: "When I pondered the scroll of the covenant, my soul was dark; until a voice from heaven broke the silence;"
opt4: "When I searched the wisdom of Egypt, my mind was troubled; until I offered burnt offerings upon the altar;"
correct: "When I thought to know this, it was too painful for me; Until I went into the sanctuary of God; then understood I their end."
explanation: Human philosophy and analytical reason failed ('too painful for me') until Asaph entered God's holy sanctuary, where eternal perspective unveiled the terrifying, abrupt end of the ungodly. Psalm 73:16-17 (KJV) - "When I thought to know this, it was too painful for me; Until I went into the sanctuary of God; then understood I their end."

question: What precarious reality and sudden catastrophic doom overtake the prosperous wicked in Psalm 73:18-19?
opt1: "Thou hast digged a pit beneath their feet: thou hast sent fire upon their dwelling in a moment;"
opt2: "Surely thou didst set them in slippery places: thou castedst them down into destruction. How are they brought into desolation, as in a moment! they are utterly consumed with terrors."
opt3: "The tempest of the Lord shall scatter them: in the twinkling of an eye shall their riches perish;"
opt4: "Thou hast bound their limbs in chains of iron: they shall be dragged down into Sheol before their time;"
correct: "Surely thou didst set them in slippery places: thou castedst them down into destruction. How are they brought into desolation, as in a moment! they are utterly consumed with terrors."
explanation: Worldly prosperity is not a solid foundation but a grease-slicked precipice ('slippery places'); in a single sudden moment, they plunge into ruin, completely consumed with panic. Psalm 73:18-19 (KJV) - "Surely thou didst set them in slippery places: thou castedst them down into destruction. How are they brought into desolation, as in a moment! they are utterly consumed with terrors."

question: How does Asaph severely rebuke his own prior bitter, short-sighted perspective in Psalm 73:21-22?
opt1: "My soul wept in darkness, and my eyes were blinded: I was as a rebellious child before the Holy One;"
opt2: "My tongue uttered vanity, and my thoughts were deceitful: I was as dry stubble before the flame;"
opt3: "Thus my heart was grieved, and I was pricked in my reins. So foolish was I, and ignorant: I was as a beast before thee."
opt4: "My spirit was hardened in pride, and I walked in darkness: I was as an unlearned stranger in Zion;"
correct: "Thus my heart was grieved, and I was pricked in my reins. So foolish was I, and ignorant: I was as a beast before thee."
explanation: Asaph repents of his resentful cynicism, acknowledging that questioning God's providence was stupid, irrational, and beast-like ('as a beast before thee'). Psalm 73:21-22 (KJV) - "Thus my heart was grieved, and I was pricked in my reins. So foolish was I, and ignorant: I was as a beast before thee."

question: What glorious assurance of lifelong guidance and eternal reception is confessed in Psalm 73:23-24?
opt1: "Yet the Lord is my shepherd in every path: he will lead me into green pastures, and crown me with life;"
opt2: "For the Almighty campeth around my soul: he shall teach me his statutes, and give me an everlasting kingdom;"
opt3: "Verily his lovingkindness shall follow my footsteps: he will preserve my life from the pit, and show me his salvation;"
opt4: "Nevertheless I am continually with thee: thou hast holden me by my right hand. Thou shalt guide me with thy counsel, and afterward receive me to glory."
correct: "Nevertheless I am continually with thee: thou hast holden me by my right hand. Thou shalt guide me with thy counsel, and afterward receive me to glory."
explanation: A pinnacle of biblical assurance: God holds the saint by the right hand, navigates mortal life through His wise counsel, and ultimately receives the believer into eternal celestial glory. Psalm 73:23-24 (KJV) - "Nevertheless I am continually with thee: thou hast holden me by my right hand. Thou shalt guide me with thy counsel, and afterward receive me to glory."

question: What supreme devotional confession of God as the soul's all-sufficient eternal portion crowns Psalm 73:25-26?
opt1: "Whom have I in heaven but thee? and there is none upon earth that I desire beside thee. My flesh and my heart faileth: but God is the strength of my heart, and my portion for ever."
opt2: "The Lord is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? the Almighty is the rock of my refuge;"
opt3: "One thing have I desired of the Lord, that will I seek after; to dwell in his holy courts all my days;"
opt4: "The Lord of hosts is my shield and my reward: though the mountains fall into the sea, I shall not be moved;"
correct: "Whom have I in heaven but thee? and there is none upon earth that I desire beside thee. My flesh and my heart faileth: but God is the strength of my heart, and my portion for ever."
explanation: The ultimate statement of pure spiritual devotion: when physical strength and emotions fail, God Himself remains the unshakable rock of the heart and the eternal inheritance. Psalm 73:25-26 (KJV) - "Whom have I in heaven but thee? and there is none upon earth that I desire beside thee. My flesh and my heart faileth: but God is the strength of my heart, and my portion for ever."

question: What practical conclusion regarding personal spiritual discipline concludes Psalm 73:28?
opt1: "Therefore will I offer sacrifices in the temple, and keep the commandments of the Most High all my days;"
opt2: "But it is good for me to draw near to God: I have put my trust in the Lord GOD, that I may declare all thy works."
opt3: "And I will sing of his righteousness before the congregation, and bless his holy name for ever;"
opt4: "So shall my soul rest in the shadow of his wings, and wait patiently for the day of judgment;"
correct: "But it is good for me to draw near to God: I have put my trust in the Lord GOD, that I may declare all thy works."
explanation: The resolution of the crisis: drawing near to God is the highest good, anchoring trust in Adonai Yahweh so as to proclaim His righteous works to the world. Psalm 73:28 (KJV) - "But it is good for me to draw near to God: I have put my trust in the Lord GOD, that I may declare all thy works."

question: What national lament over perceived abandonment and divine anger opens Psalm 74:1?
opt1: "How long, O Lord, wilt thou forget thy chosen seed? why hast thou delivered Zion into the hand of the enemy;"
opt2: "O God, why hast thou cast us off for ever? why doth thine anger smoke against the sheep of thy pasture?"
opt3: "Why standest thou afar off, O God of hosts? why hidest thou thy face in the time of great trouble;"
opt4: "Awake, O King of Israel, why sleepest thou? why dost thou suffer the heathen to trample thy courts;"
correct: "O God, why hast thou cast us off for ever? why doth thine anger smoke against the sheep of thy pasture?"
explanation: The congregation bewails national destruction under the graphic image of God's burning wrath smoking against His own covenant flock. Psalm 74:1 (KJV) - "O God, why hast thou cast us off for ever? why doth thine anger smoke against the sheep of thy pasture?"

question: What barbaric vandalism and demolition of the temple's carved woodwork is described in Psalm 74:5-6?
opt1: "The cedar beams of Lebanon were fashioned by wise craftsmen: but the heathen have burned them with fire;"
opt2: "They brought iron battering rams against the sanctuary gates, and shattered the golden doors into dust;"
opt3: "A man was famous according as he had lifted up axes upon the thick trees. But now they break down the carved work thereof at once with axes and hammers."
opt4: "The pillars of bronze were carried away to Babylon, and the cherubim broken with iron crowbars;"
correct: "A man was famous according as he had lifted up axes upon the thick trees. But now they break down the carved work thereof at once with axes and hammers."
explanation: While ancient woodsmen gained renown for felling forest timber, ruthless invaders attacked the temple's intricate carved woodwork like common lumberjacks, smashing it with axes and hammers. Psalm 74:5-6 (KJV) - "A man was famous according as he had lifted up axes upon the thick trees. But now they break down the carved work thereof at once with axes and hammers."

question: What total incineration of sacred sites throughout the land is lamented in Psalm 74:7-8?
opt1: "They burned the holy of holies with sulfur, and overturned the altar: they left no stone standing in Jerusalem;"
opt2: "They consumed the courts with flames, and mocked the priests: they plundered all the golden vessels of Zion;"
opt3: "The torch of the Babylonian consumed the tabernacle: they leveled every high place and burned the Torah scrolls;"
opt4: "They have cast fire into thy sanctuary, they have defiled by casting down the dwelling place of thy name to the ground. They said in their hearts, Let us destroy them together: they have burned up all the synagogues of God in the land."
correct: "They have cast fire into thy sanctuary, they have defiled by casting down the dwelling place of thy name to the ground. They said in their hearts, Let us destroy them together: they have burned up all the synagogues of God in the land."
explanation: A systematic scorched-earth destruction: torching the temple sanctuary to ashes and incinerating all local meeting houses of worship ('synagogues of God') throughout Judea. Psalm 74:7-8 (KJV) - "They have cast fire into thy sanctuary, they have defiled by casting down the dwelling place of thy name to the ground. They said in their hearts, Let us destroy them together: they have burned up all the synagogues of God in the land."

question: What devastating spiritual famine and loss of prophetic revelation is bewailing in Psalm 74:9?
opt1: "We see not our signs: there is no more any prophet: neither is there among us any that knoweth how long."
opt2: "The ark of the covenant is taken: the Urim and Thummim give no answer: and our priests weep in silence;"
opt3: "No vision cometh from heaven: the elders have forgotten the statutes: and none can interpret the dreams of the king;"
opt4: "The voice of the Lord is silent in Zion: the angels have departed: and no man knoweth the day of redemption;"
correct: "We see not our signs: there is no more any prophet: neither is there among us any that knoweth how long."
explanation: The ultimate grief of the exile: miraculous signs ceased, the prophetic voice fell silent, and nobody was left to tell the people how long the dark catastrophe would endure. Psalm 74:9 (KJV) - "We see not our signs: there is no more any prophet: neither is there among us any that knoweth how long."

question: What graphic mythological and historical imagery depicts God crushing Egypt at the Red Sea in Psalm 74:13-14?
opt1: "Thou didst drown Pharaoh and his chariots in the deep: thou smotest the sea monster of the Nile with thy sword;"
opt2: "Thou didst divide the sea by thy strength: thou brakest the heads of the dragons in the waters. Thou brakest the heads of leviathan in pieces, and gavest him to be meat to the people inhabiting the wilderness."
opt3: "Thou shatteredst the strength of Rahab with an east wind: thou gavest the carcasses of Egypt to the fowls of the air;"
opt4: "Thou cuttest Rahab in pieces, and woundedst the crocodile: thou threwest their captains into the depths of the sea;"
correct: "Thou didst divide the sea by thy strength: thou brakest the heads of the dragons in the waters. Thou brakest the heads of leviathan in pieces, and gavest him to be meat to the people inhabiting the wilderness."
explanation: Poetic historical typology: dividing the Red Sea, crushing the multi-headed sea-monster / Leviathan (symbolizing Pharaoh and the Egyptian empire), leaving their corpses as scavenger meat. Psalm 74:13-14 (KJV) - "Thou didst divide the sea by thy strength: thou brakest the heads of the dragons in the waters. Thou brakest the heads of leviathan in pieces, and gavest him to be meat to the people inhabiting the wilderness."

question: What cosmic authority over day, night, and seasons is proclaimed in Psalm 74:16-17?
opt1: "Thou rulest over the heavens, and the earth is thy footstool: thou commandest the stars and the moon in their courses;"
opt2: "By thy word the dawn appeareth, and the darkness fleeth away: thou governest the harvest and the rainy season;"
opt3: "The day is thine, the night also is thine: thou hast prepared the light and the sun. Thou hast set all the borders of the earth: thou hast made summer and winter."
opt4: "The universe is established by thy power: thou measutest the mountains in scales, and the waters in the hollow of thy hand;"
correct: "The day is thine, the night also is thine: thou hast prepared the light and the sun. Thou hast set all the borders of the earth: thou hast made summer and winter."
explanation: Faith anchors in the cosmic Creator: the God who ordered solar rhythms, global geography, and cyclical seasons of summer and winter will surely maintain His covenant promises. Psalm 74:16-17 (KJV) - "The day is thine, the night also is thine: thou hast prepared the light and the sun. Thou hast set all the borders of the earth: thou hast made summer and winter."

question: Under what defenseless avian metaphor does the psalmist plead for God's vulnerable people in Psalm 74:19?
opt1: "O surrender not thy little fledgling to the talons of the eagle: preserve the flock of thy sanctuary;"
opt2: "O leave not thy gentle dove among the ravenous wolves: defend the afflicted of Jacob;"
opt3: "O deliver not thy harmless sparrow into the fowler's snare: remember the outcasts of Zion;"
opt4: "O deliver not the soul of thy turtledove unto the multitude of the wicked: forget not the congregation of thy poor for ever."
correct: "O deliver not the soul of thy turtledove unto the multitude of the wicked: forget not the congregation of thy poor for ever."
explanation: A deeply tender image: the covenant community is God's gentle, harmless 'turtledove', utterly helpless before the ravenous predator mobs without divine protection. Psalm 74:19 (KJV) - "O deliver not the soul of thy turtledove unto the multitude of the wicked: forget not the congregation of thy poor for ever."

question: On what legal basis does the psalmist appeal to God concerning the violent world in Psalm 74:20?
opt1: "Have respect unto the covenant: for the dark places of the earth are full of the habitations of cruelty."
opt2: "Remember the oath made to David: for the nations have established thrones of iniquity;"
opt3: "Look upon the blood of the sacrifices: for the land is defiled with the bloodshed of the innocent;"
opt4: "Plead the cause of thy holy law: for the ungodly have filled the earth with oppression and lies;"
correct: "Have respect unto the covenant: for the dark places of the earth are full of the habitations of cruelty."
explanation: The ultimate trump card of prayer: 'Have respect unto the covenant', pleading God's unbreakable promises against a fallen globe infested with cruel barbarism. Psalm 74:20 (KJV) - "Have respect unto the covenant: for the dark places of the earth are full of the habitations of cruelty."

question: What urgent petition calls God to defend His own personal reputation in Psalm 74:22?
opt1: "Stand up, O Lord of hosts, and avenge thy sanctuary: consider how the heathen mock thy throne;"
opt2: "Arise, O God, plead thine own cause: remember how the foolish man reproacheth thee daily."
opt3: "Gird thy sword, O Almighty, and smite the blasphemers: see how the ungodly despise thy power;"
opt4: "Awake, O King of Zion, and scatter thine adversaries: remember the reproach cast upon thy name;"
correct: "Arise, O God, plead thine own cause: remember how the foolish man reproacheth thee daily."
explanation: Asaph lifts the problem above human distress: the destruction of the temple is an assault on God's own glory, urging Him to arise and litigate His own personal lawsuit ('plead thine own cause'). Psalm 74:22 (KJV) - "Arise, O God, plead thine own cause: remember how the foolish man reproacheth thee daily."

question: Who is credited with the composition of Psalm 74 in its superscription?
opt1: A Psalm of David, when he fled from Absalom
opt2: A Song of the Sons of Korah, upon Alamoth
opt3: Maschil of Asaph (a contemplative, instructional psalm by Asaph or the Asaphic guild)
opt4: A Prayer of Moses the man of God
correct: Maschil of Asaph (a contemplative, instructional psalm by Asaph or the Asaphic guild)
explanation: Inscribed 'Maschil of Asaph', indicating a deep instructional meditation composed by the prophetic Asaphic Levitical guild reflecting on national catastrophe. Psalm 74:Title (KJV) - "Maschil of Asaph."

question: What double thanksgiving opens Psalm 75:1, and what declares the nearness of God's Name?
opt1: "Bless the Lord, O our souls, bless him: for his mercy is great and his judgments are true;"
opt2: "Sing praises to the Almighty, sing praises: for his kingdom is established over all the earth;"
opt3: "Unto thee, O God, do we give thanks, unto thee do we give thanks: for that thy name is near thy wondrous works declare."
opt4: "Give thanks unto the King of glory, give thanks: for his salvation shineth from Mount Zion;"
correct: "Unto thee, O God, do we give thanks, unto thee do we give thanks: for that thy name is near thy wondrous works declare."
explanation: Gratitude is repeated with joyful emphasis: God's 'Name' (His active presence and power) is near, openly demonstrated by His supernatural wondrous works. Psalm 75:1 (KJV) - "Unto thee, O God, do we give thanks, unto thee do we give thanks: for that thy name is near thy wondrous works declare."

question: When God intervenes in human history, according to what appointed standard does He judge in Psalm 75:2?
opt1: "In the day of my wrath I will consume the heathen with unquenchable fire"
opt2: "When the set time is come I will plead the cause of the poor in Zion"
opt3: "At the appointed season I will establish the throne of David for ever"
opt4: "When I shall receive the congregation I will judge uprightly."
correct: "When I shall receive the congregation I will judge uprightly."
explanation: God Himself speaks: He has an appointed set time (mo'ed) when He will inaugurate His supreme court, judging with absolute, unyielding uprightness. Psalm 75:2 (KJV) - "When I shall receive the congregation I will judge uprightly."

question: What cosmic stability does God uphold when societal and natural structures dissolve in Psalm 75:3?
opt1: "The earth and all the inhabitants thereof are dissolved: I bear up the pillars of it. Selah."
opt2: "The mountains shake and the kingdoms fall: I stand as the everlasting rock of ages. Selah."
opt3: "The nations melt away and the kings tremble: I hold the sceptre of righteousness in Zion. Selah."
opt4: "The foundations of the world are broken: I maintain the borders of the covenant for ever. Selah."
correct: "The earth and all the inhabitants thereof are dissolved: I bear up the pillars of it. Selah."
explanation: When moral, political, and physical orders collapse into chaotic dissolution, God Himself actively supports, anchors, and stabilizes the moral pillars of the universe. Psalm 75:3 (KJV) - "The earth and all the inhabitants thereof are dissolved: I bear up the pillars of it. Selah."

question: What warning against arrogant defiance and insolent speech is delivered in Psalm 75:4-5?
opt1: "I commanded the princes, Boast not in your strength: and to the tyrants, Brandish not your swords;"
opt2: "I said unto the fools, Deal not foolishly: and to the wicked, Lift not up the horn: Lift not up your horn on high: speak not with a stiff neck."
opt3: "I warned the ungodly, Harden not your hearts: and to the proud, Walk not in vanity of mind;"
opt4: "I said unto the heathen, Mock not the sanctuary: and to the scorner, Open not your mouth in blasphemy;"
correct: "I said unto the fools, Deal not foolishly: and to the wicked, Lift not up the horn: Lift not up your horn on high: speak not with a stiff neck."
explanation: Rebels are cautioned against lifting their horn (flaunting pride) and speaking with an unbending, insolent stiff neck against the Almighty. Psalm 75:4-5 (KJV) - "I said unto the fools, Deal not foolishly: and to the wicked, Lift not up the horn: Lift not up your horn on high: speak not with a stiff neck."

question: From where does genuine earthly promotion and exaltation NOT come according to Psalm 75:6?
opt1: "neither from the sea, nor from the mountains, nor from the desert"
opt2: "neither from chariots, nor from horses, nor from mighty armies"
opt3: "neither from the east, nor from the west, nor from the south."
opt4: "neither from kings, nor from princes, nor from the elders of the gate"
correct: "neither from the east, nor from the west, nor from the south."
explanation: True sovereign exaltation originates from no earthly terrestrial direction - neither east, west, nor southern deserts. Psalm 75:6 (KJV) - "For promotion cometh neither from the east, nor from the west, nor from the south."

question: Who alone acts as the supreme Judge of human status and power in Psalm 75:7?
opt1: "For the Lord of hosts reigneth: he breaketh the crowns of kings, and blesseth the humble"
opt2: "Verily the Almighty governeth: he scattereth the proud, and exalteth the horns of the poor"
opt3: "The Holy One of Israel is King: he dethroneth empires, and planteth his chosen seed"
opt4: "But God is the judge: he putteth down one, and setteth up another."
correct: "But God is the judge: he putteth down one, and setteth up another."
explanation: God is the sole arbiter of human destiny: He deposes monarchs and elevates the humble according to His sovereign providential will. Psalm 75:7 (KJV) - "But God is the judge: he putteth down one, and setteth up another."

question: What terrifying chalice of divine indignation is held in the hand of the LORD in Psalm 75:8?
opt1: "For in the hand of the LORD there is a cup, and the wine is red; it is full of mixture; and he poureth out of the same: but the dregs thereof, all the wicked of the earth shall wring them out, and drink them."
opt2: "For the Almighty holdeth a golden vial of wrath, full of burning coals and brimstone, which he shall pour upon the heathen;"
opt3: "For the Lord hath prepared a bowl of trembling, filled with the bitter waters of judgment, to swallow up the ungodly;"
opt4: "For in his right hand is a cup of vengeance, red with the blood of oppressors, which all the nations shall drink;"
correct: "For in the hand of the LORD there is a cup, and the wine is red; it is full of mixture; and he poureth out of the same: but the dregs thereof, all the wicked of the earth shall wring them out, and drink them."
explanation: A vivid apocalyptic metaphor: God holds a cup of potent foaming red spiced wine; while the righteous are spared, the wicked are forced to drain it down to the foul, bitter dregs. Psalm 75:8 (KJV) - "For in the hand of the LORD there is a cup, and the wine is red; it is full of mixture; and he poureth out of the same: but the dregs thereof, all the wicked of the earth shall wring them out, and drink them."

question: What contrasting treatment awaits the 'horns' of the wicked versus the righteous in Psalm 75:10?
opt1: "The pride of the ungodly will I trample in the dust; but the crown of the faithful shall shine as the sun"
opt2: "All the horns of the wicked also will I cut off; but the horns of the righteous shall be exalted."
opt3: "The power of the oppressors shall be broken; but the strength of the saints shall be established in Zion"
opt4: "The weapons of the violent will I burn in the fire; but the horn of David will I multiply exceedingly"
correct: "All the horns of the wicked also will I cut off; but the horns of the righteous shall be exalted."
explanation: God strips away the aggressive predatory power ('horns') of the wicked, while exalting the dignity, honor, and authority of the righteous. Psalm 75:10 (KJV) - "All the horns of the wicked also will I cut off; but the horns of the righteous shall be exalted."

question: Why is 'the north' conspicuously absent from the directional list in Psalm 75:6 ('neither from the east, nor from the west, nor from the south')?
opt1: Because the northern tribes of Israel had already been exiled into Assyria
opt2: Because navigation by the compass was not yet known to the Hebrews
opt3: Because in ancient biblical orientation, the North (Mount Zion / the heights of heaven) was poetically identified as the transcendent abode of God Himself
opt4: Because the wind from the north was considered an unclean omen
correct: Because in ancient biblical orientation, the North (Mount Zion / the heights of heaven) was poetically identified as the transcendent abode of God Himself
explanation: Promotion does not come from east, west, or south; it comes solely from the North - where God sits enthroned in high celestial majesty. Psalm 75:6-7 (KJV) - "For promotion cometh neither from the east, nor from the west, nor from the south. But God is the judge: he putteth down one, and setteth up another."

question: To what musical tune instruction is Psalm 75 set, marking the final psalm in this sequence?
opt1: 'Shoshannim-Eduth' (Lilies of the Testimony)
opt2: 'Jonath-elem-rechokim' (The Silent Dove of Distant Lands)
opt3: 'Mahalath Leannoth' (Sickness to Afflict)
opt4: 'Al-taschith' (Destroy not), A Psalm or Song of Asaph
correct: 'Al-taschith' (Destroy not), A Psalm or Song of Asaph
explanation: Psalm 75 is the fourth and final 'Al-taschith' ('Destroy not') psalm in the Psalter (along with Psalms 57, 58, 59). Psalm 75:Title (KJV) - "To the chief Musician, Al-taschith, A Psalm or Song of Asaph."

question: Where is God renowned, and where are His sacred tabernacle and dwelling place located in Psalm 76:1-2?
opt1: "In Jerusalem is the Lord praised: his glory is upon Mount Moriah. In Shiloh was his tent, and his throne in Zion;"
opt2: "In Jacob hath God revealed his power: his name is exalted in the sanctuary. In Bethel is his house, and his dwelling in peace;"
opt3: "In the tribes of Israel is God worshipped: his presence filleth the temple. In Hebron is his glory, and his rock in Jerusalem;"
opt4: "In Judah is God known: his name is great in Israel. In Salem also is his tabernacle, and his dwelling place in Sion."
correct: "In Judah is God known: his name is great in Israel. In Salem also is his tabernacle, and his dwelling place in Sion."
explanation: Salem (the ancient name of Jerusalem, meaning 'Peace') and Mount Zion are celebrated as the chosen earthly sanctuary where God's Name is uniquely manifested. Psalm 76:1-2 (KJV) - "In Judah is God known: his name is great in Israel. In Salem also is his tabernacle, and his dwelling place in Sion."

question: What military arsenal did God shatter at Mount Zion in Psalm 76:3?
opt1: "There brake he the arrows of the bow, the shield, and the sword, and the battle. Selah."
opt2: "There he overturned the war chariots of the heathen, the iron spears, and the brass helmets. Selah."
opt3: "There he snapped the javelins of the captains, the coats of mail, and the engines of siege. Selah."
opt4: "There he broke the proud horses of Assyria, the iron shields, and the bows of steel. Selah."
correct: "There brake he the arrows of the bow, the shield, and the sword, and the battle. Selah."
explanation: At Zion, God dismantled the full apparatus of invading militarism: flaming bow arrows ('flashes of the bow'), defensive shields, slashing swords, and warfare itself. Psalm 76:3 (KJV) - "There brake he the arrows of the bow, the shield, and the sword, and the battle. Selah."

question: How does God's majestic radiance surpass the fortresses of predatory worldly empires in Psalm 76:4?
opt1: "Thy beauty outshineth the high cedars of Lebanon and the rocks of Hermon"
opt2: "Thou art more glorious and excellent than the mountains of prey."
opt3: "Thy sanctuary is more exalted than the strong towers of Babylon"
opt4: "Thy throne is higher than the ancient peaks of Bashan and Seir"
correct: "Thou art more glorious and excellent than the mountains of prey."
explanation: Worldly robber empires are likened to ferocious 'mountains of prey' prowled by beasts of plunder; God outshines them all in transcendent moral and celestial excellence. Psalm 76:4 (KJV) - "Thou art more glorious and excellent than the mountains of prey."

question: What paralyzed, comatose defeat overtook the invading warriors at God's rebuke in Psalm 76:5-6?
opt1: "The mighty captains were blinded with terror, their iron bows fell: and an angel smote them in the night watch;"
opt2: "The armies of the aliens turned back in flight, their horses stumbled: and their pride was trampled in the mire;"
opt3: "The stouthearted are spoiled, they have slept their sleep: and none of the men of might have found their hands. At thy rebuke, O God of Jacob, both the chariot and horse are cast into a dead sleep."
opt4: "The stouthearted fell upon their swords, their spears were broken: and none of their warriors could stand in Zion;"
correct: "The stouthearted are spoiled, they have slept their sleep: and none of the men of might have found their hands. At thy rebuke, O God of Jacob, both the chariot and horse are cast into a dead sleep."
explanation: Historically mirroring the destruction of Sennacherib's 185,000 Assyrian soldiers outside Jerusalem (2 Kings 19:35): mighty warriors fell into the 'dead sleep' of death, hands paralyzed. Psalm 76:5-6 (KJV) - "The stouthearted are spoiled, they have slept their sleep: and none of the men of might have found their hands. At thy rebuke, O God of Jacob, both the chariot and horse are cast into a dead sleep."

question: What rhetorical question emphasizes the absolute unendurability of divine wrath in Psalm 76:7?
opt1: "Who among the gods is like unto thee? and who can resist the thunder of thy right hand?"
opt2: "What king of the earth can endure thy judgment? and what nation shall not melt before thy face?"
opt3: "Who can abide the brightness of thy lightning? and who shall dwell with the devouring fire?"
opt4: "Thou, even thou, art to be feared: and who may stand in thy sight when once thou art angry?"
correct: "Thou, even thou, art to be feared: and who may stand in thy sight when once thou art angry?"
explanation: The doubling 'Thou, even thou' underscores absolute divine majesty: no mortal army, king, or empire can remain standing once God's holy wrath is unleashed. Psalm 76:7 (KJV) - "Thou, even thou, art to be feared: and who may stand in thy sight when once thou art angry?"

question: What global reaction overtook the earth when God arose to execute judgment in Psalm 76:8-9?
opt1: "Thou didst cause judgment to be heard from heaven; the earth feared, and was still, When God arose to judgment, to save all the meek of the earth. Selah."
opt2: "The heavens thundered and the earth melted: the kings of the world trembled when God delivered Zion. Selah."
opt3: "Thy voice shook the foundations of the mountains: the nations were put to silence when thou judgedst the poor. Selah."
opt4: "The sun was darkened at thy decree: all flesh bowed down when God established righteousness in the land. Selah."
correct: "Thou didst cause judgment to be heard from heaven; the earth feared, and was still, When God arose to judgment, to save all the meek of the earth. Selah."
explanation: When God issues His verdict from heaven to rescue all humble, oppressed sufferers ('the meek of the earth'), noisy geopolitical turmoil instantly falls into terrified, reverent silence. Psalm 76:8-9 (KJV) - "Thou didst cause judgment to be heard from heaven; the earth feared, and was still, When God arose to judgment, to save all the meek of the earth. Selah."

question: How does God's sovereignty overrule even human malice and hostility in Psalm 76:10?
opt1: "For the pride of the ungodly shall serve thy kingdom: and their wicked devices shalt thou overturn;"
opt2: "Surely the wrath of man shall praise thee: the remainder of wrath shalt thou restrain."
opt3: "Verily the sword of the enemy shall declare thy power: and their cruelty shalt thou judge with fire;"
opt4: "Because the rebellion of nations glorifieth thy name: and the fury of tyrants shalt thou extinguish;"
correct: "Surely the wrath of man shall praise thee: the remainder of wrath shalt thou restrain."
explanation: A monumental theological principle: God sovereignly compels even hostile human fury to ultimately redound to His glory, while capping and restraining any surplus malice. Psalm 76:10 (KJV) - "Surely the wrath of man shall praise thee: the remainder of wrath shalt thou restrain."

question: What command to pay vows and bring tribute to the Awe-inspiring God is issued in Psalm 76:11?
opt1: "Offer sacrifices of thanksgiving in Zion: let all kings bring gold and incense to the sanctuary of peace;"
opt2: "Keep your solemn covenants, ye children of Jacob: let surrounding nations worship at his holy mountain;"
opt3: "Vow, and pay unto the LORD your God: let all that be round about him bring presents unto him that ought to be feared."
opt4: "Bow down before his altar with fear: let the princes of the earth bring tribute unto the King of kings;"
correct: "Vow, and pay unto the LORD your God: let all that be round about him bring presents unto him that ought to be feared."
explanation: Both Israel and surrounding pagan nations are summoned to execute their sacred vows and offer tribute gifts to the awesome Sovereign. Psalm 76:11 (KJV) - "Vow, and pay unto the LORD your God: let all that be round about him bring presents unto him that ought to be feared."

question: What vine-dresser metaphor portrays God subduing arrogant rulers in Psalm 76:12?
opt1: "He will break the iron sceptres of monarchs: he shall bring down their thrones to the ground"
opt2: "He shall scatter the counsels of captains: he is a consuming fire to the rulers of the nations"
opt3: "He will prune the branches of the haughty: he shall tread their glory in the winepress of his wrath"
opt4: "He shall cut off the spirit of princes: he is terrible to the kings of the earth."
correct: "He shall cut off the spirit of princes: he is terrible to the kings of the earth."
explanation: The Hebrew yibtsor means to prune or clip grape clusters: God effortlessly snips off the arrogant spirit of worldly princes like a vintner clipping ripe grapes. Psalm 76:12 (KJV) - "He shall cut off the spirit of princes: he is terrible to the kings of the earth."

question: What historical event in King Hezekiah's reign does Psalm 76 classically celebrate in biblical commentary?
opt1: The miraculous overnight slaughter of Sennacherib's Assyrian army by the Angel of the LORD outside Jerusalem (Isaiah 37; 2 Kings 19)
opt2: David's capture of the Jebusite fortress of Mount Zion
opt3: Solomon's dedication of the golden temple in Jerusalem
opt4: The return of the Jewish exiles from Babylon under Zerubbabel
correct: The miraculous overnight slaughter of Sennacherib's Assyrian army by the Angel of the LORD outside Jerusalem (Isaiah 37; 2 Kings 19)
explanation: The Septuagint explicitly adds 'concerning the Assyrian' to the title; the imagery of sleeping warriors (v. 5) and horse/chariot cast into dead sleep (v. 6) perfectly matches the overthrow of Sennacherib. Psalm 76:5-6 (KJV) - "The stouthearted are spoiled, they have slept their sleep: and none of the men of might have found their hands. At thy rebuke, O God of Jacob, both the chariot and horse are cast into a dead sleep."

question: What agonizing nocturnal distress and unyielding grief open Psalm 77:1-2?
opt1: "I cried unto God with my voice, even unto God with my voice; and he gave ear unto me. In the day of my trouble I sought the Lord: my sore ran in the night, and ceased not: my soul refused to be comforted."
opt2: "Out of the deep have I called upon thy name, O Lord: in the night watch my spirit fainted: my eyes wept without ceasing;"
opt3: "Hear my prayer, O Almighty, in the day of calamity: my wounds bled in the dark: my heart was sore broken;"
opt4: "Unto thee, O God of Jacob, did I lift up my hands: my groaning troubled the night: my soul found no peace;"
correct: "I cried unto God with my voice, even unto God with my voice; and he gave ear unto me. In the day of my trouble I sought the Lord: my sore ran in the night, and ceased not: my soul refused to be comforted."
explanation: Intense personal anguish: Asaph cries aloud to God; his hand was stretched out unslackened through the dark night, while his inconsolable soul refused easy comfort. Psalm 77:1-2 (KJV) - "I cried unto God with my voice, even unto God with my voice; and he gave ear unto me. In the day of my trouble I sought the Lord: my sore ran in the night, and ceased not: my soul refused to be comforted."

question: How does Asaph describe his sleepless insomnia and speechlessness under God's heavy hand in Psalm 77:4?
opt1: "Sleep departeth from mine eyes: my tongue cleaveth to the roof of my mouth in terror"
opt2: "Thou holdest mine eyes waking: I am so troubled that I cannot speak."
opt3: "Thou closest my eyelids in sorrow: my lips are struck dumb with overwhelming grief"
opt4: "My soul watcheth through the dark hours: I am so faint that I can utter no petition"
correct: "Thou holdest mine eyes waking: I am so troubled that I cannot speak."
explanation: Agonizing insomnia: God Himself holds the psalmist's eyelids open, and his inner turmoil is so suffocating that he is completely paralyzed and unable to speak. Psalm 77:4 (KJV) - "Thou holdest mine eyes waking: I am so troubled that I cannot speak."

question: What six rapid-fire questions of torturing doubt assail Asaph's mind in Psalm 77:7-9?
opt1: "Why hath the Almighty forsaken Zion? will he build her walls no more? Is his covenant broken with David? shall the heathen triumph? Hath the Lord forgotten his oath? hath he rejected his sanctuary? Selah."
opt2: "Doth God sleep while we perish? will he send his prophet no more? Is his right hand withered in weakness? shall the pit swallow us? Hath he forgotten Abraham? hath his holiness departed from Israel? Selah."
opt3: "Will the Lord cast off for ever? and will he be favourable no more? Is his mercy clean gone for ever? doth his promise fail for evermore? Hath God forgotten to be gracious? hath he in anger shut up his tender mercies? Selah."
opt4: "Will the Lord keep silence in our affliction? will his ear hear no more? Is the ark delivered to the enemy? shall the altar burn no incense? Hath God despised his inheritance? hath his favor ceased? Selah."
correct: "Will the Lord cast off for ever? and will he be favourable no more? Is his mercy clean gone for ever? doth his promise fail for evermore? Hath God forgotten to be gracious? hath he in anger shut up his tender mercies? Selah."
explanation: The ultimate dark night of the soul: six heart-wrenching questions interrogating whether God's covenant mercy, faithfulness, and compassion have terminated forever. Psalm 77:7-9 (KJV) - "Will the Lord cast off for ever? and will he be favourable no more? Is his mercy clean gone for ever? doth his promise fail for evermore? Hath God forgotten to be gracious? hath he in anger shut up his tender mercies? Selah."

question: What pivotal diagnostic turning point shifts Asaph's perspective from despair to faith in Psalm 77:10?
opt1: "Then I cried, This is my sin: but I will offer sacrifices of rams upon the holy altar;"
opt2: "And I answered, This is my trial: but I will trust in the shadow of his wings;"
opt3: "So I said in my heart, This is the chastening of the Lord: but I will wait for the morning light;"
opt4: "And I said, This is my infirmity: but I will remember the years of the right hand of the most High."
correct: "And I said, This is my infirmity: but I will remember the years of the right hand of the most High."
explanation: The great breakthrough: Asaph diagnoses his dark doubts as his own subjective human weakness ('infirmity'), consciously pivoting to meditate on the objective historic triumphs of God's right hand. Psalm 77:10 (KJV) - "And I said, This is my infirmity: but I will remember the years of the right hand of the most High."

question: What therapeutic spiritual antidote does Asaph resolve to practice in Psalm 77:11-12?
opt1: "I will remember the works of the LORD: surely I will remember thy wonders of old. I will meditate also of all thy work, and talk of thy doings."
opt2: "I will inquire of the prophets: surely I will study the law of Moses day and night: I will fast in sackcloth;"
opt3: "I will go into the temple: surely I will pay my vows before the congregation: I will blow the silver trumpet;"
opt4: "I will call upon the elders: surely I will recount the battles of Joshua: I will bless his holy name;"
correct: "I will remember the works of the LORD: surely I will remember thy wonders of old. I will meditate also of all thy work, and talk of thy doings."
explanation: Replacing toxic rumination with active holy recollection: remembering, meditating on, and speaking aloud of Yahweh's ancient redemptive wonders. Psalm 77:11-12 (KJV) - "I will remember the works of the LORD: surely I will remember thy wonders of old. I will meditate also of all thy work, and talk of thy doings."

question: Where is God's way revealed, and what incomparable declaration is made in Psalm 77:13?
opt1: "Thy path, O Lord, is in the heavens: who among the mighty can compare unto thee?"
opt2: "Thy way, O God, is in the sanctuary: who is so great a God as our God?"
opt3: "Thy throne, O Most High, is in Mount Zion: who is like unto the Holy One of Jacob?"
opt4: "Thy counsel, O King, is in the secret place: who can search out the depths of thy wisdom?"
correct: "Thy way, O God, is in the sanctuary: who is so great a God as our God?"
explanation: In Hebrew, 'in the sanctuary' also means 'in holiness' (ba-kodesh): God's providential dealings are marked by pure, unblemished holiness, surpassing all counterfeit deities. Psalm 77:13 (KJV) - "Thy way, O God, is in the sanctuary: who is so great a God as our God?"

question: How did the personified waters of the Red Sea react when God approached in Psalm 77:16?
opt1: "The waves fled from thy presence: the deep sea dried up at the blast of thy nostrils"
opt2: "The ocean parted before thy feet: the great floods stood upright as an heap of walls"
opt3: "The waters saw thee, O God, the waters saw thee; they were afraid: the depths also were troubled."
opt4: "The depths melted at thy word: the roaring billows were put to silence before thy majesty"
correct: "The waters saw thee, O God, the waters saw thee; they were afraid: the depths also were troubled."
explanation: Sublime poetic personification: the waters of the Red Sea 'saw' their Creator, shuddered with convulsive terror ('were afraid'), and churned in agitated turmoil. Psalm 77:16 (KJV) - "The waters saw thee, O God, the waters saw thee; they were afraid: the depths also were troubled."

question: What cosmic tempest elements accompanied God's march through the sea in Psalm 77:17-18?
opt1: "The winds blew with fury: thick darkness covered the heavens: fire came down upon the camp of Egypt;"
opt2: "The firmament dissolved in rain: hail fell upon the mountains: and an earthquake shattered the rocky cliffs;"
opt3: "The storm overturned the chariots: the sea roared with thunderbolts: and the deep swallowed up their captains;"
opt4: "The clouds poured out water: the skies sent out a sound: thine arrows also went abroad. The voice of thy thunder was in the heaven: the lightnings lightened the world: the earth trembled and shook."
correct: "The clouds poured out water: the skies sent out a sound: thine arrows also went abroad. The voice of thy thunder was in the heaven: the lightnings lightened the world: the earth trembled and shook."
explanation: A multi-sensory theophany: torrential cloudbursts, pealing thunder, blinding lightning illuminating the cosmos, flying lightning-arrows, and seismic earthquakes. Psalm 77:17-18 (KJV) - "The clouds poured out water: the skies sent out a sound: thine arrows also went abroad. The voice of thy thunder was in the heaven: the lightnings lightened the world: the earth trembled and shook."

question: What profound mystery of divine providence is articulated in Psalm 77:19?
opt1: "Thy way is in the sea, and thy path in the great waters, and thy footsteps are not known."
opt2: "Thy counsel is hidden from the eyes of mortals, and thy works are deeper than the grave"
opt3: "Thy throne is established above the storms, and thy purpose shall not be turned aside"
opt4: "Thy chariot rideth upon the whirlwind, and no man can trace the paths of thy power"
correct: "Thy way is in the sea, and thy path in the great waters, and thy footsteps are not known."
explanation: God's pathway cuts directly through impossible roaring waters, yet He leaves no physical footprints behind - teaching faith to trust His invisible, untraceable guidance. Psalm 77:19 (KJV) - "Thy way is in the sea, and thy path in the great waters, and thy footsteps are not known."

question: What tender pastoral conclusion contrasts the terrifying tempest in Psalm 77:20?
opt1: "Thou broughtest thy children safely into the land of Canaan by the sword of Joshua"
opt2: "Thou leddest thy people like a flock by the hand of Moses and Aaron."
opt3: "Thou establishedst the tribes of Jacob in peace under the shadow of the cloud"
opt4: "Thou feddest thine inheritance with bread from heaven in the dry desert"
correct: "Thou leddest thy people like a flock by the hand of Moses and Aaron."
explanation: After thunder and splitting oceans, the psalm ends in serene pastoral gentleness: the cosmic Lord of tempests shepherds His people like a tender flock using human pastors Moses and Aaron. Psalm 77:20 (KJV) - "Thou leddest thy people like a flock by the hand of Moses and Aaron."

question: What didactic pedagogical mandate to transmit divine parables to future generations opens Psalm 78:2-4?
opt1: "Hearken, ye children, to the instruction of a father: keep the commandments of the law of Moses, that your days may be multiplied;"
opt2: "I will open my mouth in a parable: I will utter dark sayings of old ... Shewing to the generation to come the praises of the LORD, and his strength, and his wonderful works that he hath done."
opt3: "I will declare the statutes of the sanctuary unto the elders: teaching our sons the righteous judgments of God from antiquity;"
opt4: "Give ear, O Israel, to the testimony of Jacob: rehearse the mighty deeds of Joshua unto the rising generation;"
correct: "I will open my mouth in a parable: I will utter dark sayings of old ... Shewing to the generation to come the praises of the LORD, and his strength, and his wonderful works that he hath done."
explanation: Asaph undertakes a monumental historical pedagogy: unlocking 'parables' and 'dark sayings' (quoted in Matt 13:35 of Jesus) to ensure future generations never forget God's wonders. Psalm 78:2, 4 (KJV) - "I will open my mouth in a parable: I will utter dark sayings of old ... Shewing to the generation to come the praises of the LORD, and his strength, and his wonderful works that he hath done."

question: What cowardly military failure and covenant betrayal is charged against Ephraim in Psalm 78:9-10?
opt1: "The princes of Ephraim, possessing iron chariots, fled before the Amorites: they set up idols in the high places;"
opt2: "The tribe of Joseph, having trained captains, laid down their spears: they forgot the victories of the Red Sea;"
opt3: "The children of Ephraim, being armed, and carrying bows, turned back in the day of battle. They kept not the covenant of God, and refused to walk in his law;"
opt4: "The host of Ephraim, being skilled in warfare, surrendered the ark of the covenant: they broke the sabbaths;"
correct: "The children of Ephraim, being armed, and carrying bows, turned back in the day of battle. They kept not the covenant of God, and refused to walk in his law;"
explanation: Though superbly equipped with advanced weaponry ('armed, and carrying bows'), Ephraim displayed shameful cowardice in battle because their hearts were disloyal to God's covenant. Psalm 78:9-10 (KJV) - "The children of Ephraim, being armed, and carrying bows, turned back in the day of battle. They kept not the covenant of God, and refused to walk in his law;"

question: What Egyptian geographic location is identified as the theater of God's plagues and wonders in Psalm 78:12 and 78:43?
opt1: "in the plains of Memphis"
opt2: "in the delta of Goshen"
opt3: "in the valley of the Nile"
opt4: "in the field of Zoan"
correct: "in the field of Zoan"
explanation: Zoan (Tanis) was the prominent royal capital of lower Egypt during the Ramesside period, where Moses confronted Pharaoh with the plagues. Psalm 78:12, 43 (KJV) - "Marvellous things did he in the sight of their fathers, in the land of Egypt, in the field of Zoan ... How he had wrought his signs in Egypt, and his wonders in the field of Zoan:"

question: What miraculous hydrological provision gushed from the wilderness rock in Psalm 78:15-16?
opt1: "He clave the rocks in the wilderness, and gave them drink as out of the great depths. He brought streams also out of the rock, and caused waters to run down like rivers."
opt2: "He struck the flinty stone, and living water bubbled forth: satisfying all the tribes of Jacob;"
opt3: "He opened the fountains of the desert, and quenched their thirst: filling the valleys with sweet brooks;"
opt4: "He spoke to the cliff of Horeb, and it poured out rain: refreshing the camp of Israel;"
correct: "He clave the rocks in the wilderness, and gave them drink as out of the great depths. He brought streams also out of the rock, and caused waters to run down like rivers."
explanation: Not a mere trickle, but massive river-like torrents ('caused waters to run down like rivers') split from the solid flinty rock to hydrate millions of people and livestock. Psalm 78:15-16 (KJV) - "He clave the rocks in the wilderness, and gave them drink as out of the great depths. He brought streams also out of the rock, and caused waters to run down like rivers."

question: What celestial food titles are given to the manna in Psalm 78:24-25?
opt1: "the bread of life" and "the dew of glory"
opt2: "the corn of heaven" and "angels' food"
opt3: "the manna of eternity" and "the wheat of Zion"
opt4: "the fruit of paradise" and "the feast of the sanctuary"
correct: "the corn of heaven" and "angels' food"
explanation: Manna is glorified as 'the corn of heaven' and 'angels' food' (Hebrew lechem abbirim - bread of the mighty ones), sent directly from opened celestial doors. Psalm 78:24-25 (KJV) - "And had rained down manna upon them to eat, and had given them of the corn of heaven. Man did eat angels' food: he sent them meat to the full."

question: What psychological and mortal frailty of human nature did God remember in showing compassion in Psalm 78:38-39?
opt1: "For he considered that they were formed of dust; as grass of the field that withereth at noon;"
opt2: "Seeing he knew their frame; that they were as a fleeting shadow that leaveth no remembrance;"
opt3: "For he remembered that they were but flesh; a wind that passeth away, and cometh not again."
opt4: "Because he remembered the weakness of Adam; as vapor that vanisheth before the rising sun;"
correct: "For he remembered that they were but flesh; a wind that passeth away, and cometh not again."
explanation: Full of compassion, God restrained His wrath, remembering that fallen humans are frail, transient 'flesh' - like a passing breeze that blows past and never returns. Psalm 78:38-39 (KJV) - "But he, being full of compassion, forgave their iniquity, and destroyed them not ... For he remembered that they were but flesh; a wind that passeth away, and cometh not again."

question: What tragic audacity of human unbelief is exposed in Psalm 78:41?
opt1: "They rebelled against the law of Moses, and despised the counsel of the Most High"
opt2: "They hardened their hearts in the desert, and set up the golden calf in Horeb"
opt3: "They doubted his power at Kadesh, and refused to enter the land of promise"
opt4: "Yea, they turned back and tempted God, and limited the Holy One of Israel."
correct: "Yea, they turned back and tempted God, and limited the Holy One of Israel."
explanation: Unbelief commits the grotesque arrogance of 'limiting' (setting boundaries and borders upon the power and goodness of) the infinite, omnipotent Holy One of Israel. Psalm 78:41 (KJV) - "Yea, they turned back and tempted God, and limited the Holy One of Israel."

question: What tragic sanctuary abandonment occurred when God allowed the Ark to be captured in Psalm 78:60-61?
opt1: "So that he forsook the tabernacle of Shiloh, the tent which he placed among men; And delivered his strength into captivity, and his glory into the enemy's hand."
opt2: "He departed from the sanctuary of Bethel, and left his altar desolate before the Philistines;"
opt3: "He overturned the holy place of Nob, and delivered the linen ephod to the sword of Saul;"
opt4: "He removed the cloud from Gibeon, and scattered the priests of Aaron into the wilderness;"
correct: "So that he forsook the tabernacle of Shiloh, the tent which he placed among men; And delivered his strength into captivity, and his glory into the enemy's hand."
explanation: Because of Ephraim's apostasy, God permanently abandoned Shiloh, surrendering His 'strength' and 'glory' (the Ark of the Covenant) into Philistine hands (1 Sam 4:11, 21-22). Psalm 78:60-61 (KJV) - "So that he forsook the tabernacle of Shiloh, the tent which he placed among men; And delivered his strength into captivity, and his glory into the enemy's hand."

question: What tribal transfer of hegemony and sacred mountain choice is proclaimed in Psalm 78:67-68?
opt1: "He rejected the sceptre of Benjamin, and chose not the house of Saul: But chose the sons of Jesse, and Jerusalem;"
opt2: "Moreover he refused the tabernacle of Joseph, and chose not the tribe of Ephraim: But chose the tribe of Judah, the mount Zion which he loved."
opt3: "He cast off the firstborn of Reuben, and passed by the tents of Manasseh: But established the kingdom of David on Moriah;"
opt4: "He set aside the priesthood of Eli, and chose not the sons of Ithamar: But chose Zadok, and the temple of Solomon;"
correct: "Moreover he refused the tabernacle of Joseph, and chose not the tribe of Ephraim: But chose the tribe of Judah, the mount Zion which he loved."
explanation: Sovereign redemptive realignment: God rejected northern Ephraimite dominance (Joseph/Shiloh) to permanently establish royal hegemony in the tribe of Judah and Mount Zion. Psalm 78:67-68 (KJV) - "Moreover he refused the tabernacle of Joseph, and chose not the tribe of Ephraim: But chose the tribe of Judah, the mount Zion which he loved."

question: From what humble pastoral vocation did God elevate David to shepherd His nation in Psalm 78:70-72?
opt1: "He took David from the pastures of Bethlehem, from keeping the lambs: to rule the twelve tribes in righteousness and peace;"
opt2: "He called the son of Jesse from the wilderness of Paran, from tending the flocks: to lead the hosts of Israel with a rod of iron;"
opt3: "He chose David also his servant, and took him from the sheepfolds: From following the ewes great with young he brought him to feed Jacob his people, and Israel his inheritance. So he fed them according to the integrity of his heart; and guided them by the skilfulness of his hands."
opt4: "He anointed David from among his brethren, from following the cattle: to sit upon the throne of Zion with wisdom and understanding;"
correct: "He chose David also his servant, and took him from the sheepfolds: From following the ewes great with young he brought him to feed Jacob his people, and Israel his inheritance. So he fed them according to the integrity of his heart; and guided them by the skilfulness of his hands."
explanation: The shepherd boy tenderly tending nursing ewes is commissioned as the supreme Shepherd-King, pasturing Israel with two essential leadership virtues: integrity of heart and skill of hands. Psalm 78:70-72 (KJV) - "He chose David also his servant, and took him from the sheepfolds: From following the ewes great with young he brought him to feed Jacob his people, and Israel his inheritance. So he fed them according to the integrity of his heart; and guided them by the skilfulness of his hands."

question: What horrific desecration of the sanctuary and destruction of Jerusalem opens Psalm 79:1?
opt1: "O Lord of hosts, the Babylonians have breached thy walls: thy altar have they overturned; they have burned Zion with fire;"
opt2: "How long, O God, shall the enemy trample thy courts: the sanctuary of David is destroyed; Jerusalem is desolate;"
opt3: "O God, the heathen are come into thine inheritance; thy holy temple have they defiled; they have laid Jerusalem on heaps."
opt4: "Awake, O King of Israel: foreign armies have entered the holy city; they have plundered the vessels of gold;"
correct: "O God, the heathen are come into thine inheritance; thy holy temple have they defiled; they have laid Jerusalem on heaps."
explanation: A devastating communal lament over the Babylonian sack of Jerusalem: pagans invading God's inheritance, defiling the holy temple, and reducing Jerusalem to heaps of rubble. Psalm 79:1 (KJV) - "O God, the heathen are come into thine inheritance; thy holy temple have they defiled; they have laid Jerusalem on heaps."

question: What gruesome indignity was inflicted upon the unburied corpses of God's saints in Psalm 79:2-3?
opt1: "They cast their bodies into the valley of Hinnom, to be burned with fire: and none wept for the slain of Judah;"
opt2: "Their flesh was trampled under the chariot wheels of the heathen: and their bones were scattered in the wilderness;"
opt3: "They hung the bodies of the priests upon the broken walls of Zion: and wild dogs devoured their limbs in the open street;"
opt4: "The dead bodies of thy servants have they given to be meat unto the fowls of the heaven, the flesh of thy saints unto the beasts of the earth. Their blood have they shed like water round about Jerusalem; and there was none to bury them."
correct: "The dead bodies of thy servants have they given to be meat unto the fowls of the heaven, the flesh of thy saints unto the beasts of the earth. Their blood have they shed like water round about Jerusalem; and there was none to bury them."
explanation: The ultimate ancient humiliation: saints' bodies left unburied as scavenger meat for vultures and wild beasts, their blood poured out like water across Jerusalem. Psalm 79:2-3 (KJV) - "The dead bodies of thy servants have they given to be meat unto the fowls of the heaven, the flesh of thy saints unto the beasts of the earth. Their blood have they shed like water round about Jerusalem; and there was none to bury them."

question: What passionate plea for divine wrath to be redirected against godless persecutors is made in Psalm 79:6-7?
opt1: "Pour out thy wrath upon the heathen that have not known thee, and upon the kingdoms that have not called upon thy name. For they have devoured Jacob, and laid waste his dwelling place."
opt2: "Send forth thy thunderbolts upon Babylon, and burn their palaces: for they have mocked the God of heaven;"
opt3: "Avenge the blood of thy servants upon the nations: for they have torn down the gates of Jerusalem;"
opt4: "Let thy fury consume the kings of the earth: for they have plundered the heritage of Abraham;"
correct: "Pour out thy wrath upon the heathen that have not known thee, and upon the kingdoms that have not called upon thy name. For they have devoured Jacob, and laid waste his dwelling place."
explanation: Asaph appeals to divine justice: rather than consuming His covenant people, God should pour out His wrath upon ruthless pagan empires who do not call upon Yahweh. Psalm 79:6-7 (KJV) - "Pour out thy wrath upon the heathen that have not known thee, and upon the kingdoms that have not called upon thy name. For they have devoured Jacob, and laid waste his dwelling place."

question: On what grounds do the humbled survivors plead for rapid mercy and pardon in Psalm 79:8?
opt1: "Forgive our transgressions for the sake of David thy servant: let thine angels deliver us: for we faint in exile;"
opt2: "O remember not against us former iniquities: let thy tender mercies speedily prevent us: for we are brought very low."
opt3: "Look upon our tears in sackcloth: let thy lovingkindness revive our spirit: for we are crushed in the dust;"
opt4: "Pardon our sins according to the blood of the altar: let thy salvation arise: for our strength faileth;"
correct: "O remember not against us former iniquities: let thy tender mercies speedily prevent us: for we are brought very low."
explanation: Admitting their utter exhaustion and destitution ('we are brought very low'), they plead for God to forget past sins and let His tender mercies 'speedily prevent' (meet/arrive before) them. Psalm 79:8 (KJV) - "O remember not against us former iniquities: let thy tender mercies speedily prevent us: for we are brought very low."

question: What twofold reason grounds the plea for deliverance and purging of sins in Psalm 79:9?
opt1: "because of the covenant of our fathers: and for the sake of Mount Zion"
opt2: "for our weeping in captivity: and for the sake of the holy priesthood"
opt3: "for the glory of thy name: and deliver us, and purge away our sins, for thy name's sake."
opt4: "according to the multitude of our sacrifices: and for the honor of Israel"
correct: "for the glory of thy name: and deliver us, and purge away our sins, for thy name's sake."
explanation: The highest biblical motive in prayer: salvation is sought not for human merit, but purely 'for the glory of thy name' and 'for thy name's sake'. Psalm 79:9 (KJV) - "Help us, O God of our salvation, for the glory of thy name: and deliver us, and purge away our sins, for thy name's sake."

question: How does the psalmist seek to silence the pagan mockery 'Where is their God?' in Psalm 79:10?
opt1: "let fire fall from heaven upon their idols: that all nations may fear the Lord"
opt2: "rebuild the walls of Jerusalem before their eyes: that they may know thou art King"
opt3: "send forth an angel of salvation: that the heathen may bow down at thy footstool"
opt4: "let him be known among the heathen in our sight by the revenging of the blood of thy servants which is shed."
correct: "let him be known among the heathen in our sight by the revenging of the blood of thy servants which is shed."
explanation: The taunt 'Where is their God?' is answered when God publicly vindicates His justice by executing retribution for the shed blood of His martyred servants. Psalm 79:10 (KJV) - "Wherefore should the heathen say, Where is their God? let him be known among the heathen in our sight by the revenging of the blood of thy servants which is shed."

question: What petition on behalf of condemned captives is presented before God's throne in Psalm 79:11?
opt1: "Let the sighing of the prisoner come before thee; according to the greatness of thy power preserve thou those that are appointed to die;"
opt2: "Hear the weeping of the exiles in Babylon; according to thy tender mercies break their iron chains;"
opt3: "Look down upon the afflicted in the dungeon; by the strength of thine arm ransom the outcasts;"
opt4: "Behold the groaning of thy chosen seed; according to thy covenant deliver the captive daughter of Zion;"
correct: "Let the sighing of the prisoner come before thee; according to the greatness of thy power preserve thou those that are appointed to die;"
