explanation: God's ear is tuned to the faint, exhausted groans of prisoners, using His almighty power to rescue those marked for imminent execution ('appointed to die'). Psalm 79:11 (KJV) - "Let the sighing of the prisoner come before thee; according to the greatness of thy power preserve thou those that are appointed to die;"

question: What retribution is invoked upon spiteful surrounding nations who reproached the Lord in Psalm 79:12?
opt1: "And pour out unquenchable fire upon Edom and Moab: for they rejoiced at the fall of Jerusalem;"
opt2: "And render unto our neighbours sevenfold into their bosom their reproach, wherewith they have reproached thee, O Lord."
opt3: "And break the horns of the Philistines: for they mocked the sanctuary of the Most High;"
opt4: "And deliver their cities to the spoiler: for they blasphemed the holy name of God;"
correct: "And render unto our neighbours sevenfold into their bosom their reproach, wherewith they have reproached thee, O Lord."
explanation: Vengeance belongs to God: Asaph asks that neighboring malicious nations (like Edom and Ammon) receive full, complete ('sevenfold') retributive justice into their own bosom. Psalm 79:12 (KJV) - "And render unto our neighbours sevenfold into their bosom their reproach, wherewith they have reproached thee, O Lord."

question: What pastoral identity and eternal commitment to praise conclude Psalm 79:13?
opt1: "Therefore the seed of Jacob shall rejoice in the temple: and proclaim thy wondrous works unto all nations;"
opt2: "And the congregation of Israel shall bless thy holy name: we will offer sacrifices of thanksgiving continually;"
opt3: "So we thy people and sheep of thy pasture will give thee thanks for ever: we will shew forth thy praise to all generations."
opt4: "So shall the tribes of Zion celebrate thy salvation: we will sing upon the harp throughout all ages;"
correct: "So we thy people and sheep of thy pasture will give thee thanks for ever: we will shew forth thy praise to all generations."
explanation: The psalm closes with serene covenant assurance: despite national catastrophe, Israel remains God's cherished flock ('sheep of thy pasture'), vowing everlasting intergenerational praise. Psalm 79:13 (KJV) - "So we thy people and sheep of thy pasture will give thee thanks for ever: we will shew forth thy praise to all generations."

question: What phrase in Psalm 79:8 reflects the archaic King James usage meaning 'meet us with anticipated assistance'?
opt1: "let thy righteousness hold up our hands"
opt2: "let thy lovingkindness hedge our path"
opt3: "let thy salvation stay our footsteps"
opt4: "let thy tender mercies speedily prevent us"
correct: "let thy tender mercies speedily prevent us"
explanation: In 17th-century English, 'prevent' (Latin praevenire) meant 'to go before, anticipate, come to meet'; Asaph prays that God's tender mercies will hasten out to meet them before they collapse. Psalm 79:8 (KJV) - "O remember not against us former iniquities: let thy tender mercies speedily prevent us: for we are brought very low."

question: How is God addressed as the enthroned Leader of His flock, and before which three tribes does He march in Psalm 80:1-2?
opt1: "Hearken, O King of Zion, thou that guidest Judah with thy staff; thou that sittest in the holy of holies: Before Reuben, Simeon, and Levi show thy power;"
opt2: "Look down, O God of hosts, thou that pasturedst Jacob in the wilderness; thou that ridest the cherubim: Before Dan, Naphtali, and Asher reveal thy salvation;"
opt3: "Incline thine ear, O Holy One of Israel, thou that feedest thy people with manna; thou that dwellest in light: Before Judah and the house of David arise;"
opt4: "Give ear, O Shepherd of Israel, thou that leadest Joseph like a flock; thou that dwellest between the cherubims, shine forth. Before Ephraim and Benjamin and Manasseh stir up thy strength, and come and save us."
correct: "Give ear, O Shepherd of Israel, thou that leadest Joseph like a flock; thou that dwellest between the cherubims, shine forth. Before Ephraim and Benjamin and Manasseh stir up thy strength, and come and save us."
explanation: Enthroned above the mercy seat cherubim, the Shepherd of Israel is invoked to march before the three Rachel-tribes (Ephraim, Benjamin, Manasseh) which camped together immediately behind the Ark in the wilderness (Num 2:18-24). Psalm 80:1-2 (KJV) - "Give ear, O Shepherd of Israel, thou that leadest Joseph like a flock; thou that dwellest between the cherubims, shine forth. Before Ephraim and Benjamin and Manasseh stir up thy strength, and come and save us."

question: What three-step progressive refrain serves as the liturgical chorus of Psalm 80 in verses 3, 7, and 19?
opt1: "Turn us again, O God [v. 3] / O God of hosts [v. 7] / O LORD God of hosts [v. 19], and cause thy face to shine; and we shall be saved."
opt2: "Save us, O Lord our God, and gather us from among the heathen, to give thanks unto thy holy name;"
opt3: "Revive us again, O Lord, and cause thy glory to fill the sanctuary; and we shall live before thee;"
opt4: "Hearken unto our cry, O King, and heal the breaches of Zion; and we shall praise thee for ever;"
correct: "Turn us again, O God [v. 3] / O God of hosts [v. 7] / O LORD God of hosts [v. 19], and cause thy face to shine; and we shall be saved."
explanation: A climactic crescendo of divine titles: beginning with 'O God' (v. 3), elevating to 'O God of hosts' (v. 7), and peaking at 'O LORD God of hosts' (v. 19), praying for the shining face of God to bring salvation. Psalm 80:3 (KJV) - "Turn us again, O God, and cause thy face to shine; and we shall be saved."

question: What tearful diet describes the deep chastisement of God's people in Psalm 80:5?
opt1: "Thou hast given them ashes for bread; and mingled their drink with plenteous weeping;"
opt2: "Thou feedest them with the bread of tears; and givest them tears to drink in great measure."
opt3: "Thou satisfiest their hunger with the bread of adversity; and their thirst with the waters of gall;"
opt4: "Thou hast fed them with the scroll of lamentation; and filled their cup with bitter sorrow;"
correct: "Thou feedest them with the bread of tears; and givest them tears to drink in great measure."
explanation: A striking metabolic metaphor: sorrow is so all-pervasive that their solid food is tears ('bread of tears') and their beverage is tears measured out by the chalice. Psalm 80:5 (KJV) - "Thou feedest them with the bread of tears; and givest them tears to drink in great measure."

question: What horticultural allegory depicts Israel's Exodus and settlement in Canaan in Psalm 80:8-9?
opt1: "Thou didst transplant a tender cedar from the Nile: thou clearedst the wilderness, and established its boughs in Zion;"
opt2: "Thou broughtest a green olive tree out of the iron furnace: thou diggedst a trench, and wateredst it with the river of God;"
opt3: "Thou hast brought a vine out of Egypt: thou hast cast out the heathen, and planted it. Thou preparedst room before it, and didst cause it to take deep root, and it filled the land."
opt4: "Thou plantedst a fruitful vineyard in Mount Moriah: thou hedgedst it with stone walls, and built a tower in the midst;"
correct: "Thou hast brought a vine out of Egypt: thou hast cast out the heathen, and planted it. Thou preparedst room before it, and didst cause it to take deep root, and it filled the land."
explanation: Israel is personified as a delicate grapevine uprooted from Egyptian bondage, transplanted by God into Canaan, where He cleared out pagan nations so its roots filled the entire land. Psalm 80:8-9 (KJV) - "Thou hast brought a vine out of Egypt: thou hast cast out the heathen, and planted it. Thou preparedst room before it, and didst cause it to take deep root, and it filled the land."

question: What vast geographic expanse was covered by the boughs and branches of this flourishing vine in Psalm 80:11?
opt1: "Her leaves overshadowed the mountains of Lebanon, and her roots reached the wilderness of Zin"
opt2: "Her fruit filled the plains of Sharon, and her vines covered the borders of Egypt"
opt3: "Her branches extended from Dan unto Beersheba, and across the valley of Jordan"
opt4: "She sent out her boughs unto the sea, and her branches unto the river."
correct: "She sent out her boughs unto the sea, and her branches unto the river."
explanation: At its Davidic-Solomonic zenith, the national Vine covered the ideal promised borders: from the Mediterranean Sea in the west to the river Euphrates in the east. Psalm 80:11 (KJV) - "She sent out her boughs unto the sea, and her branches unto the river."

question: What wild forest beast ravages and devours the breached vineyard in Psalm 80:13?
opt1: "The boar out of the wood doth waste it, and the wild beast of the field doth devour it."
opt2: "The roaring lion of the desert doth tear it, and the jackals trample its fruitful clusters"
opt3: "The fierce wolf of the wilderness doth uproot it, and the wild ass consumeth its branches"
opt4: "The serpent of the pit hath gnawed its roots, and the fowls of heaven have plucked its fruit"
correct: "The boar out of the wood doth waste it, and the wild beast of the field doth devour it."
explanation: With the protective hedges broken down, ferocious pagan empires are likened to a destructive wild forest boar rooting up and devouring the sacred vineyard. Psalm 80:13 (KJV) - "The boar out of the wood doth waste it, and the wild beast of the field doth devour it."

question: What passionate plea calls upon God to inspect and restore this devastated vineyard in Psalm 80:14-15?
opt1: "Arise, O Lord of hosts: come down into thy garden, and restore the tender plant which thy power nurtured;"
opt2: "Return, we beseech thee, O God of hosts: look down from heaven, and behold, and visit this vine; And the vineyard which thy right hand hath planted, and the branch that thou madest strong for thyself."
opt3: "Turn thy face again, O King of Israel: look upon the vineyard of Zion, and water it with thy dew from on high;"
opt4: "Awake, O Shepherd of Jacob: heal the broken boughs of thy vine, and build up the stone hedge around thy sanctuary;"
correct: "Return, we beseech thee, O God of hosts: look down from heaven, and behold, and visit this vine; And the vineyard which thy right hand hath planted, and the branch that thou madest strong for thyself."
explanation: The community implores the celestial Gardener to look down from heaven, visit the battered vine with His grace, and restore the stock His right hand planted. Psalm 80:14-15 (KJV) - "Return, we beseech thee, O God of hosts: look down from heaven, and behold, and visit this vine; And the vineyard which thy right hand hath planted, and the branch that thou madest strong for thyself."

question: What profound Messianic titles of divine empowerment appear in Psalm 80:17?
opt1: "the anointed of thy sanctuary" and "the branch of David thy servant"
opt2: "the shepherd of Mount Zion" and "the prince of peace from everlasting"
opt3: "the man of thy right hand" and "the son of man whom thou madest strong for thyself"
opt4: "the king of glory" and "the horn of salvation for Jacob"
correct: "the man of thy right hand" and "the son of man whom thou madest strong for thyself"
explanation: A luminous Messianic prophecy: God's saving hand rests upon the Messiah - 'the man of thy right hand' and the 'son of man' whom God strengthens to accomplish redemption. Psalm 80:17 (KJV) - "Let thy hand be upon the man of thy right hand, upon the son of man whom thou madest strong for thyself."

question: What reciprocal covenant commitment of loyalty and prayer is promised in Psalm 80:18?
opt1: "So shall our feet stand firm in thy truth: revive our souls, and we will praise thee with harps;"
opt2: "Therefore will we never turn aside to idols: grant us life, and we will offer whole burnt offerings;"
opt3: "And we will walk in thy statutes day and night: renew our strength, and we will declare thy glory;"
opt4: "So will not we go back from thee: quicken us, and we will call upon thy name."
correct: "So will not we go back from thee: quicken us, and we will call upon thy name."
explanation: True spiritual revival: if God imparts life ('quicken us'), the people promise permanent perseverance, never backsliding from Him and unceasingly calling upon His Name. Psalm 80:18 (KJV) - "So will not we go back from thee: quicken us, and we will call upon thy name."

question: What musical tune and testimony instruction are specified in the superscription of Psalm 80?
opt1: 'upon Shoshannim-Eduth' (Lilies of the Testimony), A Psalm of Asaph
opt2: 'upon Gittith' (The Winepress), A Psalm of Asaph
opt3: 'upon Jonath-elem-rechokim' (The Silent Dove), A Michtam of David
opt4: 'upon Alamoth' (Maiden Sopranos), A Song for the Sons of Korah
correct: 'upon Shoshannim-Eduth' (Lilies of the Testimony), A Psalm of Asaph
explanation: 'Shoshannim-Eduth' means 'Lilies of the Testimony', indicating a lovely melody paired with solemn covenant witness, authored by Asaph. Psalm 80:Title (KJV) - "To the chief Musician upon Shoshannim-Eduth, A Psalm of Asaph."

question: What dynamic instrumental orchestra is summoned for festive celebration in Psalm 81:1-2?
opt1: "Sing aloud unto God our strength: make a joyful noise unto the God of Jacob. Take a psalm, and bring hither the timbrel, the pleasant harp with the psaltery."
opt2: "Praise the Lord with the sound of the horn: make music before the King with stringed instruments and bronze cymbals;"
opt3: "Exalt the Almighty in the sanctuary: sound the double flute and strike the ten-stringed lute in Zion;"
opt4: "Rejoice in the Holy One of Israel: blow the trumpets of victory and play upon the golden lyre with singing;"
correct: "Sing aloud unto God our strength: make a joyful noise unto the God of Jacob. Take a psalm, and bring hither the timbrel, the pleasant harp with the psaltery."
explanation: Festival joy engages the whole ensemble: singing aloud, striking the timbrel (tambourine), and blending the sweet melodies of the harp (kinnor) and psaltery (nevel). Psalm 81:1-2 (KJV) - "Sing aloud unto God our strength: make a joyful noise unto the God of Jacob. Take a psalm, and bring hither the timbrel, the pleasant harp with the psaltery."

question: What festival calendar dates are appointed for blowing the sacred shofar trumpet in Psalm 81:3?
opt1: "Sound the ram's horn at the Passover, at the evening twilight, on the day of unleavened bread;"
opt2: "Blow up the trumpet in the new moon, in the time appointed, on our solemn feast day."
opt3: "Blow the silver clarion on the Day of Atonement, in the tenth day of the month, before the mercy seat;"
opt4: "Sound the trumpet at the sunrise of the sabbath, on every new moon, in the courts of Jerusalem;"
correct: "Blow up the trumpet in the new moon, in the time appointed, on our solemn feast day."
explanation: Directing the blowing of the shofar at the New Moon (Rosh Hashanah / Feast of Trumpets) and at the full moon ('the time appointed' / Feast of Tabernacles). Psalm 81:3 (KJV) - "Blow up the trumpet in the new moon, in the time appointed, on our solemn feast day."

question: What physical burdens of Egyptian slavery did God lift from Israel's shoulders and hands in Psalm 81:6?
opt1: "I broke the iron yoke from his neck: his feet were freed from the clay of the brickfield"
opt2: "I took away the whip of the taskmaster: his hands were released from carrying stone"
opt3: "I removed his shoulder from the burden: his hands were delivered from the pots."
opt4: "I shattered the chains of Pharaoh: his arms were delivered from the oars of the galleys"
correct: "I removed his shoulder from the burden: his hands were delivered from the pots."
explanation: Divine emancipation: God lifted the heavy basket-loads off the slave's chafed shoulders and freed their hands from handling clay brick-making pots. Psalm 81:6 (KJV) - "I removed his shoulder from the burden: his hands were delivered from the pots."

question: From what mysterious theophanic location did God answer Israel, and where did He test them in Psalm 81:7?
opt1: "I spoke unto thee out of the burning bush: I tried thee in the wilderness of Sin. Selah."
opt2: "I answered thy cry from the pillar of cloud: I tested thy faith at the waters of Marah. Selah."
opt3: "I delivered thee out of the depths of the sea: I proved thy heart at the mountain of Horeb. Selah."
opt4: "I answered thee in the secret place of thunder: I proved thee at the waters of Meribah. Selah."
correct: "I answered thee in the secret place of thunder: I proved thee at the waters of Meribah. Selah."
explanation: God revealed His presence amid Sinai's dark thunderous cloud ('the secret place of thunder') and tested their faith during the water crisis at Meribah (Ex 17; Num 20). Psalm 81:7 (KJV) - "Thou calledst in trouble, and I delivered thee; I answered thee in the secret place of thunder: I proved thee at the waters of Meribah. Selah."

question: What famous promise of boundless divine generosity is conditioned upon Israel's faith in Psalm 81:10?
opt1: "I am the LORD thy God, which brought thee out of the land of Egypt: open thy mouth wide, and I will fill it."
opt2: "I am the Almighty that divided the sea: ask of me great things, and I will multiply thy cattle;"
opt3: "I am the God of Abraham thy father: stretch forth thy hands, and I will pour out my blessings;"
opt4: "I am the Holy One of Jacob: call upon my name, and I will give thee the treasures of the heathen;"
correct: "I am the LORD thy God, which brought thee out of the land of Egypt: open thy mouth wide, and I will fill it."
explanation: Like parent birds feeding nestlings, God invites His redeemed children to open their mouths wide in expectant faith, promising to fill every need with abundance. Psalm 81:10 (KJV) - "I am the LORD thy God, which brought thee out of the land of Egypt: open thy mouth wide, and I will fill it."

question: What judicial abandonment overtook Israel when they refused to hearken to God's voice in Psalm 81:11-12?
opt1: "Therefore I delivered them into the hand of the Philistines: and scattered their tribes in the wilderness;"
opt2: "So I gave them up unto their own hearts' lust: and they walked in their own counsels."
opt3: "So my wrath consumed their princes with fire: and they wandered in darkness forty years;"
opt4: "And I withdrew my presence from their camp: and left them to perish by the sword of the Amorite;"
correct: "So I gave them up unto their own hearts' lust: and they walked in their own counsels."
explanation: The most terrible judgment: when sinners persistently reject God's voice, He judicially surrenders them to the unchecked desires of their own corrupt hearts (Rom 1:24). Psalm 81:12 (KJV) - "So I gave them up unto their own hearts' lust: and they walked in their own counsels."

question: What poignant divine lament expresses God's yearning for His people's obedience in Psalm 81:13-14?
opt1: "How often would I have gathered the children of Zion, but ye refused to walk in my statutes;"
opt2: "Would that my heritage had kept my law, then had their peace flowed like an overflowing river;"
opt3: "Oh that my people had hearkened unto me, and Israel had walked in my ways! I should soon have subdued their enemies, and turned my hand against their adversaries."
opt4: "Oh that the seed of Jacob had feared my name, then had their horn been exalted above the heathen;"
correct: "Oh that my people had hearkened unto me, and Israel had walked in my ways! I should soon have subdued their enemies, and turned my hand against their adversaries."
explanation: A glimpse of the grieving heart of God: had Israel simply listened and walked in His ways, Yahweh would have effortlessly and swiftly routed all their foes. Psalm 81:13-14 (KJV) - "Oh that my people had hearkened unto me, and Israel had walked in my ways! I should soon have subdued their enemies, and turned my hand against their adversaries."

question: With what two lavish delicacies would God have satisfied an obedient Israel in Psalm 81:16?
opt1: "With clusters of grapes from Eshcol: and with rich milk and sweet wine from Lebanon"
opt2: "With the choice fat of lambs: and with rivers of pure olive oil from the presses of Zion"
opt3: "With manna from opened heavens: and with sweet pomegranates from the gardens of promise"
opt4: "He should have fed them also with the finest of the wheat: and with honey out of the rock should I have satisfied thee."
correct: "He should have fed them also with the finest of the wheat: and with honey out of the rock should I have satisfied thee."
explanation: Supernatural covenant abundance: nourishing them with the plumpest kernel of wheat ('finest of the wheat') and wild honey dripping even from barren flinty crags ('honey out of the rock'). Psalm 81:16 (KJV) - "He should have fed them also with the finest of the wheat: and with honey out of the rock should I have satisfied thee."

question: What musical instrument or rhythm setting appears in the title of Psalm 81, shared with Psalms 8 and 84?
opt1: 'upon Gittith' (A Psalm of Asaph)
opt2: 'upon Mahalath' (A Maskil of David)
opt3: 'upon Muth-labben' (A Song of Victory)
opt4: 'upon Neginoth' (A Stringed Psalm)
correct: 'upon Gittith' (A Psalm of Asaph)
explanation: 'Gittith' is associated either with a musical instrument from Gath or a joyful vintage tune chanted during the autumn grape harvest. Psalm 81:Title (KJV) - "To the chief Musician upon Gittith, A Psalm of Asaph."

question: What unknown language did Joseph encounter in Egypt according to Psalm 81:5?
opt1: "where the hieroglyphs of Pharaoh were written in stone"
opt2: "where I heard a language that I understood not."
opt3: "where the magicians spoke in the tongue of serpents"
opt4: "where foreign taskmasters shouted in an alien voice"
correct: "where I heard a language that I understood not."
explanation: Israel felt the profound alienation of exile in Egypt, dwelling among a foreign culture speaking an unintelligible pagan tongue. Psalm 81:5 (KJV) - "This he ordained in Joseph for a testimony, when he went out through the land of Egypt: where I heard a language that I understood not."

question: What solemn heavenly assize where God presides over human magistrates opens Psalm 82:1?
opt1: "The Lord of hosts sitteth upon the throne of his holiness: he reproveth the kings of the earth;"
opt2: "God standeth in the congregation of the mighty; he judgeth among the gods."
opt3: "The Almighty hath summoned the princes of Israel: he weigheth their judgments in the balances of righteousness;"
opt4: "God hath taken his place in the assembly of the elders: he rebuketh the judges of Zion;"
correct: "God standeth in the congregation of the mighty; he judgeth among the gods."
explanation: God convenes a judicial trial: standing up in the council of rulers and magistrates (titled 'gods' / elohim because they exercise delegated divine authority) to judge their conduct. Psalm 82:1 (KJV) - "God standeth in the congregation of the mighty; he judgeth among the gods."

question: What penetrating indictment of judicial corruption and partiality is delivered in Psalm 82:2?
opt1: "Why take ye bribes from the rich, and pervert the cause of the fatherless? Selah."
opt2: "How darest ye justify the ungodly for silver, and turn aside the poor in the gate? Selah."
opt3: "How long will ye judge unjustly, and accept the persons of the wicked? Selah."
opt4: "Why do ye mock the statutes of Moses, and decree unrighteous decrees against the innocent? Selah."
correct: "How long will ye judge unjustly, and accept the persons of the wicked? Selah."
explanation: God confronts civil magistrates for perverting court equity by showing favoritism to wealthy criminals ('accept the persons of the wicked'). Psalm 82:2 (KJV) - "How long will ye judge unjustly, and accept the persons of the wicked? Selah."

question: What fourfold legal mandate to protect the weak and vulnerable is commanded in Psalm 82:3-4?
opt1: "Pity the stranger and the widow: avenge the blood of the innocent: give bread to the hungry: break the yoke of the oppressor;"
opt2: "Hearken to the cry of the oppressed: vindicate the captive: execute judgment without fear: restore the heritage of the poor;"
opt3: "Open your mouth for the dumb: plead the cause of the destitute: punish the violent: establish righteousness at the gate;"
opt4: "Defend the poor and fatherless: do justice to the afflicted and needy. Deliver the poor and needy: rid them out of the hand of the wicked."
correct: "Defend the poor and fatherless: do justice to the afflicted and needy. Deliver the poor and needy: rid them out of the hand of the wicked."
explanation: The core biblical duty of civil government: actively advocating for the defenseless (orphans, poor, afflicted, needy) and rescuing them from predatory abusers. Psalm 82:3-4 (KJV) - "Defend the poor and fatherless: do justice to the afflicted and needy. Deliver the poor and needy: rid them out of the hand of the wicked."

question: What cosmic and societal catastrophe results from the willful ignorance of corrupt judges in Psalm 82:5?
opt1: "They know not, neither will they understand; they walk on in darkness: all the foundations of the earth are out of course."
opt2: "Their eyes are blinded by bribes; they wander in confusion: the land is filled with violence and tears;"
opt3: "They despise instruction, and harden their necks: the pillars of the sanctuary are shaken into dust;"
opt4: "They follow after vanity, and love deceit: the thrones of the righteous are overturned by the heathen;"
correct: "They know not, neither will they understand; they walk on in darkness: all the foundations of the earth are out of course."
explanation: When the justice system is corrupted by ignorant, darkness-loving judges, the entire moral and societal framework ('all the foundations of the earth') destabilizes into anarchy. Psalm 82:5 (KJV) - "They know not, neither will they understand; they walk on in darkness: all the foundations of the earth are out of course."

question: Which verse from Psalm 82:6 did Jesus quote in John 10:34-36 to defend His claim of divine Sonship?
opt1: "God standeth in the congregation of the mighty; he judgeth among the gods;"
opt2: "I have said, Ye are gods; and all of you are children of the most High."
opt3: "Defend the poor and fatherless: do justice to the afflicted and needy;"
opt4: "Arise, O God, judge the earth: for thou shalt inherit all nations;"
correct: "I have said, Ye are gods; and all of you are children of the most High."
explanation: Jesus cited Psalm 82:6 to argue that if mortal human magistrates commissioned with God's word were titled 'gods', it was not blasphemous for the One sanctified and sent by the Father to say, 'I am the Son of God'. Psalm 82:6 (KJV) - "I have said, Ye are gods; and all of you are children of the most High."

question: What sobering demotion and common mortal death awaits these corrupt magistrates in Psalm 82:7?
opt1: "Yet shall your glory turn to dust, and your souls go down into Sheol"
opt2: "For your sceptres shall be shattered, and ye shall perish like common clay"
opt3: "But ye shall die like men, and fall like one of the princes."
opt4: "Behold, the worms shall devour your flesh, and your crowns shall fade away"
correct: "But ye shall die like men, and fall like one of the princes."
explanation: Despite their elevated titles ('gods'), these magistrates possess zero inherent divinity; they are mortal flesh, destined to die like ordinary humans and fall like any secular prince. Psalm 82:7 (KJV) - "But ye shall die like men, and fall like one of the princes."

question: What worldwide judicial prayer concludes Psalm 82:8?
opt1: "Execute thy judgment, O Lord of hosts: for the kingdoms of the world belong unto thee;"
opt2: "Reign in righteousness, O Most High: for thou hast redeemed thy chosen people from death;"
opt3: "Stand up, O King of Zion: for thy throne endureth throughout all generations;"
opt4: "Arise, O God, judge the earth: for thou shalt inherit all nations."
correct: "Arise, O God, judge the earth: for thou shalt inherit all nations."
explanation: Human courts having failed miserably, the psalmist appeals to the supreme Sovereign to take the bench personally, inheriting and ruling all global nations with perfect justice. Psalm 82:8 (KJV) - "Arise, O God, judge the earth: for thou shalt inherit all nations."

question: What does the Hebrew title 'elohim' ('gods') specifically designate when applied to human beings in Psalm 82:1 and 82:6?
opt1: Duly appointed human civil judges and rulers acting as official representatives and administrators of God's law on earth (Exodus 21:6; 22:8-9)
opt2: Fallen angels and demonic principalities assigned to oversee pagan nations
opt3: Pagan idols carved out of cedar wood and overlaid with silver in Babylon
opt4: The ancient patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob reigning in paradise
correct: Duly appointed human civil judges and rulers acting as official representatives and administrators of God's law on earth (Exodus 21:6; 22:8-9)
explanation: In Hebrew jurisprudence, judges were called elohim because they stood in God's place to execute His justice; when they perverted justice, they invited God's direct trial. Psalm 82:1 (KJV) - "God standeth in the congregation of the mighty; he judgeth among the gods."

question: What phrase in Psalm 82:2 describes judicial partiality based on personal bribery or status?
opt1: "receive the gifts of the violent"
opt2: "accept the persons of the wicked"
opt3: "listen to the counsel of the ungodly"
opt4: "justify the deceitful for silver"
correct: "accept the persons of the wicked"
explanation: The Hebrew idiom nasa panim ('lift up the face' / 'accept the person') means granting biased judicial favor to individuals based on their wealth, rank, or bribes rather than facts. Psalm 82:2 (KJV) - "How long will ye judge unjustly, and accept the persons of the wicked? Selah."

question: Who authored Psalm 82 according to its superscription?
opt1: A Psalm of David
opt2: A Song of the Sons of Korah
opt3: A Psalm of Asaph
opt4: A Prayer of Ethan the Ezrahite
correct: A Psalm of Asaph
explanation: Psalm 82 is attributed to Asaph, fitting his prophetic concern for judicial integrity and the moral foundations of society. Psalm 82:Title (KJV) - "A Psalm of Asaph."

question: What triple plea against divine silence in the face of roaring hostile confederacies opens Psalm 83:1-2?
opt1: "Hear my voice, O Lord, in the day of trouble: be not far from me, O my Savior: For the heathen have compassed Zion;"
opt2: "Awake, O God of hosts, why sleepest thou? arise and defend thy people: For the proud have sharpened their swords;"
opt3: "Keep not thou silence, O God: hold not thy peace, and be not still, O God. For, lo, thine enemies make a tumult: and they that hate thee have lifted up the head."
opt4: "Be not silent unto our tears, O King of Jacob: look down from heaven and behold: For an army of nations hath gathered;"
correct: "Keep not thou silence, O God: hold not thy peace, and be not still, O God. For, lo, thine enemies make a tumult: and they that hate thee have lifted up the head."
explanation: Faced with a massive multi-national military encirclement, Asaph pleads with God not to remain a silent, inactive bystander ('Keep not thou silence ... hold not thy peace ... be not still'). Psalm 83:1-2 (KJV) - "Keep not thou silence, O God: hold not thy peace, and be not still, O God. For, lo, thine enemies make a tumult: and they that hate thee have lifted up the head."

question: What genocidal conspiracy against the national existence of Israel is exposed in Psalm 83:3-4?
opt1: "They have formed a league against Zion, saying, Let us burn their sanctuary: that their law may perish from the earth;"
opt2: "They have taken counsel with one accord, saying, Let us plunder their cities: that the seed of David may serve our kings;"
opt3: "They have conspired in secret, saying, Let us divide their inheritance: that none may worship the God of Abraham;"
opt4: "They have taken crafty counsel against thy people, and consulted against thy hidden ones. They have said, Come, and let us cut them off from being a nation; that the name of Israel may be no more in remembrance."
correct: "They have taken crafty counsel against thy people, and consulted against thy hidden ones. They have said, Come, and let us cut them off from being a nation; that the name of Israel may be no more in remembrance."
explanation: Total anti-Semitic annihilation: the confederate alliance schemes not merely to plunder, but to wipe Israel off the map entirely so the very memory of Israel's name is erased. Psalm 83:3-4 (KJV) - "They have taken crafty counsel against thy people, and consulted against thy hidden ones. They have said, Come, and let us cut them off from being a nation; that the name of Israel may be no more in remembrance."

question: Which ten specific nations and tribes comprise the hostile confederacy in Psalm 83:6-8?
opt1: Edom, Ishmaelites, Moab, Hagarenes, Gebal, Ammon, Amalek, Philistines, Tyre, and Assur (Assyria)
opt2: Egypt, Babylon, Syria, Medes, Persians, Hittites, Amorites, Jebusites, Moab, and Midian
opt3: Damascus, Rome, Greece, Ethiopia, Libya, Cush, Sheba, Seba, Tarshish, and Chaldea
opt4: Arameans, Keilah, Ziph, Gath, Ekron, Ashdod, Gaza, Edom, Ammon, and Canaanites
correct: Edom, Ishmaelites, Moab, Hagarenes, Gebal, Ammon, Amalek, Philistines, Tyre, and Assur (Assyria)
explanation: A ten-member hostile encirclement: Transjordan nations, desert nomads, and coastal powers joined by northern imperial superpower Assur. Psalm 83:6-7 (KJV) - "The tabernacles of Edom, and the Ishmaelites; of Moab, and the Hagarenes; Gebal, and Ammon, and Amalek; the Philistines with the inhabitants of Tyre;"

question: What two Judges-era victories at the brook of Kishon does the psalmist invoke in Psalm 83:9-10?
opt1: "Do unto them as unto the five kings of the Amorites, when the sun stood still at Gibeon;"
opt2: "Do unto them as unto the Midianites; as to Sisera, as to Jabin, at the brook of Kison: Which perished at Endor: they became as dung for the earth."
opt3: "Smite them as thou smotest the army of Pharaoh at the Red Sea, and the kings of Bashan;"
opt4: "Overthrow them as thou overthrewest the host of Sennacherib outside the gates of Jerusalem;"
correct: "Do unto them as unto the Midianites; as to Sisera, as to Jabin, at the brook of Kison: Which perished at Endor: they became as dung for the earth."
explanation: Asaph prays that God will duplicate Gideon's victory over Midian and Deborah/Barak's overthrow of Sisera and Jabin at the Kishon river, whose unburied armies fertilized the soil like dung. Psalm 83:9-10 (KJV) - "Do unto them as unto the Midianites; as to Sisera, as to Jabin, at the brook of Kison: Which perished at Endor: they became as dung for the earth."

question: Which four Midianite commanders from the Book of Judges are named in Psalm 83:11?
opt1: Sihon and Og (kings), and Balak and Balaam (princes)
opt2: Agag and Goliath (warriors), and Hadadezer and Rezon (kings)
opt3: Oreb and Zeeb (princes), and Zebah and Zalmunna (kings)
opt4: Eglon and Sisera (rulers), and Adonibezek and Nahash (captains)
correct: Oreb and Zeeb (princes), and Zebah and Zalmunna (kings)
explanation: Gideon slew Midianite generals Oreb ('Raven') and Zeeb ('Wolf') at the winepress and rock (Judg 7:25), and executed Midianite kings Zebah and Zalmunna (Judg 8:21). Psalm 83:11 (KJV) - "Make their nobles like Oreb, and like Zeeb: yea, all their princes as Zebah, and as Zalmunna:"

question: What sacrilegious motive driving the confederacy is exposed in Psalm 83:12?
opt1: "Who said, Let us carry away the ark of the covenant into our temples"
opt2: "Who said, Let us make the children of Judah our perpetual bondservants"
opt3: "Who said, Let us destroy the priesthood of Aaron from before the altar"
opt4: "Who said, Let us take to ourselves the houses of God in possession."
correct: "Who said, Let us take to ourselves the houses of God in possession."
explanation: Their brazen insolence targeted God's personal property: plotting to seize the sacred sanctuaries and grazing pastures ('houses of God') of Yahweh for themselves. Psalm 83:12 (KJV) - "Who said, Let us take to ourselves the houses of God in possession."

question: What dynamic similes of windblown tumbleweed, hurricane, and mountain wildfire are invoked in Psalm 83:13-15?
opt1: "O my God, make them like a wheel; as the stubble before the wind. As the fire burneth a wood, and as the flame setteth the mountains on fire; So persecute them with thy tempest, and make them afraid with thy storm."
opt2: "O Lord, scatter them like dust before the chariot; as dry chaff in the whirlwind: let thy lightning consume their tents;"
opt3: "Make them as melting wax before the furnace; as foam upon the raging sea: overtake them with sudden destruction;"
opt4: "Let them vanish like morning mist; as withered grass upon the housetops: drown their host in the overflowing torrent;"
correct: "O my God, make them like a wheel; as the stubble before the wind. As the fire burneth a wood, and as the flame setteth the mountains on fire; So persecute them with thy tempest, and make them afraid with thy storm."
explanation: Asaph prays that foes be spun like whirling tumbleweeds (galgal / 'a wheel'), blown like dry stubble, and consumed like a raging forest wildfire racing across mountain slopes. Psalm 83:13-15 (KJV) - "O my God, make them like a wheel; as the stubble before the wind. As the fire burneth a wood, and as the flame setteth the mountains on fire; So persecute them with thy tempest, and make them afraid with thy storm."

question: What redemptive and evangelistic purpose underlies the humiliation of the enemies in Psalm 83:16?
opt1: "Smite their princes with blindness; that they may bring silver to the sanctuary of Zion"
opt2: "Fill their faces with shame; that they may seek thy name, O LORD."
opt3: "Shatter their iron chariots; that they may bow down before the king of Judah"
opt4: "Break their proud bows; that they may confess the covenant of Abraham"
correct: "Fill their faces with shame; that they may seek thy name, O LORD."
explanation: The ultimate goal of divine discipline is not vindictive annihilation, but redemptive awakening: filling their faces with humiliating defeat so that they seek the saving Name of Yahweh. Psalm 83:16 (KJV) - "Fill their faces with shame; that they may seek thy name, O LORD."

question: What grand theological climax and revelation of God's supreme Name concludes Psalm 83:18?
opt1: "That all nations may confess that God is the Creator of heaven and earth and King of kings"
opt2: "So that the kingdoms of the world may fear the Holy One of Israel and worship at his holy hill"
opt3: "That men may know that thou, whose name alone is JEHOVAH, art the most high over all the earth."
opt4: "And all flesh shall declare that the Lord of hosts reigneth in Mount Zion for ever and ever"
correct: "That men may know that thou, whose name alone is JEHOVAH, art the most high over all the earth."
explanation: One of only four verses in the KJV Old Testament where the sacred covenant name JEHOVAH is fully rendered in all caps (along with Ex 6:3; Ps 83:18; Isa 12:2; 26:4), demonstrating His cosmic supremacy as Elyon ('the most high over all the earth'). Psalm 83:18 (KJV) - "That men may know that thou, whose name alone is JEHOVAH, art the most high over all the earth."

question: What special milestone does Psalm 83 represent in the overall structure of the Book of Psalms?
opt1: It marks the exact mathematical midpoint of the entire Old Testament
opt2: It is the concluding psalm of Book III of the Psalter
opt3: It is the only psalm in Book III written by King Solomon
opt4: It is the final psalm of the 12-psalm Asaphic collection (Psalms 50, 73-83)
correct: It is the final psalm of the 12-psalm Asaphic collection (Psalms 50, 73-83)
explanation: Psalm 83 concludes the famous Asaph collection (which began in Psalm 50 and continued through Psalms 73-83), highlighting Asaph's prophetic focus on national history and God's sovereignty. Psalm 83:Title (KJV) - "A Song or Psalm of Asaph."

question: What exclamation of delight and total soul-thirst for God's sanctuary opens Psalm 84:1-2?
opt1: "How glorious is thy temple, O King of Zion! My spirit rejoiceth in the courts of praise: my soul thirsteth for the rock of salvation;"
opt2: "How beautiful is Mount Moriah, O Lord our shield! My heart desireth to dwell in thy holy presence: my lips magnify the Almighty;"
opt3: "How excellent are thy dwelling places, O God of Jacob! My eyes weep for the courts of peace: my tongue blesseth the Holy One;"
opt4: "How amiable are thy tabernacles, O LORD of hosts! My soul longeth, yea, even fainteth for the courts of the LORD: my heart and my flesh crieth out for the living God."
correct: "How amiable are thy tabernacles, O LORD of hosts! My soul longeth, yea, even fainteth for the courts of the LORD: my heart and my flesh crieth out for the living God."
explanation: The pilgrim bursts into ecstatic adoration: God's tabernacles are supremely lovely ('amiable'), causing the entire person - soul, heart, and physical flesh - to faint with longing for the living God. Psalm 84:1-2 (KJV) - "How amiable are thy tabernacles, O LORD of hosts! My soul longeth, yea, even fainteth for the courts of the LORD: my heart and my flesh crieth out for the living God."

question: What small, humble birds find a secure sanctuary and nest near God's altars in Psalm 84:3?
opt1: "Yea, the sparrow hath found an house, and the swallow a nest for herself, where she may lay her young, even thine altars, O LORD of hosts, my King, and my God."
opt2: "Even the wild dove hath built a shelter in the cedar beams, and the fledgling in the holy place;"
opt3: "Behold, the eagle maketh her perch upon the battlements, and the turtledove beneath the altar of incense;"
opt4: "Yea, the harmless sparrow resteth under the wings of the cherubim, and the swallow in the courts of Zion;"
correct: "Yea, the sparrow hath found an house, and the swallow a nest for herself, where she may lay her young, even thine altars, O LORD of hosts, my King, and my God."
explanation: Envious of tiny, insignificant birds, the pilgrim notes that the frail sparrow and restless swallow find permanent homes and raise their young right beside the sacrificial altars of Yahweh Sabaoth. Psalm 84:3 (KJV) - "Yea, the sparrow hath found an house, and the swallow a nest for herself, where she may lay her young, even thine altars, O LORD of hosts, my King, and my God."

question: What perpetual occupation marks the beatitude of temple dwellers in Psalm 84:4?
opt1: "Blessed are the priests that minister at thine altar: they shall behold thy glory for ever. Selah."
opt2: "Blessed are they that dwell in thy house: they will be still praising thee. Selah."
opt3: "Blessed are the Levites that watch the sacred gates: their joy shall never depart. Selah."
opt4: "Blessed are the pure in heart that enter thy courts: they shall eat of the fatness of Zion. Selah."
correct: "Blessed are they that dwell in thy house: they will be still praising thee. Selah."
explanation: Permanent residency in God's presence produces unending, spontaneous worship: those who abide in His house 'will be still [continually] praising thee'. Psalm 84:4 (KJV) - "Blessed are they that dwell in thy house: they will be still praising thee. Selah."

question: How do pilgrims transform arid adversity as they journey toward Zion in Psalm 84:5-6?
opt1: "Blessed are the pilgrims who seek the city of God: when they cross the dry desert, living streams gush forth;"
opt2: "Blessed are the righteous whose steps are established: passing through the barren wilderness they find sweet manna;"
opt3: "Blessed is the man whose strength is in thee; in whose heart are the ways of them. Who passing through the valley of Baca make it a well; the rain also filleth the pools."
opt4: "Blessed is the congregation of Jacob: walking through the valley of shadow, the Lord is their shepherd;"
correct: "Blessed is the man whose strength is in thee; in whose heart are the ways of them. Who passing through the valley of Baca make it a well; the rain also filleth the pools."
explanation: The valley of Baca ('weeping' / arid balsam trees) represents barren trials; yet pilgrims anchored in divine strength turn places of tears into bubbling springs of spiritual refreshment. Psalm 84:5-6 (KJV) - "Blessed is the man whose strength is in thee; in whose heart are the ways of them. Who passing through the valley of Baca make it a well; the rain also filleth the pools."

question: What paradoxical increase of energy marks the Zion pilgrims' journey in Psalm 84:7?
opt1: "Their youth is renewed like the eagle, until they stand within the golden gates of Jerusalem"
opt2: "They run and are not weary, until they bow before the ark of the covenant in the sanctuary"
opt3: "They march without stumbling, until the light of the temple shineth upon their faces"
opt4: "They go from strength to strength, every one of them in Zion appeareth before God."
correct: "They go from strength to strength, every one of them in Zion appeareth before God."
explanation: Unlike ordinary physical journeys that induce fatigue, the spiritual pilgrimage to Zion infuses escalating divine stamina: going 'from strength to strength' until standing safely before God. Psalm 84:7 (KJV) - "They go from strength to strength, every one of them in Zion appeareth before God."

question: What famous comparative valuation of a single day in God's presence is declared in Psalm 84:10?
opt1: "For a day in thy courts is better than a thousand. I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God, than to dwell in the tents of wickedness."
opt2: "For an hour in thy sanctuary surpasseth ten thousand years of earthly glory: I had rather serve as a hewer of wood in Zion;"
opt3: "For a moment before thine altar is sweeter than all the kingdoms of the world: I had rather sit in sackcloth at thy gate;"
opt4: "For one morning in thy presence exceedeth a lifetime of earthly pomp: I had rather wash the feet of the priests in Jerusalem;"
correct: "For a day in thy courts is better than a thousand. I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God, than to dwell in the tents of wickedness."
explanation: One solitary day in communion with God eclipses a thousand days of secular pleasure; standing as a humble threshold-guard (doorkeeper) in God's house far surpasses residing in luxury inside ungodly palaces. Psalm 84:10 (KJV) - "For a day in thy courts is better than a thousand. I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God, than to dwell in the tents of wickedness."

question: What celestial and protective metaphors are ascribed to God, and what boundless promise is given in Psalm 84:11?
opt1: "For the Almighty is a rock and high tower: he will grant peace and honor: all blessings shall follow the righteous;"
opt2: "For the LORD God is a sun and shield: the LORD will give grace and glory: no good thing will he withhold from them that walk uprightly."
opt3: "For the God of hosts is our light and salvation: he will bestow lovingkindness and truth: he will satisfy the soul with good;"
opt4: "For the King of Zion is a fortress and shield: he will multiply righteousness and strength: no weapon shall prosper against the saints;"
correct: "For the LORD God is a sun and shield: the LORD will give grace and glory: no good thing will he withhold from them that walk uprightly."
explanation: God is our Sun (imparting life, warmth, and light) and our Shield (providing total defense); He bestows both saving grace in this life and celestial glory hereafter, withholding zero good things from the upright. Psalm 84:11 (KJV) - "For the LORD God is a sun and shield: the LORD will give grace and glory: no good thing will he withhold from them that walk uprightly."

question: What final beatitude seals the entire message of Psalm 84 in verse 12?
opt1: "O God of Jacob, blessed are all they that put their trust under the shadow of thy wings"
opt2: "O King of glory, blessed is the nation whose God is the Lord for ever and ever"
opt3: "O LORD of hosts, blessed is the man that trusteth in thee."
opt4: "O Holy One of Israel, blessed is the soul that hopeth in thy steadfast covenant mercy"
correct: "O LORD of hosts, blessed is the man that trusteth in thee."
explanation: The psalm culminates in the third and crowning beatitude of the chapter: ultimate human happiness and beatitude rest in unreserved personal trust in Yahweh Sabaoth. Psalm 84:12 (KJV) - "O LORD of hosts, blessed is the man that trusteth in thee."

question: Who authored Psalm 84 according to its superscription, and to what musical instrument was it set?
opt1: 'To the chief Musician on Neginoth, A Psalm of David'
opt2: 'To the chief Musician upon Shoshannim, A Maschil of Asaph'
opt3: 'To the chief Musician upon Mahalath, A Song of Heman the Ezrahite'
opt4: 'To the chief Musician upon Gittith, A Psalm for the sons of Korah'
correct: 'To the chief Musician upon Gittith, A Psalm for the sons of Korah'
explanation: Composed by the Levitical guild of the sons of Korah (temple gatekeepers and musicians) and set to the joyous vintage melody of the 'Gittith'. Psalm 84:Title (KJV) - "To the chief Musician upon Gittith, A Psalm for the sons of Korah."

question: What three distinct beatitudes ('Blessed') structure the spiritual progression of Psalm 84?
opt1: 1) Blessed are the dwellers in God's house (v. 4); 2) Blessed are the pilgrims whose strength is in God (v. 5); 3) Blessed is the believer who trusts in God (v. 12)
opt2: 1) Blessed is the king (v. 1); 2) Blessed are the priests (v. 4); 3) Blessed is Jerusalem (v. 10)
opt3: 1) Blessed are the poor (v. 3); 2) Blessed are the meek (v. 6); 3) Blessed are the pure in heart (v. 11)
opt4: 1) Blessed are the singers (v. 2); 2) Blessed are the gatekeepers (v. 8); 3) Blessed are the elders (v. 12)
correct: 1) Blessed are the dwellers in God's house (v. 4); 2) Blessed are the pilgrims whose strength is in God (v. 5); 3) Blessed is the believer who trusts in God (v. 12)
explanation: A master threefold beatitude structure: permanent sanctuary communion, pilgrim journeying in divine strength, and universal individual faith. Psalm 84:4, 12 (KJV) - "Blessed are they that dwell in thy house: they will be still praising thee ... O LORD of hosts, blessed is the man that trusteth in thee."

question: What threefold recollection of past national restoration and forgiveness opens Psalm 85:1-2?
opt1: "Lord, thou hast been favourable unto thy land: thou hast brought back the captivity of Jacob. Thou hast forgiven the iniquity of thy people, thou hast covered all their sin. Selah."
opt2: "O God, thou hast established thy sanctuary in Zion: thou hast scattered the armies of the heathen. Thou hast remembered the covenant of David. Selah;"
opt3: "The Lord hath poured out his blessing upon Jerusalem: thou hast redeemed the tribes from the iron furnace. Thou hast washed away our transgressions. Selah;"
opt4: "Thou hast built up the broken walls of Judah, O Most High: thou hast turned away the reproach of exile. Thou hast crowned thy people with peace. Selah;"
correct: "Lord, thou hast been favourable unto thy land: thou hast brought back the captivity of Jacob. Thou hast forgiven the iniquity of thy people, thou hast covered all their sin. Selah."
explanation: Post-exilic thanksgiving recounts God's historical favor: returning the exiles of Jacob, forgiving their iniquity, and completely covering (atoning for) all their sins. Psalm 85:1-2 (KJV) - "Lord, thou hast been favourable unto thy land: thou hast brought back the captivity of Jacob. Thou hast forgiven the iniquity of thy people, thou hast covered all their sin. Selah."

question: What famous revival prayer links spiritual quickening with holy joy in Psalm 85:6?
opt1: "Awake, O Lord, and pour out thy spirit: that Zion may sing praises unto thy name;"
opt2: "Wilt thou not revive us again: that thy people may rejoice in thee?"
opt3: "Restore unto us the joy of thy salvation: that our priests may minister with righteousness;"
opt4: "Heal our backslidings, O God of Jacob: that thy congregation may celebrate thy wonders;"
correct: "Wilt thou not revive us again: that thy people may rejoice in thee?"
explanation: True revival is God-centered: Asaph pleads for God to breathe new spiritual life into the community so that their joy may terminate entirely in God Himself. Psalm 85:6 (KJV) - "Wilt thou not revive us again: that thy people may rejoice in thee?"

question: What resolution to hear God's oracle of peace is paired with a warning against backsliding in Psalm 85:8?
opt1: "I will attend unto the voice of the sanctuary: for he will proclaim righteousness: but let none transgress his statutes;"
opt2: "My soul waiteth for the decree of the Almighty: for he will heal our land: but let not Israel walk after idols;"
opt3: "I will hear what God the LORD will speak: for he will speak peace unto his people, and to his saints: but let them not turn again to folly."
opt4: "I will hearken to the word of the covenant: for he will give rest unto Zion: but let the wicked cease from iniquity;"
correct: "I will hear what God the LORD will speak: for he will speak peace unto his people, and to his saints: but let them not turn again to folly."
explanation: God's promised covenant shalom ('peace') is unconditional in its source but demands holy vigilance: saints must never abuse grace by returning to their former sinful folly. Psalm 85:8 (KJV) - "I will hear what God the LORD will speak: for he will speak peace unto his people, and to his saints: but let them not turn again to folly."

question: What magnificent personification of divine attributes reconciles at the Cross in Psalm 85:10?
opt1: "Holiness and justice have embraced in Zion; grace and salvation have joined hands before the altar;"
opt2: "Lovingkindness and judgment have kissed upon the mountain; truth and peace have walked in the sanctuary;"
opt3: "Faithfulness and mercy are united in heaven; righteousness and glory have filled the temple;"
opt4: "Mercy and truth are met together; righteousness and peace have kissed each other."
correct: "Mercy and truth are met together; righteousness and peace have kissed each other."
explanation: A breathtaking theological convergence: at the Cross, God's unrelenting Righteousness and Truth satisfy divine justice, while His tender Mercy and Peace embrace the redeemed sinner. Psalm 85:10 (KJV) - "Mercy and truth are met together; righteousness and peace have kissed each other."

question: How do heaven and earth interact in mutual celebration of redemption in Psalm 85:11?
opt1: "Truth shall spring out of the earth; and righteousness shall look down from heaven."
opt2: "Mercy shall descend as gentle rain; and peace shall blossom from every hill"
opt3: "Salvation shall flow like a river; and the glory of God shall shine from the sky"
opt4: "Faithfulness shall sprout like a green vine; and holiness shall illuminate the nations"
correct: "Truth shall spring out of the earth; and righteousness shall look down from heaven."
explanation: A glorious reconciliation of creation: human fidelity and Truth sprout upward like fertile harvest shoots from earth, while heavenly Righteousness smiles downward like radiant sunshine. Psalm 85:11 (KJV) - "Truth shall spring out of the earth; and righteousness shall look down from heaven."

question: What royal herald goes before God to pave the way of His footsteps in Psalm 85:13?
opt1: "Mercy shall be his vanguard; and peace shall establish our path"
opt2: "Righteousness shall go before him; and shall set us in the way of his steps."
opt3: "His glory shall illuminate the highway; and truth shall guide our feet"
opt4: "Salvation shall march before his face; and his lovingkindness shall lead his flock"
correct: "Righteousness shall go before him; and shall set us in the way of his steps."
explanation: Righteousness acts as the royal harbinger clearing the path before God, transforming His sovereign footsteps into a secure moral highway for believers to walk in. Psalm 85:13 (KJV) - "Righteousness shall go before him; and shall set us in the way of his steps."

question: To whom is God's salvation near, and what indwelling reality results in Psalm 85:9?
opt1: "Verily his redemption is promised to the poor; that peace may reign in Jerusalem"
opt2: "Behold, his deliverance is ready for the humble; that holiness may fill the sanctuary"
opt3: "Surely his salvation is nigh them that fear him; that glory may dwell in our land."
opt4: "His mercy is extended to the seed of Jacob; that righteousness may cover the earth"
correct: "Surely his salvation is nigh them that fear him; that glory may dwell in our land."
explanation: The God-fearing experience immediate proximity to divine salvation, ensuring that the visible Shekinah glory of God permanently inhabits their commonwealth. Psalm 85:9 (KJV) - "Surely his salvation is nigh them that fear him; that glory may dwell in our land."

question: What physical agricultural blessing accompanies spiritual restoration in Psalm 85:12?
opt1: "The valleys shall be covered with corn; and the presses shall overflow with new wine"
opt2: "The mountains shall drop sweet milk; and our fields shall blossom with pomegranates"
opt3: "The desert shall become a fruitful orchard; and our cattle shall multiply exceedingly"
opt4: "Yea, the LORD shall give that which is good; and our land shall yield her increase."
correct: "Yea, the LORD shall give that which is good; and our land shall yield her increase."
explanation: Spiritual reconciliation brings tangible covenant renewal: God bestows His goodness, causing parched soil to produce bumper agricultural harvests. Psalm 85:12 (KJV) - "Yea, the LORD shall give that which is good; and our land shall yield her increase."

question: What urgent petition pleads for the cessation of divine displeasure in Psalm 85:4?
opt1: "Turn us, O God of our salvation, and cause thine anger toward us to cease."
opt2: "Heal us, O Lord our shield, and turn away the fierceness of thy wrath"
opt3: "Look upon our affliction, O King of Zion, and remove thy heavy hand from our land"
opt4: "Revive our spirits, O Most High, and extinguish the fire of thy jealousy"
correct: "Turn us, O God of our salvation, and cause thine anger toward us to cease."
explanation: Recognizing that outward restoration from Babylon is hollow without inward conversion, they pray for God to turn their hearts and extinguish His displeasure. Psalm 85:4 (KJV) - "Turn us, O God of our salvation, and cause thine anger toward us to cease."

question: Who authored Psalm 85 according to its superscription?
opt1: A Psalm of Asaph
opt2: A Psalm for the sons of Korah
opt3: A Prayer of David
opt4: A Song of Heman the Ezrahite
correct: A Psalm for the sons of Korah
explanation: Psalm 85 is inscribed to the Levitical guild of the sons of Korah, capturing their signature themes of sanctuary glory, temple peace, and covenant mercy. Psalm 85:Title (KJV) - "To the chief Musician, A Psalm for the sons of Korah."

question: What dual basis of personal helplessness and covenant devotion opens David's prayer in Psalm 86:1-2?
opt1: "Incline thine ear from heaven, O God: for I am weak and afflicted. Protect my life; for I walk in thy law: save the anointed of Zion;"
opt2: "Bow down thine ear, O LORD, hear me: for I am poor and needy. Preserve my soul; for I am holy: O thou my God, save thy servant that trusteth in thee."
opt3: "Hearken unto my supplication, O Lord: for my spirit fainted within me. Defend my head; for I love thy sanctuary: deliver thy servant;"
opt4: "Hear my voice, O Almighty: for I am encompassed with trouble. Preserve my steps; for I offer sacrifices: save the son of David;"
correct: "Bow down thine ear, O LORD, hear me: for I am poor and needy. Preserve my soul; for I am holy: O thou my God, save thy servant that trusteth in thee."
explanation: David pairs profound humility ('poor and needy') with covenant confidence: 'I am holy' (Hebrew chasid - covenant-devoted, walking in loyalty to God). Psalm 86:1-2 (KJV) - "Bow down thine ear, O LORD, hear me: for I am poor and needy. Preserve my soul; for I am holy: O thou my God, save thy servant that trusteth in thee."

question: What triple declaration of God's forgiving character and abounding mercy is confessed in Psalm 86:5?
opt1: "For the Lord is gracious, slow to anger; and abundant in lovingkindness unto the humble;"
opt2: "Because thou, O God, art merciful and just; and willing to blot out iniquity for thy name's sake;"
opt3: "For thou, Lord, art good, and ready to forgive; and plenteous in mercy unto all them that call upon thee."
opt4: "Seeing that the Almighty is full of compassion; and ready to heal the broken in heart;"
correct: "For thou, Lord, art good, and ready to forgive; and plenteous in mercy unto all them that call upon thee."
explanation: A cornerstone attribute of God: He is inherently good, eager ('ready') to pardon, and overflowing in plenteous covenant mercy (hesed) to all who pray. Psalm 86:5 (KJV) - "For thou, Lord, art good, and ready to forgive; and plenteous in mercy unto all them that call upon thee."

question: How does David affirm the absolute incomparability and exclusivity of God in Psalm 86:8 and 86:10?
opt1: "Who is like unto the Lord in the heavens? none can stand before his throne: for he is King above all gods;"

opt4: "Among the gods there is none like unto thee, O Lord; neither are there any works like unto thy works ... For thou art great, and doest wondrous things: thou art God alone."
correct: "Among the gods there is none like unto thee, O Lord; neither are there any works like unto thy works ... For thou art great, and doest wondrous things: thou art God alone."
explanation: Radical monotheism: no pagan deity compares to Yahweh in nature or miraculous deeds; He is 'God alone' without rival. Psalm 86:8, 10 (KJV) - "Among the gods there is none like unto thee, O Lord; neither are there any works like unto thy works ... For thou art great, and doest wondrous things: thou art God alone."

question: What universal eschatological worship of all created nations is prophesied in Psalm 86:9?
opt1: "All nations whom thou hast made shall come and worship before thee, O Lord; and shall glorify thy name."
opt2: "All the kingdoms of the earth shall bring tribute to Zion; and kings shall fall down at his footstool;"

correct: "All nations whom thou hast made shall come and worship before thee, O Lord; and shall glorify thy name."
explanation: Because God created all ethnic peoples, history marches toward a global climax where every nation bows in genuine worship, glorifying Yahweh's Name (Rev 15:4). Psalm 86:9 (KJV) - "All nations whom thou hast made shall come and worship before thee, O Lord; and shall glorify thy name."

question: What famous prayer for single-minded spiritual devotion and obedience is found in Psalm 86:11?
opt1: "Guide my footsteps in thy law, O God; I will keep thy testimonies: purify my mind to love thy word;"
opt2: "Teach me thy way, O LORD; I will walk in thy truth: unite my heart to fear thy name."
opt3: "Lead me in the path of righteousness, O Lord; I will meditate on thy statutes: establish my soul in peace;"
opt4: "Instruct my heart in wisdom, O Most High; I will obey thy commandments: fix my spirit upon Mount Zion;"
correct: "Teach me thy way, O LORD; I will walk in thy truth: unite my heart to fear thy name."
explanation: Recognizing the danger of a divided, distracted soul, David asks God to integrate all his affections into an undivided whole: 'unite my heart to fear thy name'. Psalm 86:11 (KJV) - "Teach me thy way, O LORD; I will walk in thy truth: unite my heart to fear thy name."

question: From what deep subterranean realm of death did God's great mercy deliver David's soul in Psalm 86:13?

explanation: David praises God for delivering him from Sheol tachtiyyah ('the lowest hell' / deepest depths of the grave), celebrating rescue from physical and spiritual destruction. Psalm 86:13 (KJV) - "For great is thy mercy toward me: and thou hast delivered my soul from the lowest hell."

question: What verbatim recitation of the classic Exodus 34:6 revelation of divine character appears in Psalm 86:15?
opt1: "The Lord God omnipotent reigneth, holy and true, forgiving iniquity and visiting the ungodly with wrath;"

explanation: David quotes the foundational Old Testament creed of divine grace revealed to Moses on Mount Sinai (Ex 34:6). Psalm 86:15 (KJV) - "But thou, O Lord, art a God full of compassion, and gracious, long suffering, and plenteous in mercy and truth."

question: How does David designate himself in his humble prayer for divine strength in Psalm 86:16?
opt1: "the son of thine handmaid"
opt2: "the anointed of thy sanctuary"

opt4: "the shepherd of Bethlehem"

explanation: Designating himself 'the son of thine handmaid' emphasizes humble, inherited covenant servanthood: born into God's household of a godly mother, belonging wholly to the Master. Psalm 86:16 (KJV) - "O turn unto me, and have mercy upon me; give thy strength unto thy servant, and save the son of thine handmaid."

question: What specific request for public vindication against enemies concludes Psalm 86:17?
opt1: "Send forth an angel of salvation; that the ungodly may tremble and flee: for thou art my high tower;"
opt2: "Shew me a token for good; that they which hate me may see it, and be ashamed: because thou, LORD, hast holpen me, and comforted me."
opt3: "Lift up the light of thy countenance; that all mine adversaries may perish: for thou hast established my throne;"
opt4: "Break the weapons of the violent; that the heathen may know thy power: for thou hast delivered my soul;"
correct: "Shew me a token for good; that they which hate me may see it, and be ashamed: because thou, LORD, hast holpen me, and comforted me."
explanation: David asks for a visible 'token for good' (an unmistakable sign of divine favor) that will silence his mockers and put persecutors to shame. Psalm 86:17 (KJV) - "Shew me a token for good; that they which hate me may see it, and be ashamed: because thou, LORD, hast holpen me, and comforted me."

question: What unique distinction belongs to Psalm 86 in the overall structure of Book III of the Psalter (Psalms 73-89)?

correct: It is the only psalm in Book III explicitly titled 'A Prayer of David'
explanation: Book III is dominated by Asaph and the sons of Korah; Psalm 86 stands as a solitary Davidic diamond, titled 'A Prayer of David'. Psalm 86:Title (KJV) - "A Prayer of David."

question: Where is God's foundation established, and what does the LORD love more than all dwellings of Jacob in Psalm 87:1-2?
opt1: "His throne is set upon Mount Moriah. The Almighty delighteth in the temple of Jerusalem more than in Shiloh;"

opt3: "His foundation is in the holy mountains. The LORD loveth the gates of Zion more than all the dwellings of Jacob."
opt4: "His glory dwelleth in the holy hills. The Holy One of Jacob honoreth Mount Zion above all the cities of Judah;"
correct: "His foundation is in the holy mountains. The LORD loveth the gates of Zion more than all the dwellings of Jacob."
explanation: Mount Zion, anchored in the sacred ridge of Jerusalem's holy mountains, is loved by God above any other residential dwelling place across all the twelve tribes. Psalm 87:1-2 (KJV) - "His foundation is in the holy mountains. The LORD loveth the gates of Zion more than all the dwellings of Jacob."

question: What famous exclamation celebrating the renown of the city of God is declared in Psalm 87:3?
opt1: "Beautiful for situation is the mountain of the Lord. Selah."

correct: "Glorious things are spoken of thee, O city of God. Selah."
explanation: John Newton's beloved hymn 'Glorious things of thee are spoken, Zion, city of our God' draws directly from this inspired, ecstatic verse. Psalm 87:3 (KJV) - "Glorious things are spoken of thee, O city of God. Selah."

question: Which historic pagan empires and surrounding nations are enumerated in the international citizen roll in Psalm 87:4?
opt1: Rahab (Egypt) and Babylon, Philistia, Tyre, with Ethiopia
opt2: Assyria and Persia, Damascus, Moab, with Ammon
opt3: Rome and Greece, Edom, Midian, with Sheba
opt4: Chaldea and Media, Amalek, Gebal, with Tarshish
correct: Rahab (Egypt) and Babylon, Philistia, Tyre, with Ethiopia
explanation: The most fierce historical persecutors (Egypt/Rahab, Babylon, Philistia, merchant Tyre, and distant Cush/Ethiopia) are included in Zion's citizenship. Psalm 87:4 (KJV) - "I will make mention of Rahab and Babylon to them that know me: behold Philistia, and Tyre, with Ethiopia; this man was born there."

question: What astounding spiritual status is conferred upon foreign converts regarding Zion in Psalm 87:4-5?
opt1: "they shall be adopted as servants: and the kings of the earth shall bring tribute"
opt2: "this man was born there ... This and that man was born in her: and the highest himself shall establish her."
opt3: "these strangers shall dwell within her gates: and the high priest shall sprinkle them"
opt4: "they shall offer sacrifices upon her altar: and the elders shall teach them the law"
correct: "this man was born there ... This and that man was born in her: and the highest himself shall establish her."
explanation: A breathtaking prophecy of spiritual regeneration: converted Gentiles are not treated as second-class aliens, but receive full native-born birthright status in Zion ('born in her'). Psalm 87:4-5 (KJV) - "behold Philistia, and Tyre, with Ethiopia; this man was born there. And of Zion it shall be said, This and that man was born in her: and the highest himself shall establish her."

question: What divine celestial census is conducted by Yahweh in Psalm 87:6?
opt1: "The Almighty shall register the tribes of Jacob, when he numbereth his saints in the book of life. Selah."
opt2: "The Lord of hosts shall record the names of the righteous, when he gathereth his flock into Jerusalem. Selah."
opt3: "The LORD shall count, when he writeth up the people, that this man was born there. Selah."
opt4: "The King shall count his jewels, when he inscribeth the redeemed in the golden roll of Zion. Selah."
correct: "The LORD shall count, when he writeth up the people, that this man was born there. Selah."
explanation: God keeps His own municipal registry: when He compiles the eternal census roll of the redeemed, He enters alongside each Gentile believer's name: 'Born in Zion!'. Psalm 87:6 (KJV) - "The LORD shall count, when he writeth up the people, that this man was born there. Selah."

question: What joyful musical climax and confession of divine life closes Psalm 87:7?

explanation: Vocalists and instrumentalists join in an ecstatic festival chorus, confessing that every life-giving fountain and refreshing spring of joy and salvation resides in God alone ('all my springs are in thee'). Psalm 87:7 (KJV) - "As well the singers as the players on instruments shall be there: all my springs are in thee."

question: What is the symbolic meaning of the name 'Rahab' in Psalm 87:4?

question: Why does Psalm 87:1 use the plural expression 'the holy mountains'?
opt1: It refers to the mountains of Sinai and Horeb in Arabia

explanation: Jerusalem is set upon a mountain ridge (Mount Moriah and Mount Zion) surrounded by defensive hills, all consecrated by God's dwelling presence. Psalm 87:1 (KJV) - "His foundation is in the holy mountains."

question: Who authored Psalm 87 according to its superscription?

question: What New Testament theological truth is foreshadowed in Psalm 87's vision of Zion?

explanation: Paul in Galatians 4:26 speaks of 'Jerusalem which is above ... which is the mother of us all', fulfilling Psalm 87's vision of citizens born from every nation into Zion. Psalm 87:5 (KJV) - "And of Zion it shall be said, This and that man was born in her: and the highest himself shall establish her."

question: What relentless nocturnal and daytime prayer opens Psalm 88:1-2?

opt4: "O LORD God of my salvation, I have cried day and night before thee: Let my prayer come before thee: incline thine ear unto my cry;"

explanation: Even in the darkest despair, faith anchors in the single ray of light in the entire psalm: addressing Yahweh as 'the God of my salvation' in unceasing day-and-night prayer. Psalm 88:1-2 (KJV) - "O LORD God of my salvation, I have cried day and night before thee: Let my prayer come before thee: incline thine ear unto my cry;"

question: What death-like state and grim military metaphor describe the sufferer in Psalm 88:4-5?

explanation: The sufferer feels discarded, 'free among the dead' (emancipated from the duties and relationships of the living like a corpse lying in a mass battlefield grave). Psalm 88:4-5 (KJV) - "I am counted with them that go down into the pit: I am as a man that hath no strength: Free among the dead, like the slain that lie in the grave, whom thou rememberest no more: and they are cut off from thy hand."

question: How does the psalmist describe the subterranean darkness and crushing weight of God's wrath in Psalm 88:6-7?

opt3: "Thou hast cast me into outer darkness: my bones are crushed beneath the waves of thy judgment. Selah."
opt4: "Thou hast shut me in the subterranean vault: thy wrath burneth like sulfur: the floods of death overwhelm me. Selah."
correct: "Thou hast laid me in the lowest pit, in darkness, in the deeps. Thy wrath lieth hard upon me, and thou hast afflicted me with all thy waves. Selah."
explanation: The ultimate isolation: buried in the 'lowest pit', smothered in pitch darkness, feeling the relentless, crushing breakers ('waves') of divine wrath pounding over his soul. Psalm 88:6-7 (KJV) - "Thou hast laid me in the lowest pit, in darkness, in the deeps. Thy wrath lieth hard upon me, and thou hast afflicted me with all thy waves. Selah."

question: What total social isolation and repulsive quarantine are lamented in Psalm 88:8?

opt4: "Mine elders have cast me out of the congregation: they close their gates against my cry"
correct: "Thou hast put away mine acquaintance far from me; thou hast made me an abomination unto them: I am shut up, and I cannot come forth."
explanation: Total ostracism (likely suffering from chronic leprosy or contagious illness): companions recoil from him as an 'abomination', permanently quarantined in solitary confinement. Psalm 88:8 (KJV) - "Thou hast put away mine acquaintance far from me; thou hast made me an abomination unto them: I am shut up, and I cannot come forth."

question: What four rhetorical questions in Psalm 88:10-12 argue that God's wonders and praises are extinguished in the grave?

opt3: "Wilt thou speak to those in the dust? shall the sepulchre echo with praise? Can the departed behold thy light? shall the dead rejoice in Zion? Selah."
opt4: "Wilt thou shew wonders to the dead? shall the dead arise and praise thee? Selah. Shall thy lovingkindness be declared in the grave? or thy faithfulness in destruction? Shall thy wonders be known in the dark? and thy righteousness in the land of forgetfulness?"

explanation: Heman marshals a desperate defense: if God allows him to die, the Lord loses an active voice of praise; dead corpses in Sheol cannot proclaim God's lovingkindness. Psalm 88:10-11 (KJV) - "Wilt thou shew wonders to the dead? shall the dead arise and praise thee? Selah. Shall thy lovingkindness be declared in the grave? or thy faithfulness in destruction?"

question: How early in the morning does the psalmist meet God with his desperate cries in Psalm 88:13?

opt4: "At daybreak shall my tears flow: before the light appeareth will I call upon thy name"

explanation: Unbroken persistence: despite feeling utterly abandoned, Heman rises before the dawn; his morning prayer 'prevents' (comes out early to meet) God at daybreak. Psalm 88:13 (KJV) - "But unto thee have I cried, O LORD; and in the morning shall my prayer prevent thee."

question: How long has the psalmist endured this chronic affliction and terror according to Psalm 88:15?

opt4: "All my life have I borne the reproach of the ungodly: my heart is overwhelmed with sorrow"

explanation: This was not an acute, temporary crisis: Heman had suffered debilitating, chronic illness and mental distress from boyhood ('from my youth up'), distracted and unhinged by divine terrors. Psalm 88:15 (KJV) - "I am afflicted and ready to die from my youth up: while I suffer thy terrors I am distracted."

question: What chilling and solitary word concludes Psalm 88:18 in the Hebrew text and KJV?

Psalm 88:18 (KJV) - "Lover and friend hast thou put far away from me, and mine acquaintance into darkness."

question: What makes Psalm 88 completely unique among all the lament psalms in the entire Psalter?
opt1: It is the only psalm that curses the day of the author's birth like Job
opt2: It is the only psalm that directly denies the existence of the afterlife

opt4: It is the only psalm that contains no transition to thanksgiving, praise, or joy; it remains enveloped in unrelieved darkness from beginning to end
correct: It is the only psalm that contains no transition to thanksgiving, praise, or joy; it remains enveloped in unrelieved darkness from beginning to end
explanation: While all other laments eventually pivot into praise or confidence, Psalm 88 maintains raw, unresolved darkness, validating the profound biblical reality that authentic faith can cry out in ongoing agony. Psalm 88:18 (KJV) - "Lover and friend hast thou put far away from me, and mine acquaintance into darkness."

question: Who is identified as the author in the detailed superscription of Psalm 88?
opt1: Heman the Ezrahite (a renowned sage and master musician, 1 Kings 4:31; 1 Chronicles 15:17-19)

question: What twin covenant attributes of God will the psalmist sing of and establish for all generations in Psalm 89:1-2?

opt4: "I will praise the power of the Almighty day and night: thy glory shalt thou display among all nations;"
correct: "I will sing of the mercies of the LORD for ever: with my mouth will I make known thy faithfulness to all generations. For I have said, Mercy shall be built up for ever: thy faithfulness shalt thou establish in the very heavens."
explanation: The overarching dual theme of Psalm 89: God's steadfast covenant mercies (hesed) and His unwavering veracity/faithfulness (emunah), established eternally in the heavens. Psalm 89:1-2 (KJV) - "I will sing of the mercies of the LORD for ever: with my mouth will I make known thy faithfulness to all generations. For I have said, Mercy shall be built up for ever: thy faithfulness shalt thou establish in the very heavens."

question: What unconditional royal covenant sworn with an oath is recorded in Psalm 89:3-4?
