opt3: "I have established a statute with Judah my lawgiver: The sceptre shall not depart from between his feet for ever. Selah;"
opt4: "I have anointed Solomon my son, and promised unto his house: An everlasting kingdom of peace and righteousness. Selah;"
correct: "I have made a covenant with my chosen, I have sworn unto David my servant, Thy seed will I establish for ever, and build up thy throne to all generations. Selah."
explanation: God's unilateral, unconditional covenant with David (2 Samuel 7): guaranteeing that his royal seed and throne will endure throughout all perpetual generations. Psalm 89:3-4 (KJV) - "I have made a covenant with my chosen, I have sworn unto David my servant, Thy seed will I establish for ever, and build up thy throne to all generations. Selah."

question: What foundational pillars uphold God's heavenly throne, and what attributes go before His face in Psalm 89:14?
opt1: "Righteousness and holiness are the pillars of thy sanctuary: grace and salvation attend thy steps"
opt2: "Power and majesty are the foundation of thy kingdom: lovingkindness and peace herald thy presence"
opt3: "Justice and judgment are the habitation of thy throne: mercy and truth shall go before thy face."
opt4: "Eternity and glory surround thy seat: judgment and truth proceed from thy mouth"
correct: "Justice and judgment are the habitation of thy throne: mercy and truth shall go before thy face."
explanation: God's cosmic government rests upon the immovable twin moral pillars of Justice and Judgment, escorted wherever He moves by Mercy and Truth. Psalm 89:14 (KJV) - "Justice and judgment are the habitation of thy throne: mercy and truth shall go before thy face."

question: What beatitude belongs to the people who recognize the festival trumpet blast in Psalm 89:15?
opt1: "Blessed are the tribes that assemble in Zion: they shall behold the beauty of the holy temple"
opt2: "Blessed is the congregation that obeyeth the law: they shall flourish under the shadow of his wings"
opt3: "Blessed are the saints that offer sacrifices: they shall rejoice in the horn of David"
opt4: "Blessed is the people that know the joyful sound: they shall walk, O LORD, in the light of thy countenance."
correct: "Blessed is the people that know the joyful sound: they shall walk, O LORD, in the light of thy countenance."
explanation: The 'joyful sound' (Hebrew teruah) is the festival trumpet shofar blast heralding jubilee, festival communion, and royal victory, walking in the radiant favor of God's face. Psalm 89:15 (KJV) - "Blessed is the people that know the joyful sound: they shall walk, O LORD, in the light of thy countenance."

question: What divine election and sacred anointing of David are recalled in Psalm 89:20-21?
opt1: "I have found David my servant; with my holy oil have I anointed him: With whom my hand shall be established: mine arm also shall strengthen him."
opt2: "I have chosen the son of Jesse; with the horn of salvation have I consecrated his crown: my right hand shall defend him;"
opt3: "I have called David from the sheepfold; with royal garments have I clothed his majesty: my angels shall fight for him;"
opt4: "I have set David upon Mount Zion; with the sceptre of righteousness have I established his seed: my power shall uphold him;"
correct: "I have found David my servant; with my holy oil have I anointed him: With whom my hand shall be established: mine arm also shall strengthen him."
explanation: God sovereignly sought and 'found' David, consecrating him with holy anointing oil, promising the constant upholding power of His omnipotent hand and arm. Psalm 89:20-21 (KJV) - "I have found David my servant; with my holy oil have I anointed him: With whom my hand shall be established: mine arm also shall strengthen him."

question: What supreme Messianic title of preeminence above all earthly monarchs is bestowed in Psalm 89:27?
opt1: "Behold, I will crown him King of kings, and establish his dominion over all nations"
opt2: "Yea, I will make him the prince of peace, and exalt his throne above the stars of heaven"
opt3: "Also I will make him my firstborn, higher than the kings of the earth."
opt4: "Verily he shall be my beloved son, and inherit the uttermost parts of the earth"
correct: "Also I will make him my firstborn, higher than the kings of the earth."
explanation: The Davidic King is designated God's 'firstborn' (bekhor - supreme in rank, honor, and inheritance), prefiguring Jesus Christ, the 'firstborn from the dead' and 'prince of the kings of the earth' (Col 1:15; Rev 1:5). Psalm 89:27 (KJV) - "Also I will make him my firstborn, higher than the kings of the earth."

question: How does God reconcile disciplinary chastisement with His unconditional covenant fidelity in Psalm 89:30-34?
opt1: "Then will I cast them into captivity, and give their kingdom to the heathen. Yet after seventy years will I restore Zion;"
opt2: "Then will I smite their princes with pestilence, and scatter their seed. But for Abraham's sake I will show mercy;"
opt3: "Then will I take away their crown, and burn their cities. Nevertheless I will raise up the horn of David in the latter days;"
opt4: "Then will I visit their transgression with the rod, and their iniquity with stripes. Nevertheless my lovingkindness will I not utterly take from him, nor suffer my faithfulness to fail. My covenant will I not break, nor alter the thing that is gone out of my lips."
correct: "Then will I visit their transgression with the rod, and their iniquity with stripes. Nevertheless my lovingkindness will I not utterly take from him, nor suffer my faithfulness to fail. My covenant will I not break, nor alter the thing that is gone out of my lips."
explanation: Paternal discipline without covenant cancellation: rebellious Davidic sons will be scourged with disciplinary stripes, yet God's hesed remains immutable; He will never break His sworn oath. Psalm 89:33-34 (KJV) - "Nevertheless my lovingkindness will I not utterly take from him, nor suffer my faithfulness to fail. My covenant will I not break, nor alter the thing that is gone out of my lips."

question: What tragic historical collapse of the Davidic monarchy provokes the psalmist's agonizing lament in Psalm 89:38-39?
opt1: "But thou hast cast off and abhorred, thou hast been wroth with thine anointed. Thou hast made void the covenant of thy servant: thou hast profaned his crown by casting it to the ground."
opt2: "Yet the crown of Solomon is fallen, and the temple burned with fire: thou hast delivered the ark into the hands of Babylon;"
opt3: "Behold, the armies of Judah have fled, and our king is bound in bronze chains: thou hast forsaken Mount Zion;"
opt4: "For the throne of David is overturned, and his palaces are brought to ruin: thou hast forgotten thine oath;"
correct: "But thou hast cast off and abhorred, thou hast been wroth with thine anointed. Thou hast made void the covenant of thy servant: thou hast profaned his crown by casting it to the ground."
explanation: The heartbreaking paradox of the Babylonian exile: the sworn eternal covenant seemed shattered when God permitted the Davidic crown to be trampled in the dust. Psalm 89:38-39 (KJV) - "But thou hast cast off and abhorred, thou hast been wroth with thine anointed. Thou hast made void the covenant of thy servant: thou hast profaned his crown by casting it to the ground."

question: What doxology concludes Book III of the Psalter in Psalm 89:52?
opt1: "Praise the Lord from the heavens; praise him in the heights; Amen, and Amen."
opt2: "Blessed be the LORD for evermore. Amen, and Amen."
opt3: "Glory be to the Holy One of Israel throughout all generations; Amen, and Amen."
opt4: "Exalted be the King of glory from everlasting to everlasting; Amen, and Amen."
correct: "Blessed be the LORD for evermore. Amen, and Amen."
explanation: Even amid the wreckage of Jerusalem and the apparent defeat of the royal line, Book III closes with an unyielding doxology of faith: 'Blessed be the LORD for evermore. Amen, and Amen.' Psalm 89:52 (KJV) - "Blessed be the LORD for evermore. Amen, and Amen."

question: Who authored Psalm 89 according to its superscription?
opt1: Maschil of Asaph
opt2: A Psalm of David
opt3: Maschil of Ethan the Ezrahite
opt4: A Song of the Sons of Korah
correct: Maschil of Ethan the Ezrahite
explanation: Ethan the Ezrahite, along with Heman, was one of the legendary sages of Israel noted for musical and theological brilliance (1 Kings 4:31). Psalm 89:Title (KJV) - "Maschil of Ethan the Ezrahite."

question: What opening confession of God as Israel's eternal dwelling place opens Book IV in Psalm 90:1-2?
opt1: "O Lord of hosts, how amiable are thy tabernacles: from the foundation of the world thou art our fortress;"
opt2: "Lord, thou hast been our dwelling place in all generations. Before the mountains were brought forth, or ever thou hadst formed the earth and the world, even from everlasting to everlasting, thou art God."
opt3: "The Lord our God is an everlasting rock: before the heavens were stretched out, thou reignest King of glory;"
opt4: "In the shadow of the Almighty have we dwelt: before the hills were established, thou art the Holy One of Jacob;"
correct: "Lord, thou hast been our dwelling place in all generations. Before the mountains were brought forth, or ever thou hadst formed the earth and the world, even from everlasting to everlasting, thou art God."
explanation: Moses begins Book IV by celebrating God's aseity and eternity: while nomadic Israel wandered in tents with no fixed address for forty years, God Himself was their timeless home. Psalm 90:1-2 (KJV) - "Lord, thou hast been our dwelling place in all generations. Before the mountains were brought forth, or ever thou hadst formed the earth and the world, even from everlasting to everlasting, thou art God."

question: How does God's timeless eternity view a thousand human years in Psalm 90:4?
opt1: "For a millennium is as a fleeting breath, and as a drop of water in the great ocean"
opt2: "For ten thousand years are as morning dew, and as a shadow that vanisheth before the sun"
opt3: "For all the ages of the world are but as a single day, and as a moment in the heavens"
opt4: "For a thousand years in thy sight are but as yesterday when it is past, and as a watch in the night."
correct: "For a thousand years in thy sight are but as yesterday when it is past, and as a watch in the night."
explanation: To the eternal Creator, a millennium of human history shrinks down to a single yesterday that has already slipped away, or a brief 4-hour night watch (quoted in 2 Peter 3:8). Psalm 90:4 (KJV) - "For a thousand years in thy sight are but as yesterday when it is past, and as a watch in the night."

question: What botanical metaphor depicts the rapid fleeting cycle of human life in Psalm 90:5-6?
opt1: "in the morning they are like grass which groweth up. In the morning it flourisheth, and groweth up; in the evening it is cut down, and withereth."
opt2: "they are as the blossom of the almond tree: blooming in the spring, and falling to the dust before autumn"
opt3: "they are like the flower of the field: beautiful at dawn, and scorched by the desert wind at noon"
opt4: "they are as a leaf driven by the tempest: flourishing in the rain, and consumed by the fire in a moment"
correct: "in the morning they are like grass which groweth up. In the morning it flourisheth, and groweth up; in the evening it is cut down, and withereth."
explanation: Human existence is compressed into a single 12-hour vegetative cycle: sprouting fresh and green in the morning dew, cut down by the scythe and completely withered by evening dusk. Psalm 90:5-6 (KJV) - "in the morning they are like grass which groweth up. In the morning it flourisheth, and groweth up; in the evening it is cut down, and withereth."

question: Where does God place our secret sins and iniquities in Psalm 90:8?
opt1: "Thou hast recorded our transgressions in thy book, and weighed our iniquities in the balances of judgment"
opt2: "Thou hast set our iniquities before thee, our secret sins in the light of thy countenance."
opt3: "Thou hast brought our secret wickedness into the open court, and judged our deeds before the congregation"
opt4: "Thou hast exposed our hidden faults before heaven, and visited our backslidings with stripes"
correct: "Thou hast set our iniquities before thee, our secret sins in the light of thy countenance."
explanation: Nothing escapes divine omniscience: human sins hidden from public view are placed directly into the brilliant, unshielded spotlight of God's holy countenance. Psalm 90:8 (KJV) - "Thou hast set our iniquities before thee, our secret sins in the light of thy countenance."

question: What standard mortal lifespan and character of human existence are defined in Psalm 90:10?
opt1: "The measure of man's days is seventy years; and if he reach eighty in honor, yet are his steps full of vanity;"
opt2: "Our life span is as sixty years; and if by great health it be seventy, yet are our years spent in tears and trouble;"
opt3: "The days of our years are threescore years and ten; and if by reason of strength they be fourscore years, yet is their strength labour and sorrow; for it is soon cut off, and we fly away."
opt4: "Man that is born of a woman hath eighty years; yet his days are as a passing shadow, and he goeth down to the dust;"
correct: "The days of our years are threescore years and ten; and if by reason of strength they be fourscore years, yet is their strength labour and sorrow; for it is soon cut off, and we fly away."
explanation: Moses defines normal human longevity as seventy years ('threescore years and ten') or eighty ('fourscore') for the robust; yet even that peak is characterized by toil and grief, soon terminating in swift departure. Psalm 90:10 (KJV) - "The days of our years are threescore years and ten; and if by reason of strength they be fourscore years, yet is their strength labour and sorrow; for it is soon cut off, and we fly away."

question: What famous prayer for perspective and spiritual wisdom is recorded in Psalm 90:12?
opt1: "Lord, show us the measure of our frailty, that we may seek thy righteousness all our days;"
opt2: "Instruct our souls in the brevity of life, that we may walk uprightly before thy holy face;"
opt3: "Teach us to ponder the end of our years, that our minds may be established in thy fear;"
opt4: "So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom."
correct: "So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom."
explanation: A master prayer for daily living: consciously calculating the finite brevity of our days compels the heart to turn away from folly and cultivate true, eternal divine wisdom. Psalm 90:12 (KJV) - "So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom."

question: What early morning petition for divine satisfaction fuels a lifetime of gladness in Psalm 90:14?
opt1: "O satisfy us early with thy mercy; that we may rejoice and be glad all our days."
opt2: "Fill our souls at daybreak with thy lovingkindness; that our tongue may sing of thy righteousness continually"
opt3: "Refresh our spirits in the morning watch with thy grace; that we may celebrate thy salvation without ceasing"
opt4: "Satisfy our hunger with the bread of heaven; that our heart may boast in the God of our fathers"
correct: "O satisfy us early with thy mercy; that we may rejoice and be glad all our days."
explanation: Starting each day anchored in God's steadfast covenant mercy (hesed) provides deep inner contentment that sustains radiant joy throughout all of life's trials. Psalm 90:14 (KJV) - "O satisfy us early with thy mercy; that we may rejoice and be glad all our days."

question: What reciprocal proportion of joy corresponding to past suffering is requested in Psalm 90:15?
opt1: "Restore unto us double joy for all our tears, and multiply our peace according to our sorrow"
opt2: "Make us glad according to the days wherein thou hast afflicted us, and the years wherein we have seen evil."
opt3: "Give us rejoicing in Zion according to our weeping in exile, and comfort us on every side"
opt4: "Crown our heads with gladness according to our afflictions, and blot out the memory of our grief"
correct: "Make us glad according to the days wherein thou hast afflicted us, and the years wherein we have seen evil."
explanation: Moses prays that the coming seasons of divine joy and blessing will be equal in measure to the grueling forty years of desert affliction and grief they had endured. Psalm 90:15 (KJV) - "Make us glad according to the days wherein thou hast afflicted us, and the years wherein we have seen evil."

question: What double plea for divine favor and permanent vocational impact concludes Psalm 90:17?
opt1: "And let the glory of the Almighty cover our sanctuary: and prosper thou the way of thy chosen seed for ever"
opt2: "And let the peace of God dwell in our borders: and confirm thou the heritage of our fathers throughout all generations"
opt3: "And let the beauty of the LORD our God be upon us: and establish thou the work of our hands upon us; yea, the work of our hands establish thou it."
opt4: "And let the lovingkindness of the King rest upon our families: and bless thou the labor of our hands in Zion"
correct: "And let the beauty of the LORD our God be upon us: and establish thou the work of our hands upon us; yea, the work of our hands establish thou it."
explanation: The ultimate benediction: praying that the pleasantness / radiant beauty (no'am) of Yahweh rest upon mortal humans, giving enduring, permanent significance to their fleeting earthly labors. Psalm 90:17 (KJV) - "And let the beauty of the LORD our God be upon us: and establish thou the work of our hands upon us; yea, the work of our hands establish thou it."

question: Who is the unique author of Psalm 90 identified in its superscription?
opt1: David the son of Jesse
opt2: Asaph the chief musician
opt3: Solomon the king of Israel
opt4: Moses the man of God
correct: Moses the man of God
explanation: Psalm 90 is the only psalm in the entire Psalter composed by Moses, making it the oldest psalm in the Bible, reflecting the forty years of wandering in the wilderness as a generation died off. Psalm 90:Title (KJV) - "A Prayer of Moses the man of God."
